sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Most men keep a ledger they never show anyone. Not the one at the feed store or the one the bank mails out. The other one. In one column you keep what you have done right — the years married, the bills paid on time, the Sundays you did not miss, the drink you did not pour. In the other column sits everything you try not to look at. You check that ledger more than you would admit. On a good week the columns look close to even, and you feel close to God. On a bad week you do not pray at all, because you already know what the ledger says.

That is what the dust does with God’s law. It hands you the commandments as a ladder and tells you to climb. Keep enough of them and you will stand on firm ground with God. Slip off a rung and start over. And when the ladder wears you down, the dust has a second offer ready: drop the whole business. Doctrine is for men who like to argue. Words about God are only words. Be sincere, work hard, and leave the teaching to somebody else.

Both lies leave a man face-down. The ladder breaks his back, and the shrug leaves him nothing to stand on. Psalm 119:25 is the cry of a man who has found that out: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) The reviving word of 1 Timothy 1 is that God’s law is good — good enough to tell you the truth about yourself — and that the teaching Paul guards ends where no ladder ever reached: in love that flows out of a heart God has washed.

sections.heading: A Letter to a Son Left at His Post
pulls: The dust hands you God’s law as a ladder and tells you to climb. Paul hands it back to you as a mirror — and the man who looks into it long enough will run to the gospel for his life.
paras: First Timothy is a letter from an old worker to a younger one. Paul writes to Timothy, my true child in faith, a man raised by a believing mother with a Greek father in the house, whose faith lived first in your grandmother Lois, and your mother Eunice (Acts 16:1; 2 Timothy 1:5). Paul took him on the road years before. Now he has left him at Ephesus with a hard job: to stand up in front of a church and tell certain men to stop teaching what they were teaching.

On its surface the letter reads like a manual — prayer, elders, deacons, widows, money. It is that. But Paul does not open with the manual. He opens with God our Savior and the Lord Jesus Christ our hope, and within fifteen verses he will call himself the chief of sinners. Every charge in this letter grows out of that soil. Read all six chapters in one sitting before you begin. It will not take long, and you will see the rules standing on mercy. Paul is writing about how a man should behave in God’s house, and he never once lets Timothy forget whose house it is.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: A DIFFERENT DOCTRINE
paras: Paul does not soften Timothy’s assignment. He is to command certain men not to teach a different doctrine. Not suggest. Not host a discussion. Command. That sounds harsh to a man raised to think every belief deserves a chair at the table. But Paul is not guarding his own opinions. He is guarding something handed to him in trust, and a man who has been handed something in trust does not let strangers rearrange it.

Look at what the different teaching ran on: myths and endless genealogies, which cause disputes. Paul gives no details, and you do not need them. You know the kind. Teaching that is always one more chart away from the point. Talk that sends men home with something to argue about and nothing to live on. It feels deep. It breeds quarrels. It is a field plowed every spring and never planted.

Set against it is God’s stewardship, which is in faith. A steward runs a house that belongs to someone else. God has a household, and He runs it by faith — by men trusting what He has said, not by men stacking guesswork on top of it. Take that as relief. You are not required to be clever. You are required to receive what God has put in front of you and trust Him with the rest.

So ask what you have been feeding on. The podcast with a new angle every week. The comment thread. The theory about the last days your brother-in-law keeps forwarding. None of it is the same as an open Bible and a plain sentence from God. Speculation will keep you busy for years and leave you hungry the whole time.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE GOAL IS LOVE
paras: Here is the key verse of the week, and it tells you what all of God’s teaching is aimed at: the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith. Not winning. Not being right in front of other men. Love. Sound doctrine is a tool, and love is the thing the tool was made to build.

Notice where that love comes from. A pure heart. A good conscience. A faith with no mask on it. You cannot make any of the three. A man cannot scrub his heart clean with the same hands that dirtied it. This love flows out of what God has already done — a heart washed, a conscience cleansed by the blood of Christ, a faith resting on Him and not on a show. The command does not start the work. It names what grace grows. Love of this kind is fruit, not a mood you work up in the truck on the way to church, and fruit has a root.

Then Paul names the men who walked off. Having missed the mark, they turned away to vain talking. They wanted to be teachers of the law, though they understand neither what they say, nor about what they strongly affirm. Confidence without understanding. Volume without love. You have met that man. Some evenings you have been that man — sure of your point at the supper table, loud about it, and cold toward the people across from you.

Test your doctrine by where it lands. If what you know about God has made you sharper with your wife and harder on your sons, it has missed the mark somewhere along the way. Truth from God is meant to come out the far end as love.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: GOOD, IF USED LAWFULLY
pulls: The law is a plumb line hung against a crooked wall. It shows you exactly where you lean. It has never straightened a wall, and it was never meant to. That work belongs to Christ.
paras: After all that, you might expect Paul to throw the law out. He does the opposite: the law is good, if a person uses it lawfully. The trouble was never the law. The trouble was men holding it by the wrong end.

So what is it for? Law is not made for a righteous person, but for the lawless and insubordinate, for the ungodly and sinners. Then Paul runs the list. Read it slowly and you will see it walk down the Ten Commandments in their order — the godless and profane, then father and mother, murder, the marriage bed, the stealing of men, lying under oath. The law is a plumb line hung against a crooked wall. It shows exactly where the wall leans. It holds back the worst of what men would do. What it cannot do is straighten the wall.

Before you run your finger down that list looking for other men, stop at two words. Liars. Perjurers. The man who shaded the hours on the invoice. The man who said he was at the shop when he was not. Paul closes the list with any other thing contrary to the sound doctrine, and that net is wide enough to catch every man who reads it.

That is the law used lawfully. It is a mirror that tells you the truth about your face, and a mirror has never washed anyone. When you see yourself in that list and your mouth goes dry, the law is doing what God gave it to do. It is pushing you out of yourself and toward Someone else. Paul knows where it pushes, because he has been pushed there himself. The next verse names the place.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: THE GOOD NEWS ENTRUSTED
paras: Paul measures sound doctrine by one standard: it is according to the Good News of the glory of the blessed God. The law shows the sickness. The gospel brings the cure. And the cure is not another rule. It is a Person.

Here is what the law could never do and God did. Jesus Christ was born under the same law that condemns you. He honored His mother. He told the truth when the truth cost Him His life. He kept every line of the list you just read, from the inside out, without a single lapse. Then He went to the cross and took the sentence the law hands down on lawbreakers, as if He were the liar and the murderer. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us. Everything the law demanded of you, Christ has done. Everything it threatened, He has carried. Then God raised Him from the dead and set Him at His right hand — the Judge’s public word that the debt was paid in full.

So when the law drives you into the dirt, do not climb back onto the ladder. Lift your face and look at Him. His obedience is counted to you by faith alone. His blood answers every line on the list. That is the glory of the blessed God — a holy God glorified by saving lawbreakers through His own Son.

Paul says this news was committed to my trust. Through him it has come down to you. You are not handed it to improve or to update. You are handed it to believe, to keep, and to pass on whole to the men coming up behind you.

stations.verse: As I urged you when I was going into Macedonia, stay at Ephesus that you might command certain men not to teach a different doctrine.
stations.question: What teaching about God have I let into my thinking mainly because it agreed with what I already wanted to believe?
stations.gloss: to teach other or different doctrine
stations.live: Pick one idea about God you took in this year from a clip, a book or a friend. Find where Scripture plainly says it. If you cannot find it, set it down: ‘I will not add to what God has said.’
body: Heterodidaskaleō means to teach other or different doctrine. Only Paul uses it, and only in this letter — here at the start, and again in 6:3, where Paul sets it against sound words, the words of our Lord Jesus Christ. The trouble is not teaching. The trouble is the word other.

Different doctrine rarely announces itself. It comes in as an addition — Jesus plus a rule, grace plus a ladder, the gospel plus a secret the plain text supposedly missed. A man does not wake up and choose a lie. He drifts toward whatever teaching flatters him, and he calls the drift growth.

The dust wants something new to chew on, because the old news humbles it. But nothing needs adding to the words of the Lord Jesus. The news that saved Paul is still the news, and it is enough ground for any man to stand on. Christ crucified and risen does not need a sequel.

stations.verse: And not to pay attention to myths and endless genealogies, which cause disputes, rather than God’s stewardship, which is in faith.
stations.question: What story have I been paying attention to this year that has crowded out the plain account of what Christ has done?
stations.gloss: a story; later, a fable set against a true account
stations.live: When things go wrong this week, notice the story you tell yourself — that you are owed, or that you are forgotten. Answer it out loud with what happened: ‘Christ died for my sins, and He was raised.’
body: Mythos once meant simply speech or a story. In time it came to mean the opposite of a true account — a fable, a fiction. All five of its New Testament uses stand it against the truth.

Peter uses it to say what the apostles did not do: we didn’t follow cunningly devised fables; they were eyewitnesses of his majesty. The gospel is not a tale men made up to feel better. It happened, in real places, to a real Man who died and came up out of a real grave. Myths cause disputes. Facts call for faith. You are not asked to believe a feeling. You are asked to trust a Man and what He did.

The dust loves a story, especially one where you are the hero or the victim. Christ hands you a true account instead, where you are the sinner and He is the Savior. That one ends better than anything you could invent.

stations.verse: From which things some, having missed the mark, have turned away to vain talking.
stations.question: Where has my knowledge of God stopped producing love and started producing arguments?
stations.gloss: to miss the mark; to fail
stations.live: Think of the last argument about faith or church you had with someone. Ask one thing: did it leave him loved? If not, go back to him this week and start over with love.
body: Astocheō is built on a word for a mark or target. It means to miss the mark, to fail. Paul uses it three times, all to Timothy: men who missed love here, men who wandered from the faith in 6:21, and men who erred concerning the truth about the resurrection in 2 Timothy 2:18.

Notice what these men were aiming at. Not nothing. They were serious, busy, full of talk about the law. They were simply not aiming at love from a pure heart, so every shot went wide. A man can spend years sharpening his aim at the wrong target and call it devotion.

The dust says a miss is the end of you. But Paul writes the next verses as a man who missed worse than any of them. Christ does not leave men lying where their shots fell. He came for the men who missed, and He has never once missed what He aimed at.

stations.verse: But we know that the law is good, if a person uses it lawfully.
stations.question: Whose sins have I been measuring with God’s law this month, when the law was handed to me to measure my own?
stations.gloss: rightly, lawfully; as the law intends
stations.live: When you catch yourself measuring another man by God’s commands this week, stop and turn the same command on yourself. Then thank Christ by name for keeping it where you did not.
body: Built on a word meaning conformable to law, nomimōs means rightly, lawfully — used the way the thing was meant to be used. Paul writes it twice, and both times the reader is Timothy.

In 2 Timothy 2:5 the athlete isn’t crowned unless he has competed by the rules. Here the law itself has to be used by its own rules. Every tool has a right end. A chainsaw is good; grab it by the chain and it will take your hand. The law is good. Climbed like a ladder, it will crush you. Swung like a club, it will turn you into a Pharisee.

The dust wants to grab the law and climb. Used lawfully, the law points away from itself. It shows you what you are, then sends you to Christ, who kept it in your place. The mirror was never meant to be the last thing you look at.

stations.verse: For the sexually immoral, for homosexuals, for slave-traders, for liars, for perjurers, and for any other thing contrary to the sound doctrine.
stations.question: What is the teaching I sit under each week actually doing to the health of my soul?
stations.gloss: to be sound; to be healthy, in good health
stations.live: Read Luke 15:11–32 in one sitting this week. Name one place you have been living like the son still in the far country. Then come home: ‘My Father has received me back.’
body: To be sound, healthy, in good health — that is hygiainō. In Luke it is used of the body, as when Jesus says, Those who are healthy have no need for a physician. In the Greek Old Testament it most often stands for the Hebrew shalom. In Paul’s letters to Timothy and Titus it describes teaching: the sound doctrine.

So sound doctrine is healthy teaching — teaching that makes a man well. False teaching is sickness in the bloodstream. Look at Luke 15:27. The father kills the fattened calf because he has received him back safe and healthy. That is the same word. Sound doctrine is the news that brings sons home whole.

The dust would rather stay sick than admit it needs the Physician. But Christ came for the sick. Healthy teaching tells you so plainly, and then hands you over to Him. He does not lecture the sick man. He heals him and sends him home.

practices.title: READ THE LETTER WHOLE
practices.body: Sit down with 1 Timothy this week and read all six chapters in one sitting. Keep a pencil in hand. Every time Paul names mercy, grace, or the Savior, mark it. Every time he gives a charge, mark that too. When you finish, look at the page and see which comes first. You will find the charges standing on mercy, and you will read the rest of the letter that way. Mercy is the ground. The charges are what grows on it.

practices.title: RUN THE LIST ON YOURSELF
practices.body: Read 1:9–10 slowly, one line at a time, and stop at the line that names you. Do not explain it. Do not compare yourself with the man on the next line down. Confess it to God by name. Then turn a few verses forward and read 1:15 out loud. Let the law do its work, then let it hand you to Christ Jesus, who came into the world for that exact line. He knew it was there before you did.

practices.title: TEST WHAT YOU TAKE IN
practices.body: Whatever teaching you take in this week — a sermon, a podcast, a book, a video a friend sends — put two questions to it. Does it agree with what Scripture plainly says? Does it end in love from a pure heart? If it fails the first, set it down. If it passes the first and you find it is only feeding your arguments, you are using it wrong. Turn it toward love. Good teaching should leave you kinder at home.

practices.title: AIM ONE THING AT LOVE
practices.body: Name one person in your house you have been right toward and cold toward. Your wife after the argument you won. The son you corrected and never sat down with. This week do one plain act of love for that person — fix the thing that has been broken since spring, take the walk, say you were hard. Truth that never comes out the far end as love has missed its mark. Grace has been shown to you first. Let some of it run downhill.

practices.title: KEEP THE NEWS WHOLE
practices.body: Write the gospel out in four plain sentences, no longer. God is holy, and His law is good. You broke it. Christ kept it, died under its curse, and rose. Everyone who trusts Him is forgiven and counted righteous. Carry that card in your shirt pocket. Before Sunday, tell it to one man who needs it, without adding anything and without leaving anything out. If he asks a question you cannot answer, open the letter together.

title: The Good Law
subtitle: from dust to love from a pure heart
keyVerse: But the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith.

passage.text: Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ according to the commandment of God our Savior and the Lord Jesus Christ our hope;
to Timothy, my true child in faith: Grace, mercy, and peace, from God our Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
As I urged you when I was going into Macedonia, stay at Ephesus that you might command certain men not to teach a different doctrine,
and not to pay attention to myths and endless genealogies, which cause disputes, rather than God’s stewardship, which is in faith—
but the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith,
from which things some, having missed the mark, have turned away to vain talking,
desiring to be teachers of the law, though they understand neither what they say, nor about what they strongly affirm.
But we know that the law is good, if a person uses it lawfully,

as knowing this, that law is not made for a righteous person, but for the lawless and insubordinate, for the ungodly and sinners, for the unholy and profane, for murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers, for manslayers,
for the sexually immoral, for homosexuals, for slave-traders, for liars, for perjurers, and for any other thing contrary to the sound doctrine,
according to the Good News of the glory of the blessed God, which was committed to my trust.

stationsIntro: Take each verse slowly, with your Bible open beside this page. Let the verse speak before you do, then answer as a man with nothing left to hide from God.
lifeIntro: God has not left you to guess what He is like or what He wants from you. He has given you His law to show you your sin, and His Son to carry it. Let both do their work in you this week.
lifePulls: The law tells you the truth about your face. The gospel tells you the truth about Christ. You need both, in that order, and you need the second one fresh every morning of your life.
prayer: Father, You are the blessed God, and Your law is good. I have used it wrong. I have climbed it to look down on other men, and I have shrugged it off when it pointed at me. Show me my face in it today, and do not let me look away. Then show me Your Son, who kept every line of it and took its curse for us. Keep me from different doctrine and from stories I like better than the truth. Wash my heart, cleanse my conscience, and make my faith sincere. Let what I know about You come out of me as love toward my wife, my children, and the men around me. Guard the Good News You have entrusted to us, and help me pass it on whole. In Jesus’ name, amen.

bottomLine: God’s law is good. It is a mirror, not a ladder, and it was given to show you your sin, not to save you from it. Different doctrine adds to the gospel; empty talk misses the mark; but sound teaching makes a man well and ends in love from a pure heart. Look at the list in 1:9–10 until you find your line. Then look at Christ, who kept the law and carried its curse for you.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and look at the law one more time. Look at it without flinching. Look at the line that has your name on it — the lie, the hours, the coldness, the thing you would never say out loud at the shop. Look until your mouth goes dry. You are not looking to be crushed. You are looking because a man who never sees his sickness never calls for the Physician, and a man who never calls for the Physician dies in his chair with his boots on, sure he was fine.

The dust told you the law was a ladder, and you have spent years with your boots on the bottom rung. It told you, when you got tired, that doctrine did not matter and you could just be sincere. Both voices were lying to you. The law was never a ladder. It was a plumb line, and it was hung against your wall to show you that you lean. It was never meant to straighten you. It was meant to send you to the One who can. Every time it has pinned you to the ground, it was pointing past you at a cross.

So look at Him. Jesus Christ was born under that same law. He honored His father and mother. He spoke the truth when it cost Him everything. He kept every line you broke, and then He stood where lawbreakers stand and took the sentence they had earned. Paul says it in plain words: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us. The curse fell, and it fell on Him. It cannot fall on you twice.

That is the Good News of the glory of the blessed God, handed down to you whole. Take it out to the porch tomorrow morning and to the job site after that. When the ledger in the back of your head starts adding up again, answer it with a promise God has signed: Christ is the fulfillment of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes. Everyone who believes. That includes the man who has spent this week looking into the mirror. Stand up out of the dust. The law has done its work. Christ has done His.
closingVerse: But the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith.
carry: Where have you been climbing God’s law like a ladder this month, when He gave it to you as a mirror to send you running to Christ?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Every man has a line he believes God will not cross for him. Most men never say it out loud. It sits underneath the prayers. You can believe God forgives other men — the drunk who got sober, the thief on the cross, the man in your Bible study with the story everybody likes to hear. But there is a thing you did, or a thing you kept doing for years, or a thing you still do when nobody is home, and in your gut you have filed it under a different heading. Forgiven, maybe. Not quite covered. You would never say it in a prayer meeting. You live by it every day.

That is the dust talking. It says grace has a ceiling and you have been living up against it. It says you were saved by mercy but you will be kept by your record from here on. It says the best you can hope for is to be tolerated — let in the back door, handed a broom, never trusted with anything that matters. So you serve God like a man on parole, waiting for the call that says the deal is off. You keep your head down at church. You take the jobs nobody sees, partly out of love and partly to stay out of sight.

Pressed flat by that voice, you have one prayer left, and God has already put it in your mouth in Psalm 119:25: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) The reviving word of 1 Timothy 1:12–17 comes from the worst man in the room. Paul says the grace of the Lord did not stop at his line. It ran over it. The grace of our Lord abounded exceedingly. If it ran over his, it has already run over yours.

sections.heading: A Testimony in the Middle of the Orders
pulls: Grace did not stop at the edge of Paul’s sin and wait for him to climb the rest of the way. It ran over the top of everything he was — and it has already run over the line you drew for yourself.
paras: Paul has just finished with the false teachers and the right use of the law. He is about to hand Timothy his orders. Then, in the middle of it, he stops and tells his own story. He does it on purpose. The man who wrote every charge in this letter wants Timothy to know where he came from before Timothy reads another line. The young man at Ephesus will hear the gospel before he hears another rule.

And he came from a dark place. The New Testament does not hide it. Saul stood by when Stephen died, guarding the cloaks of those who killed him (Acts 22:20). He ravaged the assembly, entering into every house and dragging men and women off to prison (Acts 8:3). He went out still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord (Acts 9:1). That is the man who now writes of whom I am chief. Every word of this passage is mercy speaking in the first person, and it speaks to men who have done their own damage.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: COUNTED FAITHFUL
paras: Paul begins with thanks, and the thanks has an address: I thank him who enabled me, Christ Jesus our Lord. He does not give thanks for how well he turned out. The strength for the work came from outside him. Christ supplied it, and Paul knows it. And he calls Him Lord. The man who once fought that name now bows to it and means it.

Then look at the order of things: he counted me faithful, appointing me to service. Christ counted him faithful and appointed him. He did not wait for Paul to prove himself and then hand him a job. He put the man to work as an act of grace, and the faithfulness came along behind. A foreman who hires the man everyone warned him about is not rewarding a record. He is showing his own trust.

That turns the dust’s parole story upside down. You are not on probation with Christ, sweeping the shop until you earn the keys. If you belong to Him, He has already counted you and already put you to work — at your bench, in your marriage, with the boy who watches how you take bad news. The work is not how you get in. It is what a man does once he has been brought in.

So start where Paul starts. Before you list your failures or your plans, thank the One who enabled you. A man who knows his strength is borrowed will not boast about it, and he will not quit when it runs low. He will go back to the One who lends it, and he will find more there than he spent.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: BLASPHEMER, PERSECUTOR, INSOLENT
paras: Now Paul opens the file: I used to be a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent. He does not spread it out or soften it. Blasphemer — he spoke against the name of Jesus. Persecutor — he hunted the people who loved that name. Insolent — he did it with a sneer. Three words, and every one of them true.

Notice how he tells it. No lurid detail, and no bragging about how bad he was. Just the plain account of a man who stands far enough inside mercy that he can look straight at what he used to be. That is what grace does to a man’s past. It draws the poison out of the record without pretending it away, so it can finally be told.

Then the turn: However, I obtained mercy. Paul received it; he did not earn it. He adds because I did it ignorantly in unbelief, and a man can misread that. Ignorance did not make Paul innocent, and it did not buy him mercy. It names the blindness he was in. He thought he was serving God while he fought God. Jesus prayed from the cross for men in that same blindness: Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.

So ask what you have kept out of your own story. You may have told the softer version so long you believe it. Paul’s honesty is not a weight laid on your back. It is a door held open. You can say the hard word about yourself now, because the One who heard it first has already answered it with mercy. Christ is not waiting for you to clean the file up before you bring it to Him.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: GRACE ABOUNDED EXCEEDINGLY
pulls: Paul does not say he was the chief of sinners. He says he is. A man who walks close to Christ does not watch his sin grow smaller. He watches the grace grow larger, and it is always larger.
paras: Here is the verse this book is named for: The grace of our Lord abounded exceedingly with faith and love which is in Christ Jesus. Set it beside verse 13. Blasphemer, persecutor, insolent — and grace did not merely match it. Grace overran it. Think of the creek behind the back field after three days of rain, out of its banks, over the fence line, taking all the low ground. Paul’s sin was deep. Grace was deeper, and it was still rising.

See what came with it: faith and love which is in Christ Jesus. The faith Paul needed to receive mercy came to him with the mercy. The love that replaced his hatred came too. He did not supply the faith and let God supply the rest. All of it came from one place, and the place is a Person.

Then Paul writes the sentence he wants every church to know by heart: The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners. Faithful — you can put your full weight on it. Worthy of all acceptance — no part of it is to be held back. Christ Jesus came into the world. He took a body and went to the cross on purpose. He came to save sinners. Not to coach them. To save them.

And then the line that breaks a proud man open: of whom I am chief. Not ‘was.’ ‘Am.’ The old apostle, years into the work, still puts himself at the front of the line. A man near Christ does not see his sin getting smaller. He sees the grace getting bigger. So Paul stands at the front of that line without shame. The One who came into the world for sinners is standing there with him.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: THE PATTERN AND THE KING
paras: Why would Christ save a man like that? Paul answers: for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first, Jesus Christ might display all his patience. His conversion was not for Paul alone. It was laid out as a pattern, the chalk line snapped on the slab before the walls go up, so every man after him could see the shape of mercy.

Look at the size of it: all his patience. Not a little patience stretched thin. All of it. Christ put His full patience on display in the hardest case He could find, so no man would ever be able to say, ‘I am the exception.’ If the persecutor fits inside the line, you fit inside it too. So does your brother who quit coming. So does the man on the crew you stopped praying for. And Christ has been patient with you longer than you know.

Then Paul cannot hold it in. He breaks into praise: Now to the King eternal, immortal, invisible, to God who alone is wise, be honor and glory forever and ever. Mercy received ends in worship. The man who knows he is the chief of sinners does not end his story with himself. He ends it with the King.

That is where your story is meant to end too. Not in your record, good or bad, but in honor given to the King who saved you. The Christ who came into the world for sinners now reigns at the Father’s right hand, and He will appear again in glory. A man who has received that much mercy has nothing left to do with his last word but give it to Him.

stations.verse: Although I used to be a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent. However, I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief.
stations.question: What is the worst true word about my past that I leave out when I tell my own story?
stations.live: Write down the hardest true word about your life, before Christ or since. Set 1:15 beside it on the same page. Read the two aloud together: ‘That was me. Christ came for exactly that man.’
body: A persecutor — that is all diōktēs means. It is a noun made from the verb diōkō, and Scripture has no other verse that uses it. Paul does not use it to describe someone else. He picks it up and puts it on himself.

On the road to Damascus the risen Christ asked him, Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? Paul had been hunting believers. Jesus counted it as hunting Him. That is how close Christ holds His people. And the One Paul persecuted is the One who stopped him, blinded him, and saved him. The persecuted Lord made the persecutor His servant.

The dust wants you to bury the worst word about yourself and hope no one digs. Paul writes his into Scripture with his own hand. Mercy has made it safe to tell the truth, because the truth has already been answered at the cross. What Christ has covered, you no longer need to hide.

stations.verse: The grace of our Lord abounded exceedingly with faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
stations.question: Where am I still living as if my sin runs deeper than the grace of the Lord Jesus?
stations.live: Name the sin you believe is too big, too old, or too often repeated. Each morning this week, say the verse over it aloud: The grace of our Lord abounded exceedingly.
body: Hyperpleonazō carries hyper on its front, and the lexicon gives its meaning in two words: to abound exceedingly. You will not find it anywhere else in the New Testament — only here, in the verse this book is named for. Scripture spends it on one man’s case.

Paul could have said grace was enough. He says it ran over. Set it beside the three words before it — blasphemer, persecutor, insolent — and the point is plain. Grace did not meet Paul’s sin at the same level. It rose over it the way spring water rises over a low-water crossing and keeps coming. He says the same thing to the church at Rome: where sin abounded, grace abounded more exceedingly.

The dust says your sin runs deeper than grace can reach. Scripture answers with a word it uses only once, spoken over a man worse than you think you are. Grace does not run dry before your sin does. The creek is still over its banks.

stations.verse: The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief.
stations.question: What would change in how I treat the men around me if I believed I am the chief of sinners?
stations.live: The next time you size up another man’s sin this week, put yourself first in line instead. Say it under your breath — ‘of whom I am chief’ — and then pray for him.
body: Prōtos means first. It can mark first in time or order, and it can mark first in rank — chief, principal. Paul uses it twice in two verses. In 1:15 it is rank: of whom I am chief. In 1:16 it is order: in me first.

Notice the tense. Paul does not say he used to be chief. He says he is. A man who walks with Christ for years does not find his sin shrinking in his own eyes. He finds it larger, and the grace larger still. The man who stops ranking other sinners and takes the front of the line is the man who has understood mercy.

The dust wants you first in something — first in the argument, first on the crew, first in the room. Paul has given up every first but one. And he has met the One who says, I am the first and the last. The chief of sinners is held by the First of all.

stations.verse: However, for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first, Jesus Christ might display all his patience for an example of those who were going to believe in him for eternal life.
stations.question: Do I believe the patience Christ showed Paul was drawn wide enough to cover me?
stations.gloss: an outline, a sketch; a pattern, an example
stations.live: Think of a man you have written off as too far gone — a brother, an old friend, a man you used to work beside. Pray for him by name every day this week, starting with 1:16.
body: Hypotypōsis comes from a verb meaning to delineate, to draw out the lines of a thing. It means an outline or sketch, and so a pattern or example. Paul uses it twice, both times to Timothy — here, and in the pattern of sound words of 2 Timothy 1:13.

Christ saved Paul as an outline, the first lines drawn so every man after could see the shape of mercy. He displayed all his patience in the hardest case, the way a framer cuts the first rafter as a pattern and traces every other one off it. The persecutor was the pattern. Every sinner who believes is cut from the same board.

The dust says you are the exception, the one case the pattern does not cover. Paul was saved first so that no man could ever say that and be right. The line was drawn wide on purpose, and you are inside it.

stations.verse: Now to the King eternal, immortal, invisible, to God who alone is wise, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.
stations.question: What would it look like for me to live this week as a man who sees the King no one can see?
stations.live: When the things you can see press hard this week — the bill, the bad report, the empty chair — stop and speak 1:17 aloud before you speak about the problem.
body: Unseen, invisible: aoratos turns up in five New Testament verses, and every time it points at something real that the eye cannot reach — the invisible things of him in Romans 1:20, and here the King Himself.

Paul praises a King no man can see. Yet the same word turns up in Colossians: Christ is the image of the invisible God. The King you cannot see has shown you His face in His Son — the Man who came into the world to save sinners. Hebrews says Moses endured, as seeing him who is invisible. You have more to go on than Moses had. You have seen the King in Christ.

The dust says only what you can see is real — the balance, the scan, the frost on the field in May. Paul ends his testimony praising the One he cannot see, because he has already met Him. The things you can see are passing. The King is not.

practices.title: TELL THE STORY STRAIGHT
practices.body: Paul tells his story in three moves: what I was, what Christ did, what I am now. Write yours on one sheet of paper. Do not polish the first part or pad the last. Use plain words, the way Paul used blasphemer and persecutor. Then tell it to one man this week — a son, a friend, a neighbor. The point is not your story. The point is the Savior in it, and the man listening may need Him more than you know.

practices.title: LEARN THE FAITHFUL SAYING
practices.body: Learn 1:15 word for word this week. Write it on a card and keep it where your hands go every day — the dash, the tool bench, the lunch pail. Say it when you wake. Say it before you eat. Say it in the dark when the old file opens and starts reading itself to you. Paul called it faithful. Put your whole weight on it and see if it gives. It has held the chief of sinners. It will hold you.

practices.title: GIVE UP RANKING OTHER MEN
practices.body: Watch for the moment this week when you measure another man’s sin and come out ahead — the drunk uncle, the coworker who cheats on his hours, the man in the news. Stop right there. Put yourself first in line, where Paul put himself. Then do one thing for that man you would want done for you. Mercy received turns into mercy given, or it was never understood. The man you looked down on is a man Christ came for.

practices.title: PRAY FOR THE ONE YOU WROTE OFF
practices.body: Name the man you believe is too far gone. Write his name down. Pray for him every day this week, and use 1:16 as you pray: Christ displayed all His patience in the worst case so that men like this one would believe. If you can, reach out to him once — a call, a text, a cup of coffee — and say nothing preachy. Just be there. Christ was patient with you for years before you ever looked up.

practices.title: END EACH DAY IN PRAISE
practices.body: Paul ends his testimony with the King, not with himself. Do the same this week. Before you sleep each night, read 1:17 aloud — even if the day went badly, even if it went well. Let your last word of the day be honor given to God, not a review of your own performance. A man who ends the day in praise sleeps on mercy instead of on his record. The King will still be King when the alarm goes off.

title: Grace Abounding
subtitle: from dust to mercy for the chief of sinners
keyVerse: The grace of our Lord abounded exceedingly with faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.

passage.text: I thank him who enabled me, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he counted me faithful, appointing me to service;
although I used to be a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent. However, I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief.
The grace of our Lord abounded exceedingly with faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief.
However, for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first, Jesus Christ might display all his patience for an example of those who were going to believe in him for eternal life.
Now to the King eternal, immortal, invisible, to God who alone is wise, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

stationsIntro: These five verses are a converted man’s testimony. Read them as the record of what Christ does with sinners, and answer each question as one of them.
lifeIntro: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and He has saved you. What follows is the answer of a man who has already received mercy. None of it is the price of getting it.
lifePulls: Christ did not save Paul in spite of how bad he was and then hide the file. He saved him first and put him on display, so the worst man you know — even you — would never have to wonder.
prayer: Father, I thank You for Christ Jesus our Lord, who enabled me and counted me faithful when I was not. You know my file better than I do. You know what I was and what I still am. I have no defense to make. I am the chief of sinners, and I need mercy. Thank You that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and that He did not stop short of me. Let Your grace abound exceedingly over the sin I thought was too deep. Make me patient with the men I have written off, as You have been patient with me. Give me plain words to tell my story, and let the Savior be the center of it. To You, the King eternal, immortal, invisible, God who alone is wise, be honor and glory forever. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, I thank You for Christ Jesus our Lord, who enabled me and counted me faithful when I was not.
You know my file better than I do. You know what I was and what I still am.
I have no defense to make. I am the chief of sinners, and I need mercy.
Thank You that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and that He did not stop short of me.
Let Your grace abound exceedingly over the sin I thought was too deep.
Make me patient with the men I have written off, as You have been patient with me.
Give me plain words to tell my story, and let the Savior be the center of it.
To You, the King eternal, immortal, invisible, God who alone is wise, be honor and glory forever.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Paul calls himself a blasphemer, a persecutor and an insolent man, then says the grace of the Lord abounded exceedingly over every bit of it. Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and Paul puts himself first in line. He was saved as a pattern, so no man can claim to be the exception. Stop living on parole. Tell your story straight, quit ranking other men, and end each day in praise to the King.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and look at who Christ came for. He came for the blasphemer who cursed His name. He came for the persecutor who dragged His people out of their houses. He came for the insolent man who sneered while he did it, and for the young man who held the coats while Stephen died. And He came for you — with the file you keep shut, the line you drew, the thing you still do when nobody is home. He did not come for the men who had it together. There were none. He came for sinners, and He found you.

The dust told you there was a ceiling on grace and that you had been living up against it. It told you that you came in the back door and would be watched from here on. But grace has no ceiling. It has a flood stage, and Paul says it went over. The grace of our Lord abounded exceedingly. It did not stop at his line, and it has not stopped at yours. You are not on parole. You were counted faithful and put to work by the same Lord who saved you.

Look at what it cost Him. Christ Jesus came into the world. He left the glory He had with the Father and came down into the very dust you are lying in. He took the blasphemer’s place and the persecutor’s place and your place, and He bore the judgment for all of it on the cross. Then He rose, alive in the body they buried, and He met the persecutor on the Damascus road and called him by name twice. He has not used up the patience He spent on Paul. He has all of it still, and He spends it on you this morning.

So hold on to this when Tuesday comes and the old file falls open: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners. It is a faithful saying. Put your whole weight on it; it will not give. And when you have put your weight on it, do what Paul did. Lift your head out of your own story and finish with the King — eternal, immortal, invisible — who has made the chief of sinners His own. He will not hand you back to the dust. He did not save Paul to drop him, and He did not save you to drop you. Honor to Him. Glory to Him. Forever and ever.
closingVerse: The grace of our Lord abounded exceedingly with faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
carry: Where have you drawn a line you believe God’s grace will not cross — when the chief of sinners tells you it abounded exceedingly over his?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Most men pray the way a man walks into the county office to fight a tax bill. He has his papers in order. He has rehearsed what he will say. He expects to wait a long time, and he expects to lose. Somewhere along the way you learned to think of God like that — far off, behind a counter, open only to the man who can make a strong enough case. So you make your case. You stack up the good week. You leave out the bad night. And when the case looks thin, you don’t go in at all. You stay out in the parking lot with the engine running, telling yourself you will try again when you have a better week to show.

The dust says you stand before God alone and plead your own file. It says the distance between heaven and a man like you is yours to close, and that you will never close it. Job sat in the ash and felt that distance: There is no umpire between us, that might lay his hand on us both. The same dust tells you that the men over you — the boss, the governor, the names you mutter at during the evening news — are past the reach of prayer, so you don’t bother.

Flattened by that distance, you can still pray the words of Psalm 119:25, the one thing a man in the ash can say: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) The reviving word this week is one sentence that ends the argument before you begin it: For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. He did not come to help you argue your case. He came to pay it off.

sections.heading: A Charge Handed to a Young Man
pulls: The dust tells you to stand before God alone and plead your own file. Paul says the case was taken out of your hands — one Mediator stood in the gap, and He paid with Himself.
paras: Paul writes to Timothy, my true child in faith. He had left him at Ephesus to command certain men not to teach a different doctrine (1:3). Timothy was the son of a believing Jewish mother and a Greek father, a young man the brothers at Lystra and Iconium spoke well of (Acts 16:1–2). The sincere faith that lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice had taken root in him (2 Timothy 1:5). Now he had been handed hard ground and men who wanted to argue.

In 1:18 Paul picks that charge back up. He broke off to tell his own story — the blasphemer who obtained mercy, the chief of sinners — and only then does he hand Timothy the fight. That order matters. Before a man is sent into the work, he is shown the grace that put him there. And when Paul names the first work of the church in chapter 2, it is not a program or a campaign against the culture. It is prayer, and under the prayer stands the one Mediator who opened the door for it.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE GOOD WARFARE
paras: Paul hands Timothy the charge the way an old foreman hands a younger man the keys to the site: I commit this instruction to you, my child Timothy. Notice the word child. Before Paul gives the order, he names the bond. Timothy is not hired help. He is family, and the charge comes to him inside that warmth.

Then the charge itself: that by them you may wage the good warfare. The prophecies spoken over Timothy earlier were God’s word about him, given ahead of time — ground to stand on when the work went hard and the men he faced would not listen. Paul tells him to fight by them. A man does not fight on his own say-so. He fights on what God has said.

And Paul calls the warfare good. Not easy. Good. It is good because the One who sends you into it is good, and because the outcome was settled at the cross before the first blow was swung. You fight from inside His win, not to find out whether He wins. The war was decided on a hill outside Jerusalem and announced at an empty tomb.

That changes how you carry the ordinary fights of your week. The temptation that waits for you after everyone else is asleep. The man at work who keeps baiting you. The slow pull to quit on your marriage in your head while you still sleep in the house. These are the good warfare itself, and you are not in it alone. Paul does not tell Timothy to scrape together courage from the bottom of the barrel. He reminds him whose word he carries, and that word is enough to stand on.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: FAITH AND A GOOD CONSCIENCE
paras: How is the fight waged? Holding faith and a good conscience. Two things in the grip at once. Faith holds on to Christ. A good conscience keeps the hands clean enough to keep holding. Let go of the second and the first will slip. A rope does a man little good if his hands are greased with something he refuses to wash off.

Paul shows what happens when a man lets go: which some having thrust away made a shipwreck concerning the faith. Thrust away is a hard phrase. These men did not drift off. They shoved the good conscience aside like a man kicking a sagging fence post out of his way, and the faith went down after it. A man who keeps a sin he knows God hates, and keeps it on purpose, will not keep his doctrine long. The conscience goes first. The creed follows.

Paul names two of them: Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I delivered to Satan. That is church discipline at its hardest — put out of the fellowship, back into the world where Satan works. But read the purpose clause: that they might be taught not to blaspheme. The aim is a lesson, not a grave. Paul wants them back.

And remember who is writing. A few lines earlier he called himself a blasphemer (1:13). He knows the road those two men are on because he walked it, and mercy met him there. The grace that stopped Paul is the grace he is reaching after them with. Discipline in the church of Christ is mercy with its sleeves rolled up, and it is never the last word God means to speak to a straying man.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: PRAY FOR ALL MEN
pulls: You do not get to God by a better argument. There is one Mediator, the man Christ Jesus, and He did not plead your case with words. He gave Himself as the ransom.
paras: Then Paul turns from the fight to the first thing: I exhort therefore, first of all, that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and givings of thanks be made for all men. The therefore ties it to everything above. A church that has been shown mercy asks mercy for those who have not seen it yet.

He names the hard names: for kings and all who are in high places. Paul adds no condition. No line about only the good ones, or only the ones who vote your way. That cuts across the way most men talk about whoever holds office. You can name a ruler’s sin plainly. But the man who complains about the governor at the feed store and never once prays for him has skipped the first instruction. And remember that Paul himself had once been the kind of man most believers would have left off the list.

Paul gives the aim: that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life in all godliness and reverence. Not a soft life. A settled one, where the church can worship and work without being torn up by every storm in the capital.

And under the aim he sets the reason. This prayer pleases God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and come to full knowledge of the truth. That is God’s real goodwill. He has no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11). The offer of Christ is free, and it goes out to every kind of man — the king and the hired hand, the official and the inmate. You do not get to decide who is past reaching. God has already told you to pray for them, and He means it.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: ONE GOD, ONE MEDIATOR
paras: Why pray for every kind of man with any hope at all? Because of verse five: For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. One God, so no man answers to a different judge. One Mediator, so no man reaches God by a different door. Not a priest you pay, not a saint you court, not your own good record. One.

Paul says the man Christ Jesus. The One who stands between God and you stands on both sides. He is God, and He took on flesh and bone — a real man, with hands that worked wood and lungs that drew breath. He knows the weight of dust because He wore it. Job wished for an umpire who could lay a hand on both. Here He is. Because He is a man, He is not ashamed to stand beside you. Because He is God, His standing settles the matter.

What did He do in the middle? He gave himself as a ransom for all. He did not bargain. He paid, and the price was Himself. God’s goodwill reaches every kind of man, and the offer stands open to all who hear it. And the ransom did not fall short of what it was paid for. Jesus said, I lay down my life for the sheep, and of those sheep, They will never perish (John 10:15, 28).

Then Paul says he was appointed a preacher and an apostle to carry that news, and he swears to it: I am telling the truth in Christ, not lying. A ransom paid must be announced. Paul was the man sent to cry it out to the Gentiles. And the same news is now in your mouth for the man at the next bench.

stations.verse: I commit this instruction to you, my child Timothy, according to the prophecies which were given to you before, that by them you may wage the good warfare.
stations.question: What word from God am I actually standing on when the fight in my week turns hard?
stations.live: Write down one promise from God’s word you will stand on this week — a promise, not a feeling. Read it before the hardest conversation on your calendar: ‘I fight on what God has said.’
body: Strateia is an expedition, a campaign, warfare carried on over time — not a single scuffle in a parking lot. Only Paul uses it, twice, and both times as a picture: here, and in 2 Corinthians 10:4, the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh.

So the fight handed to Timothy is long. It runs through ordinary days — the meeting with the hard man, the night alone with the old temptation, the slow work of saying the same truth again to people who are tired of hearing it. A campaign is carried through seasons, not settled in one swing.

The dust wants you to think the fight is yours to win by grit, and that losing one skirmish means the war is lost. Paul calls the warfare good because Christ has already taken the field. You fight inside a victory, with weapons God supplies and a word He has spoken over you.

stations.verse: Holding faith and a good conscience, which some having thrust away made a shipwreck concerning the faith.
stations.question: Where am I pushing away a good conscience by keeping a sin I know God hates?
stations.live: Name the sin you have been keeping with your eyes open. Confess it to God today and to one brother before Sunday: ‘I will not thrust this conscience away. Christ’s blood cleans it.’
body: Nauageō joins the word for a ship to a verb meaning to break: to suffer shipwreck. In 2 Corinthians 11:25 Paul uses it of his own body in the sea: Three times I suffered shipwreck. Here he uses it of a man’s faith.

Paul knew what a breaking hull sounds like. He knew the wreck does not begin with the sinking. It begins with a crack nobody bothered to fix. Hymenaeus and Alexander did not wake up one morning as false teachers. They thrust away a good conscience first, and the faith went down after it.

The dust says one kept sin is small and will stay small. Paul says a ship breaks from the inside. But no conscience is too fouled for Christ. His blood will cleanse your conscience from dead works (Hebrews 9:14), and a cleaned conscience holds the faith fast. The hull can be mended while the ship is still afloat.

stations.verse: For kings and all who are in high places, that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life in all godliness and reverence.
stations.question: When did I last pray by name for the men and women who hold authority over me?
stations.live: Pick one official over you and one boss at work. Pray for each by name every morning this week, for their good and their salvation, before you read a word of news about either one.
body: Quiet, tranquil: this is the one verse where ēremos shows up, rendered tranquil, and it stands beside a word of close meaning, quiet. Paul doubles the idea on purpose. He wants the church to have a still life — not idle, but undisturbed, free to worship and to work.

Look at how Paul expects that life to come: by prayer for kings and all who are in high places. Not by fear of them. Not by grabbing for control of them. By praying for them. The church’s quiet is not won by deciding who rules. It is asked from God, who rules the rulers.

The dust says your peace hangs on who wins the next election, so you carry the news around like a stone in your boot. Paul sends you past every office to the throne above them all. The tranquil life is a gift you ask for, and God our Savior is pleased to hear the asking.

stations.verse: Who gave himself as a ransom for all, the testimony in its own times.
stations.question: What am I still trying to pay God for when Christ has already given Himself as the ransom?
stations.gloss: a ransom; the price paid to set a captive free
stations.live: Each time you catch yourself trying to make it up to God this week — the extra effort, the quiet self-punishment — stop and say it plainly: ‘Christ Jesus gave Himself as a ransom. It is paid.’
body: Antilytron means a ransom — the price paid to set a captive free. Paul is the only writer who uses it, and only here, building on the common word for ransom. Jesus spoke the same way of His own death: He came to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45).

Look at what Paul names as the price. Not silver. Not a lamb from the flock. Himself. The Mediator did not stand between God and you holding someone else’s money. He paid with His own life, on a Roman cross, and the Father raised Him from the dead to show the payment was received.

Psalm 49 says no man can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him. The dust agrees, then tells you to keep trying anyway. The gospel agrees and points to the one Man who could. The ransom is paid. Stop making installments on a debt that is closed.

stations.verse: To which I was appointed a preacher and an apostle—I am telling the truth in Christ, not lying—a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.
stations.question: Who in my life has never heard me say plainly that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners?
stations.live: Name one man who needs to hear it. Before the week is out, tell him in plain words what Christ did for you: ‘Christ Jesus came to save sinners. He saved me.’
body: Kēryx is a herald — the man sent out to cry a message in public. Three verses carry it: two of Paul (here and 2 Timothy 1:11) and one of Noah, a preacher of righteousness (2 Peter 2:5). In the Greek Old Testament it names the herald of Nebuchadnezzar’s decree (Daniel 3:4).

A herald does not write the news. He carries it. He does not improve it or soften it to suit the crowd. His job is to say it loud and say it straight. Paul calls himself the herald of the ransom — the news that the man Christ Jesus gave Himself for sinners.

The dust tells you that you would have to be a smooth talker to speak of Christ. A herald needs only the message and the nerve to open his mouth. You are not the author of the good news. You only pass it on, the way someone once passed it to you.

practices.title: FIGHT ON WHAT GOD HAS SAID
practices.body: God has spoken over you in His word, the way prophecy was spoken over Timothy. Find the promise you most need this week and write it on a card for your shirt pocket or the visor. When the temptation comes, or the hard man, or the old fear, take it out and read it. Do not wait to feel brave. Paul told Timothy to wage the good warfare by the word given to him, not by his own nerve. The promise holds when your nerve does not.

practices.title: KEEP SHORT ACCOUNTS WITH YOUR CONSCIENCE
practices.body: Christ’s blood cleans a fouled conscience, so you never have to hide one. Each night this week, before you sleep, run back over the day and name to God anything your conscience flagged — the cutting word, the hour on the phone, the shaded number on the invoice. Confess it plainly. Don’t argue it down or save it for later. A crack patched tonight is a hull that holds tomorrow, and a man who keeps his conscience clean keeps his grip on the faith.

practices.title: PRAY FOR THE NAMES ABOVE YOU
practices.body: God rules the rulers, and He has told you to pray for them. Write down the names: the president, the governor, the sheriff, the county commissioner, your boss and his boss. Pray down that list once a day this week. Ask for their salvation, for wisdom, and for a quiet life for the church. Give thanks for one thing about each of them. You will find it hard to curse a man you have been praying for since Monday. Prayer has a way of changing the man who prays.

practices.title: COME BY THE ONE DOOR
practices.body: There is one Mediator, and He has already paid. When you fail this week, do not hang back for three days to show God you are sorry, and do not try to work your way back in. Go straight to Him in the name of the man Christ Jesus, the same hour. Say what you did. Thank Him that the ransom covers it. A man who has a Mediator does not need to build his own case before he can pray. The case was made at the cross.

practices.title: SAY IT LIKE A HERALD
practices.body: Paul was appointed to carry the news of the ransom, and the news has reached you. This week, tell one man in plain words what Christ has done — at the shop, on the porch, over lunch. Skip the polish. Start with your own story, the way Paul started with his: I was the kind of man Christ came for. Then name Him: the one Mediator, who gave Himself as a ransom. A herald’s job is to say it, not to close the sale.

title: One Mediator
subtitle: from dust to the ransom paid for all
keyVerse: For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all, the testimony in its own times.

passage.text: I commit this instruction to you, my child Timothy, according to the prophecies which were given to you before, that by them you may wage the good warfare,
holding faith and a good conscience, which some having thrust away made a shipwreck concerning the faith,
of whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I delivered to Satan, that they might be taught not to blaspheme.
I exhort therefore, first of all, that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and givings of thanks be made for all men:
for kings and all who are in high places, that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life in all godliness and reverence.
For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Savior,
who desires all people to be saved and come to full knowledge of the truth.
For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus,
who gave himself as a ransom for all, the testimony in its own times,
to which I was appointed a preacher and an apostle—I am telling the truth in Christ, not lying—a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.

stationsIntro: Take each verse slowly, with your Bible open, and let it say its piece before you answer. Where a Greek word is opened, let it press the verse down into the ground of your own week.
lifeIntro: The Mediator has already stood in the gap, and the ransom has already been paid. These practices are not how you get to God. They are what a man does once he knows he has been brought near.
lifePulls: God our Savior has given one Mediator to stand between Himself and men. Pray like a man who knows the door is open — for himself, and for every man he would rather leave off the list.
prayer: Father, You are the one God, and You have given us one Mediator. Thank You for the man Christ Jesus, who stood between You and me and gave Himself as my ransom. I stop pleading my own case. I come in His name alone. Keep faith and a good conscience in my grip, and where I have shoved my conscience aside, wash it in His blood. I pray for those who rule over us, and for the men over me at work: save them, and give us a quiet life in godliness. I pray for the man I would rather leave off the list. You desire his salvation; make me desire it too. Make me a plain herald of what You have done for sinners like me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You are the one God, and You have given us one Mediator.
Thank You for the man Christ Jesus, who stood between You and me and gave Himself as my ransom.
I stop pleading my own case. I come in His name alone.
Keep faith and a good conscience in my grip, and where I have shoved my conscience aside, wash it in His blood.
I pray for those who rule over us, and for the men over me at work: save them,
and give us a quiet life in godliness.
I pray for the man I would rather leave off the list. You desire his salvation; make me desire it too.
Make me a plain herald of what You have done for sinners like me.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Paul hands Timothy a good warfare, telling him to fight it holding faith and a good conscience, because men who shove the conscience aside wreck the faith. Then he sends the church to pray for every kind of man, since God our Savior desires all people to be saved. Under all of it stands one God and one Mediator, the man Christ Jesus, who gave Himself as a ransom. Stop pleading your case. Pray, and pass the news on.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and look at who stands between you and God. Look at the One who stands where Job wished an umpire would stand. Look at the One who stands where you have been trying to stand yourself for years, with your papers and your excuses and your list of good weeks. Look at the One who stands there alone because He needs no help — the man Christ Jesus, God in flesh and bone, with one hand on the Father and one hand on you. He is not waiting for you to qualify. He has already taken His place.

The dust has had you pleading your own file for a long time. Rehearsing the defense. Counting the good days. Staying away when the case looked weak. Put the file down. Your case is not being argued. It was settled, and it was settled by payment. He gave Himself as the ransom. The price was not your effort, and it was not paid in part. It was Him, all of Him, given over on the cross and accepted by the Father, who brought Him up out of the grave alive to say the debt was cleared.

And He is not idle now. The Man who paid for you is the Man who prays for you; Scripture says he lives forever to make intercession for them. When you pray for the governor you do not trust, for the man at work who mocks you, for the son who has gone quiet on the phone, your prayer does not go in alone. It goes in through Him. The door you could never open has a Man standing in it, and He is holding it for you, and He has never once let it swing shut on a man who came in His name.

So go out this week as a man with an open door behind him. Hold faith and a good conscience, and when the conscience gets fouled, bring it straight back to the blood that cleans it. Pray for every kind of man, because God desires their salvation and has told you so. And when someone asks how a man like you can stand before God, give them the herald’s plain news: there is one God, and one Mediator, and the ransom has been paid in full by the man Christ Jesus, who walked out of the grave and lives to bring every ransomed man home.
closingVerse: For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all, the testimony in its own times.
carry: Where are you still standing before God pleading your own case, when the man Christ Jesus has already stood there for you and paid the ransom with Himself?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: A lot of men leave the praying to someone else. The wife prays at supper. The pastor prays on Sunday. Your grandmother prayed for you for years, and you knew it, and it was a comfort, and it was hers. Your part, you figured, was the work — the paycheck, the roof, the oil change, the hard word when the boy needs one. You would carry the load. Somebody else could carry the prayers. And if anyone asked, you would say you believe in prayer. You just never seem to get around to it, and nobody in your house has heard you do it out loud in years.

The dust says a man leads with his hands full and his jaw set. It says prayer is soft work, and that the real strength in a house belongs to the man who can fix what breaks, raise his voice when he has to, and hold a grudge longer than the other fellow. Then the same dust turns around and tells you that if you ever do pray, you had better clear out the anger and the doubt on your own first, or keep your mouth shut. So the man who most needs to pray is the man who feels least fit to, and he stays quiet.

When you find out how little your own strength holds up, the first honest prayer is the short one in Psalm 119:25: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) The reviving word this week is one verse, and it is aimed straight at you: I desire therefore that the men in every place pray. Before Paul says one word about who teaches or leads in the church, he tells the men to pray — and to come with hands lifted, not clenched.

sections.heading: Hard Ground, Read in the Light
pulls: Paul’s first word to the men of the church is not take charge. It is pray. Lift your hands to God empty and open, and let the grudge and the argument fall out of them on the way up.
paras: The second half of this chapter is hard ground. Paul speaks to the men, then to the women, then reaches back to Adam and Eve in the garden. Read it as the next paragraph of a letter that opened with mercy for a blasphemer and a persecutor. The therefore of 2:8 ties it to the one Mediator and the ransom paid for all (2:5–6). Nothing here walks back 1:15. Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and every line that follows is written to people He saved.

This study is written to men, so the weight of the week sits where Paul sets his first weight: on 2:8. When the text turns to the women of the church, it honors them — their godliness, their good works, their place as learners of the word. When it speaks of order in the church, it grounds that order in how God made the man and the woman, not in one being worth less than the other. Read slowly. Read as a man who has been shown mercy and has no room to boast.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: HOLY HANDS IN EVERY PLACE
paras: I desire therefore that the men in every place pray. The therefore reaches back to verse five. There is one God and one Mediator, and the ransom is paid; so the door stands open, and the men are to walk through it. Paul does not start with a list of duties. He starts with access, and then he tells the men to use it. Grace comes first. The prayer is what a forgiven man does with the open door.

In every place means wherever the church gathers to worship, and the habit runs out from there into every place a man stands — the shop floor, the back field, the hospital waiting room, the side of his own bed. Prayer is not a room in the house. It is the air the house breathes. A man who prays only in church has a building he visits, not a Father he lives with.

Lifting up holy hands. Lifted hands were the posture of prayer among God’s people long before Paul. Solomon spread out his hands toward heaven at the altar (1 Kings 8:22). The psalmist asks God to receive the lifting up of my hands like the evening sacrifice (Psalm 141:2). Lifted hands are empty hands. A man cannot grip a tool, a bottle or a grudge and lift his hands to God at the same time. Something has to be set down.

And the hands are holy. Not because you scrubbed them. Isaiah heard God say of His people, Your hands are full of blood (Isaiah 1:15), and the same chapter answers it: Though your sins are as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow (Isaiah 1:18). Your hands are holy because Christ’s were nailed. You lift them as a washed man, not as a man trying to get clean.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: WITHOUT ANGER AND DOUBTING
paras: Then Paul names the two things men most often carry into prayer: without anger and doubting. Start with the anger. The grudge against the brother who cheated you. The edge in your voice with your wife that has been there since Tuesday. The slow burn at the boss. A man can stand in church with his hands up and his teeth clenched.

Jesus said, Whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone (Mark 11:25). Peter told husbands to live with their wives giving honor to the woman, as joint heirs of grace, that your prayers may not be hindered (1 Peter 3:7). Anger at home stops the mouth of prayer. It is hard to lift a hand to God that you just slammed on the table.

Then the doubting. That is the argument that runs in a man’s head — the case he keeps building against a brother, and the case he keeps building against God. He prays with one eye on heaven and the other on his own backup plan. He asks and then argues with the answer before it comes. That is not humility. It is a man who has not yet decided whether God can be trusted with the outcome.

Here is the ground under both. You do not drop the grudge to earn a hearing. You drop it because you have been forgiven a far larger debt, just as God also in Christ forgave you (Ephesians 4:32). And you do not end the argument by winning it. You end it by looking at the One who stands between God and you. The Mediator is real, the ransom is paid, and a man who knows that has nothing left to argue about.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: ADORNED WITH GOOD WORKS
pulls: Adam was formed first, from the dust, and Adam sinned with his eyes open. A man finds no ground for pride in this passage — only a call to go first in prayer and first in serving.
paras: In the same way Paul turns to the women. They too come to God in worship, and he wants them to adorn themselves in decent clothing, with modesty and propriety — not with braided hair, gold, pearls, or expensive clothing, but with good works, which is appropriate for women professing godliness. Paul honors them. He counts them full members of the household of faith, women whose true beauty is not what can be bought at a jeweler’s counter but what their hands do in the name of Christ.

Then: Let a woman learn in quietness with full submission. Notice first that she is to learn. She is a student of the word, sitting where Mary sat when she sat at Jesus’ feet, and heard his word (Luke 10:39). Timothy himself first learned the faith from two women, his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (2 Timothy 1:5).

Then the plain line: But I don’t permit a woman to teach, nor to exercise authority over a man. Paul is speaking of the gathered church, and of the work of teaching and governing the congregation. That work he gives to qualified men, and he lists who they are in the very next chapter. It is not a ruling on whether a woman is wise or able. It is an order God has set in His house, and both the man and the woman in it are His.

And it lands hardest on you. Before the Lord gave His men any work, He knelt with a towel and washed their feet. Then He said, If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet (John 13:14). A man washed like that leads without a raised voice. He starts low, in the same place his Lord knelt.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: FORMED FIRST, SAVED THROUGH FAITH
paras: Paul grounds the order in creation, not in the customs of any city: For Adam was formed first, then Eve. Formed — from what? Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground (Genesis 2:7). First in order is not first in worth. Male and female he created them, both in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), and neither is the woman independent of the man, nor the man independent of the woman, in the Lord (1 Corinthians 11:11).

Then: Adam wasn’t deceived, but the woman, being deceived, has fallen into disobedience. The woman was deceived. Adam was not — which means he went in with his eyes open. Paul writes elsewhere that through the one man’s disobedience many were made sinners (Romans 5:19). A man who reads this verse and feels proud has not read it.

Then the hardest line: but she will be saved through her childbearing, if they continue in faith, love, and sanctification with sobriety. Say plainly what it cannot mean. No woman earns salvation by bearing children, and no woman without children is shut out. Salvation is Christ’s work, received by faith alone: for by grace you have been saved through faith (Ephesians 2:8). Paul is naming the life in which saved women continue — their ordinary callings, motherhood among them for many — marked by faith, love and holiness with a sound mind.

And remember the first promise after the fall. God told the serpent that the woman’s offspring would crush him: He will bruise your head (Genesis 3:15).
