The deception in the garden was answered through a woman’s Child, born to a woman (Galatians 4:4), the One who shall save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21). Hold that as a connection, not a work: a woman was deceived first, and a woman carried the Savior every believer trusts.

stations.verse: I desire therefore that the men in every place pray, lifting up holy hands without anger and doubting.
stations.question: What am I holding on to this week that keeps my hands from being lifted to God in prayer?
stations.live: Each morning this week, before your feet hit the floor, open your hands palm-up and pray for your household by name: ‘Lord, I hold nothing back from You. Bless them.’
body: Epairō means to lift up, to raise. Nineteen verses use it — for lifting eyes, voices, heads and hands. Jesus, lifting up his eyes to heaven, prayed to the Father on the night He was betrayed (John 17:1). In 2 Corinthians 10:5 the passive form names every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God.

So the same word points a man two ways. He can lift his hands to God, or he can lift himself up against God. Paul wants the first. The man who prays with his hands raised has admitted he holds nothing worth keeping back.

The dust says your hands are too dirty to raise. The tax collector thought so too. He wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast and begged for mercy (Luke 18:13). Jesus said that man went down to his house justified (Luke 18:14). Mercy lifts what shame keeps down, and a forgiven man may raise his hands as high as he likes.

stations.verse: I desire therefore that the men in every place pray, lifting up holy hands without anger and doubting.
stations.question: Am I staying away from prayer until I can scrub my own hands clean enough to lift them?
stations.live: Before you pray tomorrow, confess one thing your hands did this week that shames you. Then thank Christ for it by name: ‘The Holy One has made these hands holy. I will lift them.’
body: Holy, devout, right before God: hosios shows up eight times. It describes the man fit to be an overseer (Titus 1:8). It is said of God: For you only are holy (Revelation 15:4). And it names the Messiah Himself, your Holy One, whom God would not leave in the grave to see decay (Acts 2:27).

In 2:8 Paul hangs the word on a man’s hands, and the hands stand for the whole man — what he did, what he held, what he took. Holy hands are hands set apart for God, not hands that have never touched dirt.

Hebrews 7:26 says where that holiness comes from: a high priest holy, guiltless, undefiled. The dust says your hands must be clean before you can lift them. The gospel says the Holy One has washed them. You come as a man made holy, not as a man working to make himself so. The washing is finished.

stations.verse: I desire therefore that the men in every place pray, lifting up holy hands without anger and doubting.
stations.question: What argument have I been running in my head that follows me every time I try to pray?
stations.live: Write down the argument you keep having in your head. Bring it to God out loud, then lay it down: ‘You have shown me Your hands. I am done building my case.’
body: Dialogismos is a thought, a reasoning, an inward questioning. Of its fourteen uses, some are private and some are public. It can be private doubt: Why do doubts arise in your hearts? (Luke 24:38). It can be open quarrel: An argument arose among them about which of them was the greatest (Luke 9:46). Paul tells the church to do all things without complaining and arguing (Philippians 2:14).

Set beside anger in 2:8, it covers both the silent doubt and the spoken dispute. One sours a man toward his brother. The other sours him toward heaven. Both choke prayer before it gets out of his mouth.

The dust keeps the argument running so the prayer never starts. But look at Luke 24. The risen Christ stood among doubting men, asked why the doubts rose, and said, See my hands and my feet. The argument ends at His wounds, because a God who bled for you can be trusted with what you were arguing about.

stations.verse: In the same way, that women also adorn themselves in decent clothing, with modesty and propriety, not just with braided hair, gold, pearls, or expensive clothing.
stations.question: When I praise the women in my house, do I name the godliness and good works Paul calls their true adorning?
stations.live: Pick your wife, your daughter or your mother. Tell her one good work of godliness you have seen in her this month, plainly and without flattery: ‘I saw what you did. It honored Christ.’
body: Sōphrosynē means soundness of mind, good sense, sanity — the opposite of madness — and so self-control, sobriety. It turns up three times, and two are in this paragraph: modesty and propriety in 2:9, and sanctification with sobriety in 2:15. The third is Paul’s own answer to Festus, that he was not out of his mind but speaking words of truth and reasonableness (Acts 26:25).

So Paul brackets the women’s section with this word. It is a sound mind about what matters — a woman whose worth does not hang on gold or pearls, because her glory is in the good works of a godly life. It is the same sound mind Paul claimed for himself.

The dust teaches men to prize in women what can be bought and worn. That is a man’s sin as much as anyone’s. God prizes the hidden person of the heart (1 Peter 3:4), and a man given a sound mind by grace learns to praise what God praises.

stations.verse: Let a woman learn in quietness with full submission.
stations.question: Where has my own talking kept me from learning God’s word in quietness this past month?
stations.live: At church this Sunday, and in your Bible each morning, say nothing about the passage until you have heard it through twice. Then pray: ‘Teach me before I talk.’
body: Hēsychia is quietness, stillness, silence. A crowd in Jerusalem fell into it when Paul spoke to them in Hebrew (Acts 22:2). Paul uses it twice here, in 2:11 and 2:12. And he lays it on working men in 2 Thessalonians 3:12: that they work with quietness and eat their own bread.

So quietness is not a word for women only. It comes from the same family as the quiet life of 2:2 that Paul wants for the whole church. In 2:11 it is the posture of a learner — someone sitting under the word, letting it teach before she speaks.

The dust says quiet is weakness and the loudest man wins. But the Son of God went to the cross and didn’t open his mouth (Isaiah 53:7), and His silence before His accusers bought your peace. A man made quiet by that grace can finally hear, and what he hears is a Father who has already spoken peace.

practices.title: PRAY FIRST IN YOUR HOUSE
practices.body: The door to the Father is open, and Paul tells the men to walk through it. This week, don’t wait to be asked. Pray aloud at supper yourself. If you are married, take five minutes each night to pray with your wife, even if it comes out clumsy. If you live alone, pray by phone with a brother twice this week. Lead the prayers in your house the way you would take the heavy end of a load. Your children need to hear their father talk to God.

practices.title: SETTLE THE GRUDGE BEFORE YOU PRAY
practices.body: God in Christ forgave you a debt you could never pay. So name the person you are angry with — the brother, the boss, the ex, the neighbor across the fence line. Before you pray tomorrow, forgive him before God by name, out loud. If you owe him an apology for your part, make it this week. Jesus tied prayer and forgiveness together, and a man cannot lift a hand to God that is still curled into a fist. Open it first.

practices.title: HONOR THE WOMEN NEAR YOU
practices.body: Peter calls husbands and wives joint heirs of the grace of life, and Paul honors women who profess godliness with good works. Make a short list of the women of faith God has put in your life — your wife, your mother, the older woman at church who prays for your kids. Thank each one this week, by name, for a specific good work. Then pray for each one by name. Honor is a debt a man pays with his mouth, and it costs him nothing but the words.

practices.title: LEARN IN QUIETNESS YOURSELF
practices.body: God speaks to you in His word, and a learner keeps his mouth shut long enough to hear. Pick one chapter for this week — 1 Timothy 2 will do. Read it every morning without a commentary, a podcast or a phone in reach. Write down one thing it says that you had not seen. On Sunday, listen to the sermon the same way. The quiet life Paul wants for the church starts with men who listen before they hold forth.

practices.title: LEAD BY SERVING
practices.body: The Lord and Teacher washed His disciples’ feet, and He has washed you. If God has given the men the work of leading in His house, then lead the way He did. This week, take on one job at home or church that nobody thanks a man for — the dishes, the nursery, the stacking of chairs, the trip to the shut-in. Do it without mentioning it. Authority in Christ’s house is carried on a servant’s back, the way He carried it to the cross.

title: Without Anger or Doubting
subtitle: from dust to prayer in every place
keyVerse: I desire therefore that the men in every place pray, lifting up holy hands without anger and doubting.

passage.text: I desire therefore that the men in every place pray, lifting up holy hands without anger and doubting.
In the same way, that women also adorn themselves in decent clothing, with modesty and propriety, not just with braided hair, gold, pearls, or expensive clothing,
but with good works, which is appropriate for women professing godliness.
Let a woman learn in quietness with full submission.
But I don’t permit a woman to teach, nor to exercise authority over a man, but to be in quietness.
For Adam was formed first, then Eve.
Adam wasn’t deceived, but the woman, being deceived, has fallen into disobedience;
but she will be saved through her childbearing, if they continue in faith, love, and sanctification with sobriety.

stationsIntro: Read each verse slowly and let it land before you answer it. Most of this week’s words sit in one verse, 2:8, so stay there long enough to let it search your hands.
lifeIntro: Christ has washed your hands, forgiven your debt and opened the Father’s door. What follows is a man walking through that door with his hands up — first in prayer, first in serving, and last in the argument.
lifePulls: The man Christ Jesus opened the way to the Father and lifted His wounded hands over men who had failed Him. Your hands are holy because of His. Lift them, and let the grudge drop on the way up.
prayer: Father, You have opened the way to Yourself through the one Mediator, and I come in His name. Thank You for washing my hands in the blood of Christ when I could not make them clean. I lift them to You now, empty. Take the anger I have carried against the people You have put near me. I let it go, because You forgave me far more. Quiet the argument in my head. I trust You. Teach me to pray first in my house, and to lead by serving, not by force. Thank You for the women of faith You have put in my life. Make me a man who honors them. Teach me to learn in quietness before I speak. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You have opened the way to Yourself through the one Mediator, and I come in His name.
Thank You for washing my hands in the blood of Christ when I could not make them clean.
I lift them to You now, empty.
Take the anger I have carried against the people You have put near me. I let it go, because You forgave me far more.
Quiet the argument in my head. I trust You.
Teach me to pray first in my house, and to lead by serving, not by force.
Thank You for the women of faith You have put in my life. Make me a man who honors them.
Teach me to learn in quietness before I speak.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Paul’s first word to the men is pray — in every place, with holy hands lifted, without anger and doubting. Your hands are holy because Christ washed them. Then Paul honors godly women, adorned with good works and learning the word, and sets order in the church on creation, not on worth. Adam sinned with open eyes, so you have no room to boast. Drop the grudge. End the argument. Lift your hands and go first.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and then lift your hands. Lift them empty, because you have nothing to bring that God needs. Lift them open, because you are not hiding a stone or a grudge in them anymore. Lift them holy — not because you scrubbed them, but because the Holy One has washed them in His own blood. Lift them in every place: at the head of your table, at the side of your bed, on the job site before the crew pulls in, in the waiting room when the news is bad.

The dust has taught you to lead with a set jaw and a closed fist. To carry the grudge home and set it on the supper table. To argue with God in your head and call it thinking. Christ did not lead you that way. He did not come at you in anger. He came with all His patience for the chief of sinners, and He bore the wrath your sin had earned so that none of it would be left over for you. He took the blows so you could have the open hand.

Remember the last thing the disciples saw before He went up. The risen Lord, with the nail marks still in His hands, led them out as far as Bethany, and he lifted up his hands, and blessed them. Then, While he blessed them, he withdrew from them, and was carried up into heaven. The last sight those men had of Him was hands raised in blessing over men who had run away. He has not lowered them. That is still His posture toward you, on your worst morning as much as your best.

So pray this week as a man standing under those hands. Settle the grudge before the sun goes down. Bring the argument to God and leave it there. Honor the women who have prayed for you longer than you have prayed for anyone. Go first in prayer and first in serving, and when your arms get heavy, remember whose hands are raised over you. The word given that day still stands: This Jesus, who was received up from you into the sky, will come back in the same way as you saw him going into the sky — and the hands that blessed at Bethany will be the hands that welcome you home.
closingVerse: I desire therefore that the men in every place pray, lifting up holy hands without anger and doubting.
carry: What grudge or argument are you still holding in your hands this week, when the risen Christ has His own hands lifted over you in blessing?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Read a list like this one and you will do one of two things with it. You will hand it to someone else, or you will hang yourself with it. The first move is easy. This is for the pastor, for the elders, for the men whose names are printed in the bulletin. You stack chairs and give what you can, and the list is none of your business.

The second move comes later, at night, when you read it again and find yourself missing from every line. Without reproach — and you think of the thing nobody at church knows about. The husband of one wife — and you think of the first marriage, the papers, the years you would rather not name. Not a drinker — and you think of the cooler in the back of the shop. Gentle — your son could tell you about gentle. By verse 7 the list has become a fence line, and you are on the wrong side of it.

The dust tells you God hands out a list like this the way a foreman hands out a punch list: finish it, and then you are worth keeping. Or it tells you the list was never about you at all. Both are lies, and both leave a man right where he is. Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a man flat on the floor of that lie: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV)

And the word that revives him is the one Paul has already set over this whole letter: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief. A list written after that sentence is not a gate. It is a portrait of what grace grows in a man — first in the men who lead, and then, through them, in every man who follows.

sections.heading: A Faithful Saying About a Good Work
pulls: The list in 1 Timothy 3 is not a gate you climb over to reach God. It is a portrait of what His grace grows in a man who has already been carried through the gate.
paras: Paul left Timothy at Ephesus to command certain men not to teach a different doctrine. Those men were desiring to be teachers of the law, though they did not understand what they were saying. Wanting the chair was never their problem. Wanting it without the life was. So Paul does not answer bad teachers with a program. He answers them with men of a certain kind.

He calls the man an overseer. Years before, when Paul sent for the leaders of this same church, Acts records that he called to himself the elders of the assembly, and Paul told those elders that the Holy Spirit had made them overseers (Acts 20:17, 28). One office, two names. And Paul opens this chapter with the same words he used for the gospel itself — this is a faithful saying. The trustworthy news that Christ saves sinners came first. The trustworthy news about the men who shepherd those sinners comes second, and it rests on the first.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: A GOOD WORK WORTH WANTING
paras: Someone who seeks to be an overseer desires a good work. Paul does not scold the man who wants it. He calls the wanting good, because the thing wanted is good. But look at what the man wants. Not a seat. Not a title. A work. Oversight in the church is a man bending over other men’s souls the way a farmer bends over a sick calf at two in the morning — not because the calf is his trophy, but because it is his charge.

That changes what desire looks like. The man who wants the title will want the meeting and the vote. The man who wants the work will already be doing it before anyone asks him. He calls the widower on Sunday afternoon. He opens the Bible with the young couple who cannot stop fighting. He prays for other men by name. Desire for this office shows up first as care, long before it shows up as a nomination. If no one ever gives him the title, he will keep doing the work anyway, and he will not keep a tally of it.

And there is a reason the work is good. Someone did it first. Peter writes to scattered believers, you were going astray like sheep; but now you have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls. Christ is the first Overseer. He watched over you while you ran. He came looking, and He found you, and He carried you back on His own shoulders. Every elder in every small church works under that Shepherd, keeping watch over a flock that is not his, bought with blood that was not his. The work is good because it is Christ’s work, put into the hands of ordinary men.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: WITHOUT REPROACH
paras: The overseer therefore must be without reproach. That phrase stands over the whole list like a roof over a barn. Everything after it fills in what it means. And look how plain the rest of verse 2 is: the husband of one wife, temperate, sensible, modest, hospitable, good at teaching. There is nothing here a camera would want. No gift for crowds. No head for money. These are the marks of a man you would trust with your house key. Paul is not hunting for a celebrity. He is looking for a man whose life holds up when you look at it close.

The husband of one wife names a man whose heart and eyes and hands belong to one woman. If you are divorced, or married again, hear this before anything else: your past is not outside the reach of 1:15. The church must weigh hard cases with care, and this page will not rule on yours. But the blood of Christ does not stop at the courthouse door. The faithfulness this verse asks of you begins today, with the wife you have or the purity you keep, and it is fruit of mercy, never the fee for it. And every husband, office or no office, owes his wife a man whose eyes stay home.

Then come four quiet words. Temperate: clear in the head. Sensible means sound in judgment. Modest: ordered and decent, not loud about himself. Hospitable: his door opens. A man like that is not built by willpower. He is grown, the way the fruit of the Spirit grows. Gentleness, and self-control are fruit, and fruit does not come from straining at the branch. It comes from being joined to the vine. Stay joined, and the fruit will come in its season.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: GENTLE IN HIS OWN HOUSE
pulls: The place God grows an elder is the same place He grows every man: the supper table, the back porch, the long drive home. Your house is where your faith is tested before the church ever sees it.
paras: Verse 3 moves from what the man is to what he is not: not a drinker, not violent, not greedy for money, but gentle, not quarrelsome, not covetous. Read it slowly. Nearly every item is a way a man uses his strength on other people. The bottle takes the edge off him and puts it on his family. The slammed door. The argument he has to win. The money he has to have. In the middle of all that noise Paul sets one word, gentle, and lets it stand alone.

Before you are asked to be gentle, see how you have been handled. Christ won’t break a bruised reed. He has ruled you with strength that never crushed you. Now Paul walks the man home: one who rules his own house well, having children in subjection with all reverence. And he gives the reason: how could someone who doesn’t know how to rule one’s own house take care of God’s assembly? Notice the word Paul chooses for the church. He does not say run it. He says take care of it, the way you would care for something that could break.

Your house is where your faith is tested before anyone at church sees it. Your wife knows whether your gentleness is real. Your children know whether your rule is reverent or only loud. That is not a threat. It is a mercy, because the place God grows an elder is the same place He grows every man: the supper table, the back porch, the long drive home from a ballgame. If your house is in pieces, do not perform harder at church. Go home and ask forgiveness first. A man who has been forgiven much can say the words without choking on them.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: ROOTED BEFORE RAISED
paras: Not a new convert, lest being puffed up he fall into the same condemnation as the devil. Paul is not insulting young believers. He is protecting them. A seedling set out in August heat scorches before it roots. Put a man in charge of souls before his roots are down, and the title will do to him what the sun does to the seedling. He will swell. Pride was the devil’s sin before it was ever yours, and it has not changed its methods.

Paul measures maturity by roots, not by birthdays. A man of sixty can be a new plant. A man of thirty can be deep. What tells the difference is the list itself — whether the gentleness, the clear head and the open door have had time to show up in hard weather. God is not in a hurry with you, and the church should not be either.

Then verse 7 turns the man around to face the road: he must have good testimony from those who are outside, to avoid falling into reproach and the snare of the devil. The men at the feed store, the neighbor across the fence, the crew you worked beside for eleven years — they have a vote here. Not on doctrine. On whether you pay what you owe, keep your word, and speak well of people behind their backs.

None of this is a ladder to God. Christ Jesus is the one man whose whole life was without reproach, and He was condemned in your place. Him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf. The testimony that saves you is His. The good testimony your neighbors see in you is the evidence that He is still at work.

stations.verse: This is a faithful saying: someone who seeks to be an overseer desires a good work.
stations.question: When I picture myself serving in Christ’s church, what exactly is my hand reaching for?
stations.live: Write down one thing you have been reaching for at church or at work. Next to it, write who it serves. If the plain answer is you, hand it back to God in one sentence of prayer.
body: Oregō means to reach, to stretch out. Used of a man, it pictures him stretching himself toward something — reaching after it, grasping at it. Only three verses use it, and together they tell a story.

In Hebrews 11:16 the fathers of the faith desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. In 1 Timothy 6:10 the same verb is used of men grasping after money, and they come back pierced with sorrow. Here in 3:1 the reach is toward oversight, and Paul calls it a good work. The arm is the same arm. What it reaches for makes all the difference.

The dust says ambition is either everything or a sin. Oregō says the reach is not the problem; the object is. A man who has been reached for by Christ can stretch toward a work for others without needing it to make him somebody. Christ already made him somebody when He made him His own.

stations.verse: The overseer therefore must be without reproach, the husband of one wife, temperate, sensible, modest, hospitable, good at teaching.
stations.question: Is there a place in my life where someone could take hold of a real fault and use it against the name of Christ?
stations.gloss: above reproach; nothing to take hold of
stations.live: Name one thing a man could grab and hold against Christ’s name in your life — an unpaid debt, a broken promise, a tab you hide. Settle it or confess it before Sunday.
body: Anepilēmptos is built from a negative and the verb epilambanō, to take hold of. A man without reproach gives the accuser nothing to grab. The word is stronger than its near neighbors: it means not only that a man has a good report, but that he deserves it. Every use of it sits in this one letter: 3:2, 5:7 and 6:14.

That does not mean sinless. It means no live handle — no hidden account, no open grudge, no pattern a neighbor could name. Paul uses the word again near the end, charging Timothy to keep the commandment without spot, blameless, until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ.

The dust wants you to believe a man is either spotless or finished. Christ took hold of every charge against you and carried it to the cross. Because nothing can be held against you there, you can stop hiding the handle here and let Him take it away.

stations.verse: The overseer therefore must be without reproach, the husband of one wife, temperate, sensible, modest, hospitable, good at teaching.
stations.question: When someone in my house asks what the Bible says, do I have anything plain and true to hand them?
stations.live: Pick one verse from this week’s passage. Learn it well enough to explain it in two minutes. Then explain it to your wife, your son, or a man at work before the week is out.
body: Didaktikos means apt at teaching, able to teach. Paul uses it twice, and both times he is writing to Timothy. Of all the overseer’s marks, it is the one that is a skill as much as a trait of character.

But look where Paul puts it the second time: The Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, able to teach, patient. Teaching sits between gentle and patient. The man who is able to teach is not the man who wins arguments at the parts counter. He is the man who knows the Word well enough to hand it over plainly and kindly, and then to wait.

The dust says you are no teacher, so leave the Word to the pastor. Every father teaches something, whether he opens his mouth or not. Christ taught you first, slowly and with patience, and you know more of Him than you think.

stations.verse: Not a drinker, not violent, not greedy for money, but gentle, not quarrelsome, not covetous.
stations.question: What does the drink I reach for at the end of the day do to the man my family has to live with?
stations.live: If drink has a grip on your evenings, tell one man this week, plainly. If it does not, ask your wife whether it ever frightens her. Then listen without defending yourself.
body: Paroinos is built on oinos, wine. It describes a man given to wine, a drinker whose evenings keep company with the bottle. Its one other use is Titus 1:7, in another list for overseers, where the World English Bible says not given to wine.

Paul does not say wine is evil. He names a man whose nights belong to it. In the same verse comes not violent, and the two often travel together. The bottle loosens the tongue and the hand, and the people closest to it pay first.

The dust says you need something to take the edge off. Christ offers more than a dulled edge. He gives His Spirit, and Paul sets the two side by side: Don’t be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit. The empty place the drink keeps trying to fill was made for Him.

stations.verse: Not a new convert, lest being puffed up he fall into the same condemnation as the devil.
stations.question: Where have I been trying to look further along in the faith than God has actually grown me?
stations.live: Name one place you have wanted to look further along than you are. Tell God the truth about it, and thank Him for the slow work of roots: ‘You planted me. You will finish it.’
body: Neophytos is built on neos, new, and it means newly planted. The Greek Old Testament uses it of young plants, as in Psalm 128:3, your children like olive plants around your table. This verse is its lone appearance in the apostles’ letters, and here it means a new convert.

Paul’s worry is pride. A plant set out too soon in hard sun does not grow tall; it wilts or it swells. Put a man over souls before his roots are down and the title will puff him up, lest being puffed up he fall. The danger is not his youth. It is the weight laid on him before he can carry it.

The dust says you are behind, that other men are further along and you had better catch up fast. God is a patient farmer. He planted you, and He tends what He plants. He who began a good work in you will complete it. Roots grow in the dark and take seasons. Let them.

practices.title: PRAY FOR YOUR ELDERS BY NAME
practices.body: Christ gave His church overseers as a gift. Thank Him for yours this week, by name. Then pray for them — not for their comfort but for their character. Ask that they would be without reproach, gentle at home, clear in the head, and kept from pride. Pray the list over them line by line. Then tell one of them you did, and ask what you could carry to lighten his load. Men who watch over souls are rarely asked how their own souls are doing.

practices.title: READ THE LIST AT YOUR OWN TABLE
practices.body: Take the words of verses 2 and 3 home. Read them to your wife and ask which of them she sees growing in you, and which one she most wants to see. Do not argue with her answer. Thank her for it. Your house is the first place God grows this list in a man, and the people under your roof see it before anyone at church does. Pray over her answer before you go to sleep.

practices.title: OPEN YOUR DOOR
practices.body: The overseer is to be hospitable, and so is every man who has been welcomed by Christ. Even His enemies said of Him, This man welcomes sinners, and eats with them. Invite someone to your table this week who cannot pay you back — a widower, a new family, a younger man from church. Keep it simple. Burgers in the backyard count. An open door is a sermon your neighbors can read, and it costs less than you fear.

practices.title: CHECK YOUR NAME ON THE ROAD
practices.body: Verse 7 asks for good testimony from those outside the church. Think of the men who know you away from Sunday — your boss, your crew, the man you sold the tractor to. Is there a debt unpaid, a promise broken, a deal you shaded? Pick one and set it right this week. Do it as a man Christ has already set right, because His name is on you now and goes wherever you go.

practices.title: WATER A NEW PLANT
practices.body: Find one man newer to the faith than you. Do not hand him a church job. Hand him your time. Read a chapter of this letter with him once this week, and talk about what it says Christ has done before you talk about what it asks of him. Roots grow slowly and out of sight. Be the man who brings the water and then waits, the way someone once waited on you.

title: Above Reproach
subtitle: from dust to a life worth following
keyVerse: This is a faithful saying: someone who seeks to be an overseer desires a good work.

passage.text: This is a faithful saying: someone who seeks to be an overseer desires a good work.
The overseer therefore must be without reproach, the husband of one wife, temperate, sensible, modest, hospitable, good at teaching;
not a drinker, not violent, not greedy for money, but gentle, not quarrelsome, not covetous;
one who rules his own house well, having children in subjection with all reverence;
(but how could someone who doesn’t know how to rule one’s own house take care of God’s assembly?)
not a new convert, lest being puffed up he fall into the same condemnation as the devil.
Moreover he must have good testimony from those who are outside, to avoid falling into reproach and the snare of the devil.

stationsIntro: These five words come from one short list, and each one is a mirror before it is a measure. Read the verse, answer the question plainly, and let the Greek send you back to the grace that made you before it tells you what to become.
lifeIntro: God has already given you the Shepherd and Overseer of your soul, and He has put His Spirit in you to grow what this list describes. These practices do not earn a place. They make room for fruit.
lifePulls: Every line of this list was first a line in the life of Christ. He is the Overseer who watched over you while you ran, and the marks He asks of you are the ones He is growing in you.
prayer: Father, You sent Christ Jesus into the world to save sinners, and I am one of them. He is the Shepherd and Overseer of my soul, and He came looking for me while I ran. Thank You for the men You have set over Your church here. Keep them without reproach, gentle at home, clear in mind, and free from pride. Where my house carries the marks of my temper or my silence, give me the courage to ask forgiveness first. Keep the drink, the money and the need to win from ruling me. Grow in me what this list describes, not so I can earn a place with You, but because I already have one in Christ. Root me deep before You raise me up, and guard me from the snare of the devil. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You sent Christ Jesus into the world to save sinners, and I am one of them.
He is the Shepherd and Overseer of my soul, and He came looking for me while I ran.
Thank You for the men You have set over Your church here. Keep them without reproach, gentle at home, clear in mind, and free from pride.
Where my house carries the marks of my temper or my silence, give me the courage to ask forgiveness first.
Keep the drink, the money and the need to win from ruling me.
Grow in me what this list describes, not so I can earn a place with You, but because I already have one in Christ.
Root me deep before You raise me up, and guard me from the snare of the devil.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Paul calls the overseer’s work good, and then he describes the man who does it: without reproach, faithful to one wife, sober, gentle, open-handed, able to teach, rooted, well thought of on the road. The list is for elders first. It is also the shape of every man Christ is growing. It is fruit of His mercy, never a ladder to it. Go home first. Let the roots go down.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, to the One who met this list before you ever read it. Look at the man who was without reproach, whose enemies searched for a charge and had to bring in false witnesses to make one. Look at the man who was gentle, who would not break a bruised reed or snuff out a dimly burning wick. Look at the man who opened His table to sinners and taught them with patience. Look at the man who was never a new plant in any of this, because He was the Word before the first seed fell into the ground.

The dust has handed you this chapter as a verdict. You read without reproach and you remember. You read the husband of one wife and old papers come up out of the drawer. You read gentle and you hear your own voice in the hallway last Tuesday night. The list feels like a door with your name scratched off the frame. But this list was never meant to stand alone. It stands under 1:15, and 1:15 stands over you: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief.

So look at what He did with your reproach. He took it. He was counted a sinner so you could be counted clean, and He went down into death carrying charges you could never answer. The grave could not keep Him. He walked out of it alive, and He lives now as the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls. He watches over you tonight the way no elder ever could — without sleep, without favorites, without ever growing tired of you. He knows His sheep by name, and yours is on His lips.

And He is coming again. Peter tells the men who keep His flock that when the chief Shepherd is revealed, you will receive the crown of glory that doesn’t fade away. Hold that on Tuesday. The Overseer of your soul will appear, and every man He has grown will stand before Him clothed in His record, not his own. The elder and the man who stacks the chairs will wear the same robe, and neither of them will have woven it. Go home. Be gentle. Open the door. The good work is His, and He will finish it.
closingVerse: This is a faithful saying: someone who seeks to be an overseer desires a good work.
carry: Which line of this list have you been using to keep yourself at a distance from God, when Christ has already met it for you and is growing it in you by His Spirit?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: There is a kind of man every church runs on and almost nobody names. He unlocks the building at six. He fixes the leak over the nursery. He drives the van to the nursing home, carries the casserole to the widow, and knows which family is behind on the light bill and sees that it gets paid without a word. He will never preach. He is not sure his name is written down anywhere. If you asked him, he would say he just helps out.

The dust has two things to say to that man. The first is that his work does not count — that the real ministry happens up front, and he is only the help. The second is worse, because it sounds like praise. It tells him his service is how he keeps his place. Every Saturday at the church is a deposit. Every fixed pipe buys a little more standing with God. Miss a few weeks and the balance runs low. Let a younger man take over the van route and he wonders whether God still needs him.

Both lies leave a man tired. One empties his work of meaning. The other loads it with a weight it was never built to carry. Worn flat between them, you have only the old words left to pray: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV)

And the word that revives him comes at the end of this passage. Paul says those who serve well do gain a standing. But he says where their boldness rests: in the faith which is in Christ Jesus. The work matters. The ground under it is Christ. Paul has already told you what kind of ground that is: The grace of our Lord abounded exceedingly.

sections.heading: Servants in the Same Way
pulls: The dust tells the man at the back of the church that his work does not count, or that it is how he earns his place. Paul tells him something better: the standing is real, and it rests in Christ Jesus.
paras: Paul has just described the overseer. Now he turns to a second group with three words: Servants, in the same way. The World English Bible calls them servants, which is the plain sense of the office most churches call deacon. Paul greets the same two groups in another letter, writing to the saints at Philippi with the overseers and servants, so the pattern was not unique to Ephesus.

Scripture does not hand over a full job description for these men. Acts 6 gives a picture of the kind of work: the apostles asked the church to select from among you, brothers, seven men of good report, full of the Holy Spirit and of wisdom, so that widows would be fed and the Word would not be neglected. What 1 Timothy gives instead is character. Paul cares less about what the servant does with his hands than about what kind of man the hands belong to.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: ONE TONGUE, ONE HAND
paras: Servants, in the same way, must be reverent, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for money. In the same way. The servant is held to the same kind of life as the overseer. There is no second shelf of holiness for the men who set out the folding tables. Every office in the church is service, and every servant answers to the same Lord. The man with the keys to the building and the man with the pulpit Bible kneel at the same rail.

Look at the shape of the list. Reverent: a man who carries weight because he takes God seriously, not himself. Not double-tongued: the same story to the pastor and to the men at the fuel pump. Not addicted to much wine. Not greedy for money. Most of it has to do with what comes out of a man’s mouth or into his hand. A servant handles people’s trouble and, often enough, people’s money. He hears things. He knows who is behind on rent and whose marriage is cracking. If his tongue splits and his hand closes, the people he serves get hurt at the very place they are weakest.

But hear what comes before the charge. The Lord these men serve is the One of whom Peter writes, neither was deceit found in his mouth. He never told one man one thing and another man something else. He never reached for gain. He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and went lower than any deacon will ever have to go. Every servant in His church works under a Master who has already done the hard part, and who does not ask a man to kneel anywhere He has not knelt first.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: A HELD FAITH, A CLEAN CONSCIENCE
paras: Verse 9 goes underneath the behavior: holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience. A servant is not only a pair of hands. He holds something. The mystery of the faith is what God once kept hidden and has now made known in Christ, and Paul will open it wide a few verses on. Here he wants to know where the man keeps it. In a pure conscience.

That joins two things men like to pull apart. Some men hold the truth tightly and live loosely; the doctrine is clean and the conscience is a junk drawer. Other men keep a tender conscience and vague beliefs. Paul will have neither. The faith is held in a clean conscience the way water is held in a whole bucket. Knock a hole in the bucket and it does not matter how good the water was. You will carry it across the yard and arrive with nothing.

So where does a clean conscience come from? Not from working harder to feel innocent. Hebrews answers plainly: how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without defect to God, cleanse your conscience from dead works to serve the living God? Watch the order. First the blood cleanses. Then the cleansed man serves. A servant in Christ’s church does not scrub his own conscience to qualify. He brings it to the cross, has it washed, and then picks up the toolbox.

This is the line between service and slavery. The man who serves to get clean will never feel clean enough. The man who has been made clean serves because the weight is already gone. He can carry a neighbor’s load, because his own was lifted off at the cross.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: TESTED FIRST, AT HOME TOO
pulls: Before any man in the church tests you, God has already declared you blameless in His Son. The testing does not decide your standing. It shows what His grace has been growing in you.
paras: Let them also first be tested; then let them serve if they are blameless. A testing comes before the work. Not an exam with a pass mark, and not a trap. It is the church watching a man over time, the way a crew watches a new hand for a season before anyone gives him the keys to the skid steer. You do not test him because you hope he fails. You test him because people are going to lean on him.

Then Paul turns to the house. Their wives in the same way must be reverent, not slanderers, temperate, and faithful in all things. And: Let servants be husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own houses well. A man’s service at church does not happen in a sealed room. His home is the first place the testing happens, and his wife stands beside him in it. If he is kind at the food pantry and cold at his own supper table, the test has been given already. The church does not need to invent a trial for him. His own kitchen has been running one for years.

Every man reading this is being tested, office or no office. Your wife hears how you speak of other people. Your children see whether your faith and your money point the same direction. That is not a cause for fear. It is the slow, ordinary way God proves what He has grown. And the blamelessness Paul asks of servants is first a gift before it is ever a reputation. Christ has reconciled in the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and without defect and blameless before him. Before any man tests you, God has already declared you clear in His Son.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: A GOOD STANDING AND GREAT BOLDNESS
paras: For those who have served well gain for themselves a good standing, and great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus. Paul ends with a promise, not a warning. Service done well is not wasted. It gains something. The hours spent in the church kitchen and the cold mornings in the parking lot are not poured out on the ground.

It gains a good standing: a step, a footing, a place to stand among the people of God. The man who has served for twenty years without a title is not invisible. The church knows where he stands, and so does God. But this footing is not a rung on a ladder leaning against heaven. No man climbs into the favor of God by setting up tables. The ladder runs the other way, and Christ came down it. He humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. Every step down was a step toward you.

It also gains great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus. A man who has served faithfully does not grow proud of his record. He grows bold in his Lord. He has watched Christ keep him through a hundred small obediences and a hundred failures, and he speaks of Him with less fear. That boldness has no swagger in it. It rests where every believer’s boldness rests: In him we have boldness and access in confidence through our faith in him.

So the servant’s reward is real, and it was never the price of his salvation. Jesus said, I am among you as one who serves. Kneel where He knelt. You will find the ground under your knees is solid rock. It is the same ground He stood on when He rose.

stations.verse: Servants, in the same way, must be reverent, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for money.
stations.question: When I talk about a man who is not in the room, would I say the same words if he walked in?
stations.live: This week, catch yourself the first time you say something about a man that you would not say to his face. Go back and either say it to him plainly or take it back.
body: Dilogos is built from dis and legō. Outside the Bible it could describe a man given to repeating himself. In its single New Testament use, here, it most likely means double-tongued — near kin to the talebearer of Proverbs 11:13, who betrays a confidence.

A double-tongued man says one thing to the pastor and another in the parking lot. He agrees with the man in front of him and corrects him behind his back. In a servant this does deep harm, because he goes from house to house and hears the troubles of many families. A split tongue carries poison between homes.

The dust says a little shading keeps the peace. Christ never spoke two ways to you. His word to sinners has always been one word, and He kept it at the cross. A man held by that word can afford to say one thing himself, in every room he walks into.

stations.verse: Servants, in the same way, must be reverent, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for money.
stations.question: Where am I willing to take a dollar that I would not want my pastor to watch me take?
stations.live: Look over one invoice, expense report or tax line you filled out this year. If anything on it is shaded, fix it this week and pay what you owe, without excuses.
body: Aischrokerdēs is made from aischros and kerdos, and it means greedy of base gain. It names a man who will take money the low way. Titus 1:7 is the only other place it is found, and there the World English Bible renders it greedy for dishonest gain.

Servants in the church often handle money and always handle need. A man hungry for shameful profit will find a way to make the need pay him. At work it looks like a padded invoice, cash off the books, a deal shaded so the other man does not notice.

The dust says you have to look out for yourself because nobody else will. Christ looked out for you at the cost of everything He had: the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. A man bought that dearly does not need to cheat for a few dollars more.

stations.verse: Let them also first be tested; then let them serve if they are blameless.
stations.question: When I am being watched and tested by others, where do I find ground that lets me stand without fear?
stations.gloss: blameless; with no charge against him
stations.live: Ask an older man at church to tell you one thing he has seen in you that concerns him. Thank him. Then say it aloud: ‘No charge can stand against me in Christ. I can hear this.’
body: Anenklētos is built from a negative and enkaleō. It means not to be called to account: a man against whom no charge sticks. Paul uses it five times, and three of them sit in his lists for leaders in the church.

The other two carry the gospel. Christ died to present you holy and without defect and blameless before him, and Paul promises that He will also confirm you until the end, blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. The church tests a servant to see whether he is blameless before men. God has already made him blameless before Himself.

The dust says you are one charge away from ruin. In Christ every charge has been brought, answered and paid. Who could bring a charge against God’s chosen ones? It is God who justifies. Let the church test you. You have nothing left to hide, and nothing left to prove to the One who already declared you clear.

stations.verse: Their wives in the same way must be reverent, not slanderers, temperate, and faithful in all things.
stations.question: What did I say about another person this week that did the accuser’s work for him?
stations.live: For one week, say nothing about anyone that you have not first said about him to God in prayer. When you catch yourself, stop mid-sentence: ‘That is not my trade anymore.’
body: Diabolos means slanderous, one who accuses falsely. As a noun it names a slanderer, and in the Greek Old Testament it usually stands for Satan, the Accuser. It turns up thirty-five times between Matthew and Revelation. In 3:11 it is the word behind not slanderers. Four verses earlier, the same word names the snare of the devil.

Paul uses one word for the devil and for the slanderer, and the overlap is the point. When a tongue tears down another person, it is doing the devil’s trade. The side comment about the pastor’s wife. The story of a brother’s failure told one time too many. The grudge passed along as a prayer request.

The dust says it is only talk. But the Accuser has met his match. Christ took on flesh that through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death, that is, the devil. You belong to the One who silenced the accuser. Do not keep his shop open.

stations.verse: For those who have served well gain for themselves a good standing, and great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus.
stations.question: What standing am I still trying to earn from God that Christ has already secured for me?
stations.live: Name one quiet service you did this year that nobody thanked you for. Thank God for the chance to do it, and say plainly: ‘My standing is in Christ. This was a gift, not a payment.’
body: Bathmos comes from bainō, to step. It means a step, and from there a degree or a standing. The Greek Old Testament uses it for the steps on the sundial of Ahaz, when the shadow went ten steps backward as a sign to Hezekiah. This verse is its lone appearance in the New Testament.

Paul says the man who serves well gains a good step — a place to stand among God’s people, a footing the church knows and trusts. Faithful service is not wasted. Over the years it lays down solid ground under a man, and others learn to put their weight on it.

The dust turns that step into a ladder and tells you to climb toward God. But no rung reaches heaven. Christ came down every step to the cross, rose again, and was lifted to the right hand of the Father, and He is your standing there. Service gives you footing among men. Grace has already given you footing with God.

practices.title: SAY ONE THING IN EVERY ROOM
practices.body: Christ never spoke two ways to you. This week, check your tongue against verse 8. Before you speak of anyone who is absent — the pastor, your boss, your brother-in-law — ask whether you would say it with him standing beside you, close enough to hear. If not, keep it to yourself, or go say it to him with care. Let one word go out of you in every room, the same word, and see what it does to your sleep.

practices.title: OPEN THE BOOKS AT HOME
practices.body: Servants in Paul’s church were not to be greedy for money. Sit down with your wife this week and go over the money together: what comes in, what goes out, and where it goes. Hide nothing. If there is a debt or an account she does not know about, tell her now. A man whose ransom has been paid in full does not need a secret drawer, and his wife should never have to wonder.

practices.title: ASK TO BE TESTED
practices.body: Verse 10 says servants are tested first. Do not wait to be examined; invite it. Ask an elder or an older man you respect to watch your life for a season and tell you what he sees. Do not argue with him. You have already been declared blameless in Christ, which means you can afford to hear where you are not yet what grace is making you. A man with nothing left to defend can listen.

practices.title: GUARD THE ABSENT
practices.body: Verse 11 forbids slander, which is the devil’s own trade. This week, when the talk at work or after church turns against someone who is not there to answer, be the man who changes the subject or speaks one true good word about him. If you know something against him, take it to him, not to the room. Christ has silenced the accuser for you. You do not have to run the accuser’s errands for anyone else.

practices.title: SERVE WHERE NO ONE IS LOOKING
practices.body: Christ took a towel at supper and washed feet that would run from Him by morning. Pick one job at church this week that nobody wants and nobody will thank you for — the restrooms, the gutters at the widow’s house, the parking lot after a storm. Do it well. Do not mention it. Your standing with God was settled at the cross. This is a son working in his Father’s house, with nothing to prove and nothing to buy.

title: Tested First
subtitle: from dust to a good standing in Christ
keyVerse: For those who have served well gain for themselves a good standing, and great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus.

passage.text: Servants, in the same way, must be reverent, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for money,
holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience.
Let them also first be tested; then let them serve if they are blameless.
Their wives in the same way must be reverent, not slanderers, temperate, and faithful in all things.
Let servants be husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own houses well.
For those who have served well gain for themselves a good standing, and great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus.

stationsIntro: Five words from Paul’s short list for servants, each one a test and each one met first in Christ. Read the verse, sit with the question, and let the Greek send you back to the grace that holds you up.
lifeIntro: This week is not about earning a title in the church or a higher rung with God. Christ has already taken the form of a servant and secured your standing with the Father. These practices are the ordinary work of a man who stands on that ground.
lifePulls: Christ knelt with a towel before He was nailed to a cross. Every servant in His church kneels where He knelt, and finds the ground under his knees is solid rock.
prayer: Father, Your Son came not to be served but to serve, and He gave His life as a ransom for me. He knelt with a towel and went down to the cross, and You raised Him up and seated Him at Your right hand. Thank You that my standing with You rests on Him and not on my work. Make my tongue single. Where I have said one thing to a man’s face and another behind his back, forgive me. Loosen my grip on money, and keep me from taking any gain I would have to hide. Wash my conscience in His blood, so I can serve You clean and not afraid. Keep the men and women who serve our church faithful in all things, and make me faithful beside them. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, Your Son came not to be served but to serve, and He gave His life as a ransom for me.
He knelt with a towel and went down to the cross, and You raised Him up and seated Him at Your right hand.
Thank You that my standing with You rests on Him and not on my work.
Make my tongue single. Where I have said one thing to a man’s face and another behind his back, forgive me.
Loosen my grip on money, and keep me from taking any gain I would have to hide.
Wash my conscience in His blood, so I can serve You clean and not afraid.
Keep the men and women who serve our church faithful in all things, and make me faithful beside them.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Paul holds the servants of the church to the same kind of life as the overseers: reverent, single-tongued, sober, free from shameful gain, holding the faith in a clean conscience, tested first, faithful at home. Service done well is never wasted. It gains a footing among God’s people and boldness in Christ. But it never buys standing with God. Christ went down every step to the cross so you could stand.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and watch the Servant who went first. See Him rise from supper and lay aside His outer garments. See Him wrap a towel around His waist and pour water into the basin. See Him kneel at the feet of men who would scatter before morning, and wash the road dust from every one of them, the betrayer’s feet included. See Him stand again, and walk out into the dark toward a cross He could have refused.

The dust told you your service was too small to count, or else that it was the coin you paid to stay in God’s favor. Look at the basin. The Lord of glory did not serve to earn a standing. He already had one, and it was the highest there is. He served because He loved you. He went down every step — the towel, the trial, the whip, the cross, the grave — until there was nowhere lower to go, and He went that low for the man who still keeps score.

Then the Father raised Him. The tomb that took Him could not hold Him, and He did not climb a ladder out of it; He was lifted. He has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God, and from there He lives forever to make intercession for every servant in His church — for the man who unlocks the doors at six, for the man who carries the casserole, and for the man who forgot to do either this week and feels it. He prays for you by name, and He has never once been too tired to ask the Father for you.

So here is what you can hold on Tuesday. Paul promises that He will also confirm you until the end, blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. Blameless. Not because you passed every test, but because He passed them all and then handed you His record. Go and serve without fear. Pick up the towel. Fill the basin. Your standing is not on a ladder. It is in Him, at the right hand of the Father, and nothing can move Him from there. On the day He appears, He will not ask you for your hours. He will call you His own.
closingVerse: For those who have served well gain for themselves a good standing, and great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus.
carry: What service have you been carrying as a payment to God, when Christ has already gone down every step for you and hands you a towel instead of a ladder?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Most men think godliness is a project. A list taped inside a cabinet door. Read more, pray longer, lose your temper less, quit the second drink. You have bought the books on being a better husband and a steadier father, and a few of them helped for a week. Then the old man came back to work in your boots, the temper flared over supper, the phone stayed lit past midnight, and the list went into the drawer with the others.

The dust says godliness is something you build — that if you find the right method and grind long enough, you will finally become the man God wants, and He will finally be glad to see you. So you keep a ledger. Good weeks go in one column and bad weeks in the other, and you never quite know what the total says. That ledger has worn a groove in you, and you lie in it, face to the dirt, with nothing left to say but this: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV)

The reviving word of 1 Timothy 3 is that the secret of godliness has a name, and the name is not yours. Paul stops in the middle of his instructions about overseers and deacons and breaks into confession: the mystery of godliness is great. Then he tells you what the mystery is. God was revealed in the flesh. Before Paul says another word about how a man ought to live, he points you to the God who came down to live among men.

sections.heading: A Church Manual With a Song in the Middle
pulls: The dust says godliness is a project you build until God is finally glad to see you. Paul says the mystery of godliness is a Person, and He came down into the flesh to find you.
paras: For three chapters Paul has been setting the church in order — false teachers, prayer, men and women in worship, the men who would oversee and the men who would serve. He left Timothy at Ephesus to deal with all of it (1:3). He hoped to come himself before long. In case he was held up, he wrote it down. Timothy was a young man with a hard post and false teachers to face, and Paul gave him what he would need when no one else was there.

Then, before the warnings of chapter 4, he lays out what holds the whole letter up. Six short lines about Christ: His coming in the flesh, His vindication, His being seen, preached, believed, and received up. Paul does not argue for them. He states them, the way a man reads off the names on a deed. Every rule before these lines and every charge after them leans on them. Read chapters 3 and 4 of 1 Timothy in one sitting this week, and notice how the instruction stops to worship before it goes on.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: WHEN A LETTER HAS TO STAND IN
paras: These things I write to you, hoping to come to you shortly. Paul wanted to be in the room. He wanted to put a hand on Timothy’s shoulder and walk him through it. He could not, so he wrote. A letter is what a man sends when he cannot get there himself, and this letter had to carry his full weight.

That is still how Christ orders His church. You do not get Paul at the door. You get his words, and they are enough. That you may know how men ought to behave themselves in God’s house. Notice what he calls the church before he says one more word about conduct. He calls it God’s house. A household. Not a club you joined or a business you pay into, but the home of a Father who has taken in sons. That order matters for you. Paul does not tell Timothy how men ought to behave so they can earn a way in. The behavior is for men already under the roof. You were brought in by mercy — Paul himself was, of whom I am chief — and then you are taught the ways of the house. A family has its ways because a Father sits at the head of the table, and the sons learn them by living there. No son earns his place at that table. He is born or brought into it.

So when you read the charges in this letter — to overseers, to deacons, to men and women, to the rich, to Timothy himself — do not read them as the bar you must clear to be let in. Read them as the shape of a house you already live in, built by the One who carried you through the door.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE PILLAR AND THE GROUND
paras: Which is the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth. Paul stacks up the names. God’s house. The assembly of the living God. Then two building words: pillar and ground. A pillar holds a load up where it can be seen. A footing keeps it from shifting. God has set His truth on the church the way a roof is set on posts.

That is a heavy sentence for a small congregation in a rented hall with a coffee pot that leaks. But the weight does not come from the people. It comes from the God they belong to. He is the living God, and He has chosen to hold His truth up in the world through ordinary men and women gathered around His word. The church does not make the truth. It carries it, and it is carried by it.

This cuts against two errors in you. One is the man who thinks he can keep the faith alone — a Bible on the dash and no one in his life who can ask him a hard question. Paul knows nothing of a solo Christian. The truth stands on a pillar, and the pillar is the assembly. The other error is the man who thinks the whole thing rests on him, that if he slips the truth falls down. It will not. The house is God’s, the truth is His, and under it all lies Jesus Christ Himself, the one foundation, laid once and laid for good (1 Corinthians 3:11).
So go to church this week as a man going home. You are not going there to be graded. You are going to stand with other men under a truth none of you holds up alone.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: THE MYSTERY HAS A NAME
pulls: There is a Man in glory right now with scars in His hands. He came all the way down into your flesh, and He went all the way back up still wearing it. Your godliness hangs on Him.
paras: Without controversy, the mystery of godliness is great. Paul has been talking about conduct. Now he names its root. In his letters a mystery is no riddle. It is a secret God kept and has now opened: the mystery which has been hidden for ages and generations. But now it has been revealed to his saints (Colossians 1:26).

Here is the first line of the secret. God was revealed in the flesh. Godliness starts with God coming down into a body — hands, lungs, a back that ached from a carpenter’s bench, skin that could be torn, feet that walked dirt roads — and never with a man climbing up toward Him. The eternal Son took real flesh, and in that flesh He lived the obedient life you have not lived and died the death you had coming.

The next line: justified in the spirit. The men who tried Him called Him a blasphemer and nailed Him up. They sealed the tomb and set a guard. The grave could not keep Him. When the Father raised Him, the verdict of that courtroom was thrown out. Paul says Christ was declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:4). Heaven reversed earth’s sentence. And because He was declared in the right, you who trust Him are declared righteous in Him. He was raised for our justification (Romans 4:25).

So your godliness can never be a project you finish. It is the life of Another, given to you, growing from a root you did not plant. The obedience you owed, He gave. The verdict you could not win, He won. What grows in you now grows from Him.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: SEEN, PREACHED, BELIEVED, RECEIVED UP
paras: Four more lines finish the song. Seen by angels. Angels praised God over the shepherds’ field the night He was born, and angels were waiting at the empty tomb to tell the women, He is not here, for he has risen (Matthew 28:6). Heaven watched every step, from the cradle to the stone rolled back.

Preached among the nations, believed on in the world. The news did not stay in one country. It went out on the roads and across the water to Jews and Greeks, slaves and masters, rich and poor, to a town like Lystra, where a young man with a Greek father and a believing mother heard it (Acts 16:1). And it reached you. A man in your county, with your history, heard about Christ and believed. That line of the song has your name somewhere in it.

Received up in glory. The Christ who came down was taken back up, in the same body, and sat down at the Father’s right hand. He did not shed the flesh like a coat when the work was done. There is a Man in glory right now with scars in His hands, and He is there for you. He lives forever to make intercession for them (Hebrews 7:25), and you are among them.

This is the mystery of godliness. Not a better version of you. A risen, reigning Christ who came all the way down and went all the way up, and who carries in Himself everything your godliness will ever be. Look at Him long enough and you will begin to look like Him. That is the order of the whole letter: first the Christ who came, then the man He is making.

stations.verse: But if I wait long, that you may know how men ought to behave themselves in God’s house, which is the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
stations.question: Where in my life have I been trying to hold up the truth alone, apart from the assembly God set as its pillar?
stations.live: Name one man in your church you have kept at arm’s length. Call him this week, ask how he is really doing, and tell him one thing you have been carrying alone.
body: Stylos is a pillar, a column regarded above all as a support. Four verses use it: of James, Cephas and John, who were reputed to be pillars (Galatians 2:9); of an angel with feet like pillars of fire (Revelation 10:1); of the man who overcomes; and here.

Paul sets the word on the church as a whole. Not on Timothy, not on the strongest man in the pews. The assembly lifts the truth where the world can see it. Your part is to stand in that row, shoulder to shoulder with other men, not to carry the roof by yourself.

The dust says you are the only thing holding your house up, and that you are cracking. Christ answers with a promise: He who overcomes, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and he will go out from there no more. You are not the builder. He sets you in place, and He does not move you out.

stations.verse: But if I wait long, that you may know how men ought to behave themselves in God’s house, which is the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
stations.question: What am I resting my full weight on when the ground under my life begins to shift beneath my feet?
stations.live: When your heart runs cold this week, say it aloud before you do anything else: ‘My footing is Christ, not how I feel this morning.’
body: Hedraiōma appears nowhere else in the New Testament. It means a support, a bulwark, a stay — what sits under a load and keeps it from sliding. The World English Bible renders it ground.

Paul pairs it with the pillar. One lifts the truth up. The other holds it steady. A man who has poured a footing knows the difference: the post gets seen, but the footing does its quiet work below the frost line. The church is both. It shows the truth, and it keeps the truth from drifting with every new wind that blows through town.

The dust wants you to build on what you can feel — your mood, your record, last Sunday’s warmth. All of it shifts. The truth the church stands under does not, because it is about Christ, and no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 3:11). He is the ground under the ground.

stations.verse: Without controversy, the mystery of godliness is great: God was revealed in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, and received up in glory.
stations.question: Do I hold the facts about Christ as settled ground, even on the mornings when my own heart feels anything but settled?
stations.live: Write the six lines of 1 Timothy 3:16 on a card. Read them aloud each morning this week before you look at your phone, as a man joining a confession, not inventing one.
body: Homologoumenōs is an adverb, and this is the only verse in the New Testament that has it. It means confessedly — as agreed, by common consent. The World English Bible gives it as without controversy.

Paul is not saying no one ever argued about Christ. Men argued all the way to the cross. He is saying that among the people of God this is the shared confession, the thing every believer says together. You do not have to invent your faith or hold it up by your own certainty. You join a confession already standing, and you add your voice to it.

The dust thrives on a doubt that never says its name. It hints that the gospel is still an open question, that your faith is only as strong as your feelings this week. Paul plants a stake in the ground. Christ came. Christ was raised. Christ is reigning. That is settled, and your wavering does not unsettle it.

stations.verse: Without controversy, the mystery of godliness is great: God was revealed in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, and received up in glory.
stations.question: When I think about becoming a more godly man, how much of my thinking actually begins with Christ?
stations.live: Before you try to fix one habit this week, read one Gospel account of Christ each day, slowly. Let reverence for Him come before effort for Him, and let the effort grow out of what you see.
body: Eusebeia first meant reverence and in the New Testament it means reverence toward God: godliness. In Isaiah 11:2 the Greek Old Testament uses it to render the fear of the LORD. Of the fifteen New Testament verses that carry it, eight are in this letter.

So godliness is not polish. It is a man’s whole life bent toward God in reverent fear. And Paul says this godliness has a mystery at its center — the Christ who came in the flesh. Reverence grows where Christ is seen.

The dust wants godliness without Christ: a form you can keep up by grit. Paul warns of men holding a form of godliness, but having denied its power (2 Timothy 3:5). Peter tells you where the real thing comes from: his divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness. Granted. Given. Start there.

stations.verse: Without controversy, the mystery of godliness is great: God was revealed in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, and received up in glory.
stations.question: How would an ordinary Tuesday change if I believed that a living Man is reigning in glory for me right now?
stations.live: When fear about the future rises this week, take up the shield on purpose. Say aloud: ‘Jesus was received up in glory, and He is coming back the same way.’
body: Analambanō means to take up, to raise. Acts uses it three times in its first chapter for the day Christ was received up (Acts 1:2, 11, 22). It can also mean to take something up for oneself, as in taking up the shield of faith (Ephesians 6:16).

The ascension finishes what the cross began. The Christ who went down into the grave was lifted into glory, in His body, and seated at the Father’s right hand. He is not absent. He is enthroned, and from there He keeps His people and pleads for them.

The dust tells you heaven is far off and Christ is a memory. The two men in white told the disciples otherwise: This Jesus, who was received up from you into the sky, will come back in the same way as you saw him going into the sky. The One taken up will come again, bodily and once. Until then, take up the shield.

practices.title: READ THE SONG ALOUD
practices.body: Copy the six lines of 1 Timothy 3:16 onto a card and put it where you start your day — the visor, the tool bench, the bathroom mirror. Read it out loud every morning: God was revealed in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, and received up in glory. You are not reciting a fact sheet. You are joining a confession the church has spoken since Paul first wrote it down.

practices.title: GO TO GOD’S HOUSE AS A SON
practices.body: Paul calls the church the assembly of the living God. Go this Sunday as a son coming home, not as a spectator or a critic. Get there early, before the parking lot fills. Sit closer to the front than you usually do. Before the service begins, pray for the man preaching and for the man in the pew beside you by name. If you do not know his name, learn it before you leave the building.

practices.title: STAND BESIDE ANOTHER MAN
practices.body: The pillar is the assembly, not the loner. Pick one man in your church and ask him to meet you once this week — breakfast at the diner, coffee at the feed store, a walk along the fence line. Do not wait for the perfect man; pick the one God has put near you. Tell him one true thing you have been carrying alone, and ask him to pray for it. Then ask what he is carrying, and pray for that before the two of you part.

practices.title: TRADE ONE METHOD FOR ONE LOOK
practices.body: Name the method you have been leaning on to make yourself godly — a reading plan you grind through, a list of rules, a book you keep going back to. Set it down for one week. You can pick it back up later if it still serves. Each day, read one chapter of a Gospel and ask one thing of it: what does this show me of the Christ who came in the flesh? Let your godliness grow from looking at Him.

practices.title: LOOK UP ONCE A DAY
practices.body: Christ was received up in glory, and He is coming back the same way. Once a day this week, step outside — the porch at dawn, the job site at lunch, the back field at dusk — and look up at the sky for one full minute, without the phone in your hand. Say it plainly: ‘He is reigning now, and He is coming back.’ Then go back to the work in front of you as a man whose King has not gone missing.

title: God Revealed in the Flesh
subtitle: from dust to the mystery of godliness
keyVerse: Without controversy, the mystery of godliness is great: God was revealed in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, and received up in glory.

passage.text: These things I write to you, hoping to come to you shortly;
but if I wait long, that you may know how men ought to behave themselves in God’s house, which is the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
