Without controversy, the mystery of godliness is great: God was revealed in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, and received up in glory.

stationsIntro: These five words hold up one of the fullest sentences Paul ever wrote about Christ. Read the verse first and let it settle, then let the Greek press it a little deeper into you.
lifeIntro: God came down into the flesh, was raised and received up, and has set you in His house among His people. These five practices take that seriously this week. Each one starts with what He has done, and none of them asks you to climb toward a God who has already come down to you.
lifePulls: Godliness is not the price you pay to get God’s attention. It is the fruit that grows on a man whom God has met in the flesh, and the root of it is Christ, and He came to you first.
prayer: Father, the mystery of godliness is great, and You have not kept it from me. You sent Your Son into the flesh to find me in the dust. He lived the life I have not lived, and You raised Him and declared Him in the right. Angels saw Him, the nations heard of Him, and You gave me faith to believe on Him. He is received up in glory, and He prays for me there now. Keep me from trying to build my own godliness out of grit and lists. Where I have stood apart from Your church, bring me back into the house and teach me to carry the truth with other men. Make me glad to belong to Your house, and open my eyes to the brothers You have set beside me. When I look up this week, remind me that my King is coming back. In Jesus’ name, amen.

You sent Your Son into the flesh to find me in the dust.

bottomLine: Paul stops his church manual to sing, because every rule in it leans on one Person. The mystery of godliness is Christ: God revealed in the flesh, raised and declared in the right, seen by angels, preached to the nations, believed on in the world, received up in glory. You built none of it. Stop trying to manufacture godliness. Look at Him, belong to His house, and let the life grow from the root.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and see the Man who came down into the dust with you. He came down into a manger and a carpenter’s shop. He came down into hunger and weariness and the long walk between towns. He came down under the whip, onto the cross, and into a rich man’s tomb. He was not visiting. He stayed. There was no depth of the low place He refused. God was revealed in the flesh — your kind of flesh, the kind that tires and bleeds and was taken from the ground.

The dust has told you that godliness is a weight you lift alone, and you have been lifting it with a sore back for years. Set it down here, at His feet. The secret was never in your grip. It was in Him. He lived the obedient life. He bore the curse. And when men had done their worst, the Father reached into the grave and stood Him up, alive, declared in the right before heaven and earth. Every charge that could be laid against Him was answered that morning, and every charge that could be laid against you was answered in Him.

Lift your eyes higher still. Angels saw Him. The nations heard. Men in places Paul never walked heard the news and believed, and in the fullness of time the same word found you. Then He was received up in glory — not as a spirit set loose from a body, but as a Man, with hands that still bear the marks of the nails. Right now He is seated at the right hand of the Father. Right now He lives to make intercession for you. Right now your name is spoken by the One who holds all things together.

So walk out into this week under an open sky. The same Jesus who was received up will come back in the same way. The two men in white said so while the disciples stood staring at the clouds. He will come bodily, once, and every eye will see Him. Until then you belong to His house, you stand among His people, and the truth you hold is held up by Him. Take up the shield of faith, and carry it into the barn, the job site, and the house where you live. Your King is not gone. He is reigning, and He is on His way.
closingVerse: Without controversy, the mystery of godliness is great: God was revealed in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, and received up in glory.
carry: Where have you been trying to build your own godliness out of grit and lists, when the mystery of godliness is a risen Man in glory who came down into the flesh to give it to you?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Every man has watched someone walk away. The friend who led the men’s study and then quit coming. The brother-in-law who was on fire at thirty and mocks all of it at fifty. The preacher whose name came down off the sign out front. It shakes you more than you say. You sat beside some of these men. You prayed with them over a hospital bed and stood with them at a graveside. If he could leave, what keeps you from leaving?

The dust answers that question two ways, and both are lies. One says your hold on Christ is only as strong as your grip, so grip harder and hope you outlast him. The other says your body and its appetites are the enemy — that if you deny yourself enough and swear off enough, you will finally be safe. Either way the whole weight lands on you, and you are already tired from carrying it. Under that weight your knees buckle, and the psalmist’s words become your own: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV)

The reviving word of 1 Timothy 4 is that the Spirit saw the walking away coming and told the church ahead of time. The God who made the world good has not changed His mind about it. And the living God is the Savior of those who believe. You are not left to hold on by your own strength. You are fed, you are trained, and you are held. The warning in this chapter is real, but it is spoken by a Father to sons He means to keep.

sections.heading: Right After the Song
pulls: The dust says your hold on Christ is only as strong as your grip. The living God says He is the Savior of those who believe — and His hold on you never depended on the strength of your hand.
paras: Chapter 4 follows straight on from the six lines about Christ that close chapter 3. Paul has just confessed that God was revealed in the flesh. Now he warns of teachers who treat the flesh and its needs as dirty — who forbid marriage and certain foods, as if the things God made were traps. The contrast is deliberate. A gospel of God in the flesh cannot sit beside a religion that despises His creation. Paul will not let Timothy choose between loving Christ and receiving the bread on his plate with a glad heart.

Then Paul turns to Timothy himself, a young man raised on the Scriptures from childhood by his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15). Paul does not hand him a new program. He tells him what to refuse, what to feed on, and what to train for. Read 1 Timothy 4:1–10 aloud this week, slowly. Mark every place where God is the one acting, and notice how many there are before Paul gives a single command.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE SPIRIT SAW IT COMING
paras: But the Spirit says expressly that in later times some will fall away from the faith. Paul is not guessing. The Spirit said it plainly, so that when it happens the church is not caught flat-footed. Some will hear the gospel, sit under it, sing it, and then turn and walk. Do not hunt for the later times on a calendar. They began when Christ was received up and poured out His Spirit, and the church has lived in them ever since.

Paul names where the walkers go: paying attention to seducing spirits and doctrines of demons. The lie rarely sounds like a lie. It sounds holy and serious. It comes through the hypocrisy of men who speak lies, branded in their own conscience as with a hot iron. A brand burns the skin until the nerve dies. Touch the scar later and there is no feeling left. That is a conscience after years of being lied to.

Take the warning seriously, and take it straight to Christ. Hebrews says the same: watch for an evil heart of unbelief, in falling away from the living God (Hebrews 3:12). Jesus told of seed on rocky ground: these have no root, who believe for a while, then fall away in time of temptation (Luke 8:13). The ones who fall away never put down root. Those who belong to Christ are held by Him, and He said of His sheep, no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28).

So the warning is a mercy to you. A man who trembles when he reads it does not have a dead conscience. Dead nerves do not hurt. The ache you feel is the Shepherd’s hand on your shoulder, turning you back toward Him. He has not lost track of you.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: EVERY CREATURE OF GOD IS GOOD
paras: What did the liars teach? Forbidding marriage and commanding to abstain from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth. It looks like strictness. It looks like a man finally getting serious about God. But it is a lie about God — that He is stingy, that the things He made are traps, and that holiness means backing away from His world.

Paul answers from the first page of the Bible: For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected, if it is received with thanksgiving. Marriage is a gift. The steak on the grill, the cornbread in the skillet, the cold water after a long afternoon in the sun — gifts. God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good (Genesis 1:31). The fall bent the world, but it did not turn God’s gifts into garbage.

For it is sanctified through the word of God and prayer. The word tells you what a thing is and who gave it. Prayer gives thanks for it. Between the two, an ordinary supper becomes holy ground. The same bread a man wolfs down in the truck, standing at the counter, or in front of the television can be received with a bowed head, and it becomes worship.

This frees you on two sides. The man who thinks God is pleased with his misery can put down the hair shirt; Christ has already borne the curse, and no amount of going without will add to His work. The man who grabs gifts without thanks — the third helping, the drink that turns into three, the wife treated like a convenience — is shown the way back. Receive it from His hand, give thanks, and it stays a gift.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: FED BEFORE YOU ARE TRAINED
pulls: Bodily exercise runs out at the grave. Godliness holds the promise of the life which is now and of the life to come, and that promise rests on a living God, not on how hard you hold on.
paras: If you instruct the brothers of these things, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, nourished in the words of the faith, and of the good doctrine which you have followed. Look at the order. Before Paul tells Timothy to train, he reminds him that he has been fed. Being nourished is something done to a man. Timothy was raised on the Scriptures before he could lace his own boots. Someone else did the feeding.

That is your story too. You did not dig the gospel up on your own. Someone opened the word to you — a mother, a pastor, a man at work who would not let it go — and the Spirit made it bread. Christ said it of Himself: I am the bread of life (John 6:35). He is the food, and He is the One who sets it out. Every bit of strength you have for godliness comes from having been fed on Him.

Then the charge: But refuse profane and old wives’ fables. Exercise yourself toward godliness. Refuse the junk — the stories and speculations that fill a man up and leave him starving. And exercise. Paul’s word is a training word. Godliness does not fall on you like weather. It is worked into you, day after day, like hard ground broken with a hand plow, by a man who has already been fed and is now putting that food to work.

Notice that the man in training is already called a good servant of Christ Jesus. He trains as a man already taken on, because he already belongs, and a son who knows he belongs will work harder for his father than a hired man ever will.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: THE PROMISE OF LIFE
paras: For bodily exercise has some value, but godliness has value in all things, having the promise of the life which is now, and of that which is to come. Paul does not sneer at a strong back. Hard work and a body kept fit have some value. But they run out. A man can split his own firewood at seventy and still be laid in the ground at seventy-one. Godliness reaches past the grave.

And the reason is the promise. Godliness does not earn life. It holds the promise of the life which is now, and of that which is to come. God made that promise, and Christ secured it when He walked out of His tomb alive, so that those in Him will walk out of theirs. Then Paul adds, This saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance — the very words he set over Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners in 1:15.

For to this end we both labor and suffer reproach, because we have set our trust in the living God, who is the Savior of all men, especially of those who believe. Paul worked and was mocked for it, and he did not quit, because his trust was in a God who is alive. That God is good to every man. He sends rain on the field of the man who curses Him, and He holds out Christ freely to anyone who will come. And He saves, fully and for good, those who believe.

So train without fear of wasting the effort. It rests on a living God who has already promised how it ends. Labor, then, and take the reproach when it comes. The One you trust is alive, and He keeps His word.

stations.verse: But the Spirit says expressly that in later times some will fall away from the faith, paying attention to seducing spirits and doctrines of demons.
stations.question: What in my life right now is quietly drawing me to stand a little further off from Christ than I stood a year ago?
stations.live: Name the step you have taken back from Christ this year. Take one step toward Him this week, and say, ‘The Lord knows those who are His.’
body: Aphistēmi means to stand off, to depart, to withdraw. After the temptation in the wilderness the devil departed from him until another time (Luke 4:13). In the middle voice it can mean to fall away, as here and in Jesus’ parable of the seed on rocky ground.

Falling away is rarely a single leap. It is a man standing a step further back each month — skipping the Lord’s Supper, letting the Bible gather dust on the shelf, opening a door he once shut. The word is about distance before it is about disaster. Nobody wakes up one morning gone. They drift, one Sunday at a time.

The dust says you are one bad season from being lost. But Paul uses this same verb for a better departure: Let every one who names the name of the Lord depart from unrighteousness. And over that command stands a seal: The Lord knows those who are his. You are known by Him. Step back toward Him.

stations.verse: Through the hypocrisy of men who speak lies, branded in their own conscience as with a hot iron.
stations.question: Where has my conscience gone quiet about something that used to trouble me every time I did it?
stations.gloss: to sear with a hot iron
stations.live: Name one thing your conscience has stopped flagging. Bring it to God in plain words this week, then make it right with the person it touched, if there is one.
body: Kaustēriazō means to mark by branding — to burn with a hot iron. No other New Testament verse uses it, and Paul makes it a picture of the conscience. The form is a perfect passive: the burning has been done, and the mark remains.

A brand kills the nerve where it lands. Lie to your conscience long enough and it stops answering. The side comment that used to sting on the way out now comes easy. The hours you once felt bad about rounding up, you now round up without a thought. Each small lie is another press of the iron.

The dust says your conscience is too far gone. But a dead conscience does not ache, and you are reading this with an ache. Christ’s blood does what no effort can: it will cleanse your conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14). The iron is not the last word over you. The blood is.

stations.verse: For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected, if it is received with thanksgiving.
stations.question: Which of God’s good gifts have I been taking this week without a single word of thanks?
stations.live: Pray aloud before every meal this week, even on a tailgate at the job site, and name one specific thing on the plate. Once this week, thank God for your wife or a friend by name, out loud.
body: Apoblētos comes from the verb to throw away. It means fit to be thrown away, rejected. Paul uses it once, here, and he says it of nothing God made: nothing is to be rejected, if it is received with thanksgiving.

The false teachers called marriage and food unclean. Paul calls them gifts, made by God and meant to be enjoyed by His people. The word that blessed the world in the beginning still stands over your supper plate and your marriage bed. What God made, He made good, and thanksgiving puts it back in His hand where it belongs.

The dust has two lies here. One says joy is suspect, so a godly man ought to look grim. The other says gifts are owed, so a man may grab without a word. Thanksgiving answers both. It says this is good, and it came from my Father. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above (James 1:17).

stations.verse: If you instruct the brothers of these things, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, nourished in the words of the faith, and of the good doctrine which you have followed.
stations.question: What is actually feeding my mind most days, now that I stop to count it?
stations.gloss: to nourish; to bring up in
stations.live: Pick one book of the Bible and read a chapter of it each morning this week before any screen. If you have children at home, read one of those chapters aloud to them.
body: Entrephō means to train up, to nurture — to bring someone up on something. Here it is passive and figurative: Timothy is nourished in the words of the faith. Nowhere else does the New Testament use it.

The passive matters. Timothy did not feed himself. Paul reminds him elsewhere, From infancy, you have known the holy Scriptures which are able to make you wise for salvation (2 Timothy 3:15). Other hands set the word in front of him before he could choose it. Every man who stands in Christ was fed first by another hand.

The dust wants you to believe you are on your own, scraping for scraps, too far behind to catch up. The word says you have a table. The words of the faith are still set out on it, the same words that fed Timothy, and Christ is the bread. Sit down. Eat before you work.

stations.verse: But refuse profane and old wives’ fables. Exercise yourself toward godliness.
stations.question: Which daily habit of mine is training my heart right now, whether I meant it to or not?
stations.live: Choose one small act of godliness and do it at the same time every day this week — before work, at lunch, or at the end of the night shift. Keep it small. Keep it daily.
body: Gymnazō grows from gymnos, naked: first, to exercise stripped down; then, more generally, to train the body or the mind. Hebrews uses it for senses exercised to discern good and evil and for those trained by the Father’s discipline.

Training is slow and repeated. It does not happen at a conference or on a single hard weekend. It happens on ordinary days, in the same small motions — the open Bible, the closed tab, the held tongue, the prayer before the phone. Paul tells Timothy to train himself, because godliness grows in a man who keeps at it.

The dust is training you too. Peter warns of men having a heart trained in greed (2 Peter 2:14). Every heart is being shaped by something, and a man who does not choose his training has it chosen for him. But the Father has not left you to your own program. He trains you Himself, and afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness.

practices.title: TAKE THE WARNING TO CHRIST
practices.body: When you hear of a man who walked away from the faith, do not gloat and do not panic. Pray for him by name, today, and if you can, call him and tell him you have not forgotten him. Then take the warning to your own heart. The Spirit spoke expressly so you would not be caught off guard. Ask Christ to show you where you have been standing off from Him, and thank Him out loud that He keeps His own to the end.

practices.title: SAY GRACE AND MEAN IT
practices.body: Paul says the food on your plate is sanctified through the word of God and prayer. Every meal this week, stop before you eat — at home, on the road, on an upturned bucket at lunch — and give thanks in plain words for the specific food and the hands that grew and made it. Do the same once a day for the people God has put in your house. Gifts received with thanks stay gifts, and a grateful man is hard to tempt with the next thing.

practices.title: LET YOUR CONSCIENCE SPEAK
practices.body: A branded conscience goes numb one lie at a time. Sit quietly for ten minutes early in the week and ask God to wake up what has gone quiet in you. Then go back and fix one small thing you have let slide — the hours you rounded up, the tool you borrowed and kept, the apology you never made. Do it because the blood of Christ has already cleansed you, never as a way to buy the cleansing.

practices.title: EAT BEFORE YOU WORK
practices.body: Timothy was nourished in the words of the faith before he was ever told to train. Each morning this week, read Scripture before you read anything else, and leave the phone in another room until you have. Start with the Gospel of Mark, one chapter a day, and underline one line in each chapter that shows you Christ. You are not filling a quota or earning a mark. You are sitting down at a table someone else has set.

practices.title: TRAIN SMALL AND DAILY
practices.body: Paul says exercise yourself toward godliness. Pick one small, concrete motion — five minutes of prayer before you start the truck, a psalm at lunch, a walk with your wife after supper where you ask how she is and listen. Do the same thing at the same time every day this week, even on the days you do not feel it. Godliness grows like a crop, by small daily work under a sky you do not control.

prayer: Father, Your Spirit told Your church plainly what was coming, and You have not left me in the dark. Keep me from standing off from Christ one quiet step at a time. bottomLine: Some will fall away, and the Spirit said so ahead of time. Their consciences go numb one lie at a time, and their religion turns against the good things God made. You are called the other way: receive God’s gifts with thanks, feed on the words of the faith, and exercise yourself toward godliness. You train because you have been fed, and the promise rests on the living God, not on your strength.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and see who is holding you. The living God has not let go of you. He saw the falling away coming and told you ahead of time. He made the world good and set it before you to enjoy. He fed you His word before you knew you were hungry, by hands He chose and sent. He holds out the promise of life now and life to come, and He does not take it back.

The dust has told you that your faith is only as strong as your hold on it, and some mornings your hands are weak. You have watched other men walk away and wondered, lying awake, when your turn would come. Hear it plainly, and let it settle in your bones: the ones who stood off had no root. You were not planted in your own soil. You were planted in Christ, and He said of His sheep that no one would snatch them out of His hand. Your grip on Him is real, but His grip on you is what holds.

Look at what He did to make that promise good. The Son of God took on a body like yours. He kept the law you broke, every line of it, on ordinary days in an ordinary town. He went under the full weight of the Father’s judgment for every lie you told your conscience and every gift you grabbed without thanks. And when they laid Him in the ground, the ground could not hold Him. He rose with a body that will never wear out, the first sheaf of a harvest that includes you. When the trumpet sounds and He appears, the graves of His people will open like a plowed field in spring.

So train this week, but train as a man with a promise in his pocket. Godliness has the promise of the life which is now, and of that which is to come. The life which is now: a cleansed conscience, a marriage held as a gift, bread received with thanks, a word to feed on each morning. The life to come: a raised body that will not ache or fail, a new earth, and the face of the living God who is the Savior of those who believe. Bodily exercise ends at the grave, however hard a man has worked. This promise starts there, and it does not end.
closingVerse: For bodily exercise has some value, but godliness has value in all things, having the promise of the life which is now, and of that which is to come.
carry: What would change this week if you trained for godliness as a man already fed by Christ and already promised life, instead of as a man holding on harder to keep from falling?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: A man carries a private estimate of how much his life counts, and it runs low. Too young to be listened to. Too old to start over. Too plain to lead anyone. The man who runs a saw all week and mends the pasture gate on Saturday figures that the word example belongs to preachers, and that what he does with his Bible before daylight is between him and the coffee pot. Nobody follows a man like him, he thinks, and nobody would notice if he quit.

Under that lie sits a second one. The dust says that once a man is saved, the rest is coasting. You were baptized, you believed, the matter is closed — so the reading can slide, the gift can sit, and nobody needs to look hard at the man in the mirror. A man who believes that will not fall all at once. He will thin out. Weeds will come up through the gravel of his days, and he will call it a busy season. He still sits in the pew. He still bows his head over supper. But the roots have stopped going down.

Psalm 119:25 is the prayer of a man who has felt that thinning in his own bones: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) Notice where the reviving comes from. Not from a fresh burst of effort. From the word. That is a prayer a coasting man can pray the morning he wakes up and sees the weeds. And 1 Timothy 4:11–16 is Paul telling a young man the same thing — that God means to keep him, and the people near him, by the very word he is tempted to let slide.

sections.heading: A Young Man Left at Ephesus
pulls: The dust says a saved man can coast. Paul says the same word that found you is the word that keeps you, and a man who stays close to it is a man God is keeping.
paras: Paul calls Timothy my true child in faith (1:2). He met him at Lystra, the son of a believing Jewish mother and a Greek father, a disciple the brothers spoke well of (Acts 16:1–2). The faith had lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice before it lived in him (2 Timothy 1:5). Then Paul left him at Ephesus to command certain men not to teach a different doctrine (1:3). Paul trusted him. He had sent him on hard errands before, into Macedonia ahead of him (Acts 19:22). This was a hard post for anyone. It is harder for a man some thought too young to hold it.

The letter never gives Timothy’s age. It says only that he was young enough to draw contempt. Paul does not answer that contempt with a pep talk. He answers it with the gospel Timothy already holds, a handful of charges plain enough to nail above a workbench — read, urge, teach, use the gift, keep at it, watch yourself — and a promise at the end that turns the whole passage: you will save both yourself and those who hear you.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: LET NO MAN DESPISE
paras: Command and teach these things. The things are the ones Paul has just set down — the good doctrine, the training in godliness, the hope fixed on the living God. Timothy is not told to invent a message. He is handed one. That matters before anything else, because a man who has to make up his own authority will either swagger or shrink. A man who has been handed the word can stand still and say it.

Then: Let no man despise your youth; but be an example to those who believe, in word, in your way of life, in love, in spirit, in faith, and in purity. Paul cannot stop older men from looking down on Timothy. Timothy cannot stop them either. What he can do is give the contempt nothing to stand on. Six places a man lives: his mouth, his daily conduct, his love, his spirit, his trust, his purity.

Read the list again and you will find no talent for speaking in it and no credential. A man answers contempt with a life, and the life is not his own product. Paul has already told Timothy where godliness comes from — the mercy shown to the man who called himself chief of sinners, set out as a pattern for everyone who would believe after him (1:16). The example Timothy gives is an example of grace received. That is why a young man can give it. That is why you can give it at sixty, with a past. Your words at supper, the way you handle the fuel bill, your eyes when the house is asleep — these are where a believing man is watched and followed.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE WORD READ ALOUD
paras: Until I come, pay attention to reading, to exhortation, and to teaching. Paul hopes to come. Until he does, Timothy is not to fill the gap with himself. He is to fill it with the word read, the word pressed home, and the word explained.

The reading is the public reading of Scripture in the gathered church. Long before Ephesus, God’s people stood in the open while the Levites read in the book, in the law of God, distinctly; and they gave the sense, so that they understood the reading (Nehemiah 8:8). At Nazareth Jesus stood up to read, and when He had read from Isaiah He told the room, Today, this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing (Luke 4:16, 21). The Scriptures were always pointing at Him. Reading them aloud is how a church hears its Savior speak.

Then exhortation: the word pressed against the life, urging and comforting. The same Scripture that tells a man he is forgiven tells him to forgive his brother, and exhortation is the work of saying both out loud to people who would rather hear neither. Then teaching: the word laid out so a man can follow it. Nothing here depends on the reader being clever. It depends on the word being read. For a man who has never stood behind a pulpit, this lands close to home. The church you sit in on Sunday is fed by these three tools, and so is the house you lead. A father who reads Scripture aloud at the table, plainly, without a speech attached, is doing what Paul handed Timothy. Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God (Romans 10:17). Your children’s ears are good ground. Sow there.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: THE GIFT AND THE PROGRESS
pulls: God does not save a man and then leave him to keep himself. He keeps him by the same word that found him, and He uses that man’s steady, ordinary faith to reach the people at his table.
paras: Don’t neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the elders. Look at every verb attached to the gift. It was given. It is in him. The elders laid hands on him to mark it out. Timothy did not earn it, buy it, or grow it from his own seed. What do you have that you didn’t receive? (1 Corinthians 4:7). His gift was for ministry among the saints at Ephesus. Yours may sit in a different shop. But every believer has been handed something by the grace of God, and grace does not hand out dead weight.

Neglect is how gifts go quiet. Not by a decision — by drift. A man stops reading because mornings got crowded. He stops teaching the boys at church because somebody else could. He lets the hands that were laid on him go idle, and the tool rusts where he left it. Nobody announces it. One spring he notices the gift has gone quiet, and he cannot say when it happened.

So Paul says: Be diligent in these things. Give yourself wholly to them, that your progress may be revealed to all. Progress is a word with ground under it. A row of corn shows it. A barn going up shows it, rafter by rafter. Paul expects Timothy’s growth to be visible — not finished, not flawless, but moving. He is not asking for a show. He is describing what happens when the word gets into a man: it bears fruit where people can see it. Progress is never the price of God’s favor. It is what His favor does when it is given room.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: CONTINUE, AND BE KEPT
paras: Pay attention to yourself and to your teaching. The order is pointed. Timothy is to watch his own soul first, then what comes out of his mouth. A man can guard his doctrine and let his heart go to seed. He can also love Jesus warmly and grow loose with the truth about Him. Paul will have neither. Watch the man. Watch the message.

Then the promise that makes some men uneasy: Continue in these things, for in doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you. Paul is not teaching Timothy to save himself by effort. This same letter has already said why Christ came — to save sinners (1:15) — and Timothy is one of them. Salvation is God’s work, beginning and end. But God does not save without means. He saves through the word read, believed, held, and spoken. The man who continues in the gospel is the man God is keeping by the gospel. His perseverance is not the payment. It is the road the Savior walks him down to the end.

That is why continue is good news. The One who began the work does not drop it halfway. He who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6). Christ is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, seeing that he lives forever to make intercession for them (Hebrews 7:25). Your continuing rests on His living. And those who hear you — your wife, your sons, the man on the night shift who listens to how you talk — are reached by the same word through a plain, steady life. God uses a man who stays.

stations.verse: Let no man despise your youth; but be an example to those who believe, in word, in your way of life, in love, in spirit, in faith, and in purity.
stations.question: When another man looks down on me this week, what do I reach for first to answer him?
stations.gloss: to think little of; to look down on
stations.live: When someone sneers at you this week — at work, at church, in your own house — do not answer with a defense. Answer with one plain act of kindness toward that person, and let it stand.
body: Kataphroneō means to think little of, to despise. Nine New Testament verses carry it. Jesus uses it of the servant who cannot serve two masters, who will hold to one, and despise the other (Luke 16:13). Paul uses it of the man who despises the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience (Romans 2:4).

Some at Ephesus thought little of Timothy. Paul does not tell him to argue his way out of it. He tells him to give the contempt nothing to stand on — a life of word, conduct, love, faith and purity, all of it fruit of a grace he did not grow.

The dust wants you to spend your strength on what men think of you. But the same word is used once of Jesus. He endured the cross, despising its shame (Hebrews 12:2). He thought little of the shame because He set His love on you. A man held by that love can let contempt fall where it falls.

stations.verse: Until I come, pay attention to reading, to exhortation, and to teaching.
stations.question: How often is Scripture read out loud in my house, plainly, with nothing of mine added to it?
stations.gloss: reading; the public reading of Scripture
stations.live: Read one chapter of 1 Timothy aloud this week — to your wife, your children, or an empty room. Add no comment. Let the word be heard as it stands, and trust God to do His own work with it.
body: Anagnōsis could mean recognition in older Greek, but it also means reading. Each of the three times the New Testament has it, the reading is the public reading of Scripture. In the synagogue at Antioch, Paul was asked to speak after the reading of the law and the prophets (Acts 13:15). The Greek Old Testament uses it in Nehemiah 8:8, where the law was read and the sense was given.

In 2 Corinthians Paul says that at the reading of the old covenant the same veil remains — and then, in Christ it passes away (3:14). Reading alone does not open blind eyes. Christ opens them through the reading. That is why Timothy is to keep it at the center.

The dust says Scripture read aloud is too plain to do anything. It wants a story, a joke, a fresh angle. God has always worked through the plain reading of His word. Read it in your house. Christ still takes the veil away, often through words a man has heard a hundred times.

stations.verse: Don’t neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the elders.
stations.question: What gift has God put in my hands for His people that I have quietly let go idle?
stations.gloss: to be careless of; to neglect
stations.live: Name the gift — teaching, serving, encouraging, giving, a strong back — that you have let sit. Put it to work once this week for someone in your church, and tell no one you did.
body: Ameleō means to be careless, not to care; with an object, to neglect it. Matthew, Hebrews and this letter use it, four verses in all. In Jesus’ parable of the wedding feast, the invited guests made light of it, and went their ways, one to his own farm, another to his merchandise (Matthew 22:5).

Look at those guests. They did not hate the king. They had a farm to see about. Neglect seldom looks like rebellion. It looks like a full calendar. Hebrews uses the same verb for the gravest neglect of all: how will we escape if we neglect so great a salvation (Hebrews 2:3).

The dust says a gift can wait until life settles down. Life does not settle down. But the gift is still there. It was given, not earned, and the Giver has not taken it back. Christ did not make light of you. He came all the way down for you and finished the work. Pick up what He put in your hands.

stations.verse: Be diligent in these things. Give yourself wholly to them, that your progress may be revealed to all.
stations.question: When my mind is free to wander, what does it settle on and turn over again and again?
stations.gloss: to give care to; to practice; to ponder
stations.live: Copy one verse from this passage onto a card and carry it in your shirt pocket. Each time your mind drifts this week — on break, at the feed store counter — take it out and turn it over.
body: Meletaō is built on meletē, care. It means to attend to, to practice, and also to study and ponder. In the Greek Old Testament it chiefly translates the Hebrew verb hagah. Outside this verse the New Testament has it once, in Psalm 2 as the believers prayed it in Acts: the peoples plot a vain thing (Acts 4:25).

So one verb covers a man turning over God’s word and nations turning over a vain scheme. Every man is chewing on something. Paul tells Timothy what to chew on — the reading, the teaching, the gift — and to give himself wholly to it.

The dust wants your idle mind for its own plots: the grudge, the purchase, the argument you replay at the stoplight. Christ gave Himself wholly for you. He does not ask for your leftovers. He offers you His word as bread worth chewing all day, and the man who chews on it finds his thoughts slowly bending toward Christ.

stations.verse: Pay attention to yourself and to your teaching. Continue in these things, for in doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you.
stations.question: If someone watched me closely for a month, what would they learn about how I keep my own soul?
stations.gloss: to hold toward; to give attention to
stations.live: Set one fixed time each day this week — before work, after the dishes — to read, pray, and ask yourself one question: ‘Am I still holding to the gospel I was given?’
body: Epechō means to hold upon, to hold out, and to hold the mind toward a thing — to give it attention. Paul uses it of holding up the word of life (Philippians 2:16). Luke uses it of the lame man at the temple gate, who listened to them, expecting to receive something from them (Acts 3:5).

That beggar is a fair picture of what Paul wants. Eyes fixed, hands open, waiting on a gift. Timothy is to hold his attention that way on his own life and his teaching — not in dread, but as a man who expects God to give through His word.

The dust says watching yourself means staring at your sins until you sink. Paul points another way. Watch yourself the way that lame man watched Peter: expecting. He went into the temple walking. Christ still keeps those who keep looking to Him, and He has never sent a man away empty-handed for looking too hard.

practices.title: ANSWER CONTEMPT WITH A LIFE
practices.body: Somebody will think little of you this week — a boss, a son, a man at church. Paul does not tell Timothy to argue. He tells him to be an example in word, conduct, love, faith and purity. Pick the one of those six where you know you are weakest — maybe your words, maybe your purity — and give it attention in plain sight. Christ thought little of the shame of the cross for your sake. You can let a sneer go unanswered for His.

practices.title: READ IT OUT LOUD
practices.body: Read Scripture aloud in your house at least three times this week. Start with 1 Timothy 4. Do not explain it unless someone asks. The church has always been fed by the word read, urged and taught, and your household is a small church. Let your wife and children hear the word in your voice before they hear anything else from you that day. If you live alone, read it aloud anyway; the word was made to be heard, and your own ears need it.

practices.title: PICK UP THE TOOL
practices.body: Name the gift God has given you for His people. Teaching a boys’ class. Fixing what breaks at the church building. Sitting with the sick. Giving. It was given, not earned, and it was given to be used. Gifts go quiet by drift, so do not wait to feel ready. Put a date on the calendar this week, tell your pastor or an elder what you mean to do, and do one thing with what He put in your hands.

practices.title: ASK WHERE IT SHOWS
practices.body: Paul wanted Timothy’s progress revealed to all. Ask your wife, or a friend who will tell you the truth, one question: where have you seen the word change me this year? Listen without defending. If they can name something, thank God for it — that was His work. If they cannot, do not despair, and do not argue with them. Ask Him to grow it, and open the word again tomorrow. The growth is His to give.

practices.title: KEEP WATCH AT NIGHT
practices.body: Each night this week, before you sleep, ask two plain questions. Did I stay near the word today? Did I say anything about God that was not true? Confess what needs confessing. Then rest on Christ, who lives to intercede for those who come to God through Him. Watching yourself is not dread. It is a man staying close to the One who saves him, the way a man on a ridge in a storm stays close to the fence wire.

title: Watch Yourself
subtitle: from dust to a life that saves
keyVerse: Pay attention to yourself and to your teaching. Continue in these things, for in doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you.

passage.text: Command and teach these things.
Let no man despise your youth; but be an example to those who believe, in word, in your way of life, in love, in spirit, in faith, and in purity.
Until I come, pay attention to reading, to exhortation, and to teaching.
Don’t neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the elders.
Be diligent in these things. Give yourself wholly to them, that your progress may be revealed to all.
Pay attention to yourself and to your teaching. Continue in these things, for in doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you.

stationsIntro: Five words in six verses, and each one names a way a man either stays near the word or drifts from it. Read the verse first, answer it plainly, then let the Greek press it a little deeper.
lifeIntro: God has put His word in your hands, given you gifts you did not earn, and promised to finish what He began in you. These practices are ways of staying where He has set you — near the word, in plain sight, for your own soul and for those who hear you. None of them earns a thing. Each one puts you where grace has promised to meet you.
lifePulls: Your continuing in the faith rests on Christ’s continuing for you. He lives to intercede, and a man who keeps close to His word is a man He is keeping.
prayer: Father, You sent Your Son into the world to save sinners, and You saved me. You put Your word in my hands and gave me gifts I did not earn. When men look down on me, let me answer with a life that shows Your grace. Keep me near the reading of Your word, in my house and in Your church. Don’t let me neglect what You have given me to use. Watch over my heart and my teaching, and keep me from drifting. Keep me to the end, and use my plain life to reach those who hear me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You sent Your Son into the world to save sinners, and You saved me.
You put Your word in my hands and gave me gifts I did not earn.
When men look down on me, let me answer with a life that shows Your grace.
Keep me near the reading of Your word, in my house and in Your church.
Don’t let me neglect what You have given me to use.
Watch over my heart and my teaching, and keep me from drifting.
Keep me to the end, and use my plain life to reach those who hear me.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Timothy was young, posted to a hard church, and looked down on. Paul did not hand him a strategy. He handed him the word: read it, urge it, teach it, use the gift you were given, give yourself wholly to these things, and watch your own soul. You do not save yourself. God keeps a man by the gospel he keeps, and uses that steady man to reach the people who hear him.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, from the shelf where the Bible sat closed. Lift them to the Savior who came into the world for sinners and does not leave His work half done. Lift them past the man who looked down on you this week. Lift them past the Bible gathering dust on the shelf and the gift you let sit idle. Lift them past the years you think you wasted and the progress you cannot see. Lift them to the One who has not let go of you through any of it, who knew every slack season before it came and set His love on you anyway.

The dust told you that a saved man can coast, and that if you have coasted too long the road has closed behind you. Neither is true. Paul wrote to a young man under pressure and told him to keep reading, keep teaching, keep watching his own heart — not because Timothy’s grip was holding him up, but because God had put His word in Timothy’s hands and meant to keep him by it. The same word is in yours. Open it again tomorrow. It has not changed its mind about you.

Look at Christ. He thought little of the shame of the cross and endured it for the joy set before Him. He broke out of death with the work finished, and He has not stopped working since. He lives forever to make intercession for those who draw near to God through Him. When you stumbled this year, He did not resign. When you went quiet, He kept speaking for you at the Father’s right hand. Your continuing in the faith rests on His living. You hold on because He holds you, and His hands do not tire.

So go back to the plain things this week. Read the word out loud. Use the gift. Watch your heart and your words. Let the people at your table see a man being kept. You do not need to be impressive. You need to be near the word, and stay there, and let God do in plain sight what only God can do. The promise stands at the end of the chapter like a cornerstone set in the ground: in doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you — because the One who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.
closingVerse: Pay attention to yourself and to your teaching. Continue in these things, for in doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you.
carry: Where have you let the word, or the gift God gave you, slide into neglect — and what would it look like this week to pick it up again, trusting Christ to keep you by it?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: The dust keeps a short map of a man’s obligations. It draws a line around his own skin, maybe around his paycheck, and calls everything outside the line somebody else’s problem. The widow two roads over is the church’s business. His mother in the care home is his sister’s business. The older man at church who talks too long after the service is nobody’s business at all. A man can live a whole life that way and call it minding his own affairs.

The dust has a lie for the people outside that line, too. If you are old, it says your use is spent. If you are left alone, it says you have been forgotten. If you are young and restless, it says the people who came before you are in the way. It sorts people by what they can give back, and it keeps a man so busy with his own wants that he never looks up from them. He ends up alone in a full house, and he does not know how he got there.

The lonely map ends in the dirt. A man who has followed it that far learns an old prayer by heart: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) The word that revives him here is a word about a household. In 1 Timothy 5:1–16 God does not hand the church a program. He hands it a family, and He shows the men in it how fathers, brothers, sons and providers carry themselves.

sections.heading: From Timothy’s Soul to God’s House
pulls: The dust draws a line around a man’s own skin and calls everything outside it somebody else’s problem. God draws a family, and He puts the man inside it.
paras: Paul has spent the end of chapter 4 on Timothy’s own life — his example, his reading, his gift, his watch over himself. Now he turns outward. Earlier he told Timothy he was writing that you may know how men ought to behave themselves in God’s house (3:15). Chapter 5 shows what that house looks like on an ordinary weekday: an older man who needs correcting, a widow with no one left, a son who owes his mother, a church deciding whom it will support. None of it is glamorous. All of it is the gospel worked out in a family that has to share a roof, a budget and a Lord’s Table.

Most of the passage concerns widows. The words were written to a first-century church, but the shape of the need has not changed: a woman whose husband is gone, whose hands are not as strong as they were, whose bills still come. God has always paid attention to her. His law protected her, His prophets defended her, and His Son noticed a poor widow’s two small coins in the temple treasury. He is a father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows (Psalm 68:5). Before Paul asks any man to provide, he shows him the God who already does. Every charge in this passage stands on that ground. The Father looks after the widow first, and then He sends His sons.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: FATHERS AND BROTHERS
paras: Don’t rebuke an older man, but exhort him as a father; the younger men as brothers; the elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, in all purity. Paul does not tell Timothy to stop correcting people. A pastor who never corrects is no pastor, and a brother who never speaks up is not much of a brother. He tells him how to do it — not with a fist, but with a family name.

An older man who has gone wrong is still to be spoken to as a father: with respect, with an appeal, with the honor due his years. Younger men are brothers, equals rather than projects. Older women are to be treated as a man treats his own mother. Younger women are sisters, and the guard on that relationship is stated plainly: in all purity. A man who would never let his hands or his eyes wander toward his own sister has his rule for every younger woman in the church.

Where did this family come from? Not from Timothy’s good manners. Christ made it. He said, whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother (Matthew 12:50). He is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11) — He, the holy Son, who had every right to be ashamed of you. The church is a household because the Son of God took sinners out of the dust and gave them His own Father. When you speak to an old man at church this Sunday, you are speaking to a brother of Christ old enough to be your father. Speak like it. Christ already speaks to you as a brother.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: A RETURN FOR THE YEARS
paras: Honor widows who are widows indeed. Honor here is more than a kind word. In the verses that follow it means real support: food in the pantry, a roof that holds, someone looking in on her. The word indeed matters. Paul is about to separate the widow who has no one from the widow who has family close by.

But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let them learn first to show piety toward their own family and to repay their parents, for this is acceptable in the sight of God. Mark the word first. Before the church takes her on, her own children and grandchildren are to learn godliness at home. Paul calls it piety, and he sets that piety in the kitchen of a widowed mother, not in a pew.

A son cannot pay his mother back. Nobody settles the account of a thousand meals and the nights she sat up with a feverish boy. But he can make a return. He can carry in the groceries, fix the leak under the sink, sit on the porch and hear the same story again. God calls that acceptable in the sight of God. Notice it is not the price of His acceptance. The Son of God already secured that for you at the cross. This is what a son made right with God looks like with his mother. And the commandment did not expire when you left home. Honor your father and your mother (Exodus 20:12) still has groceries in it, and the Son who kept that commandment perfectly kept it for you.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: LEFT ALONE, HOPING IN GOD
pulls: From the cross, while He was paying for your sin, Jesus provided for His mother. A man who carries his own household is following that Savior, not buying his way to Him.
paras: Now she who is a widow indeed and desolate, has her hope set on God, and continues in petitions and prayers night and day. Here is the widow with no one. Paul does not describe her only by what she has lost. He describes her by where she has put her weight, the way an old fence post leans its whole load on the brace beside it. Left alone, she has set her hope on God, and she spends her nights in prayer. Luke tells of Anna, a widow for about eighty-four years, who didn’t depart from the temple, worshiping with fastings and petitions night and day (Luke 2:37) — and who lived to see the Christ child carried in.

But she who gives herself to pleasure is dead while she lives. The contrast is hard and true. A life spent on its own comfort is a walking grave, whatever its age. A man can spend his evenings on a screen and his money on himself and be dead while he lives.

Then the verse men remember: But if anyone doesn’t provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith, and is worse than an unbeliever. Say it plainly. A man provides for his own. Unbelievers know that much; plenty of them work double shifts for their families. A man who names Christ and walks away from his own contradicts the faith he names. But hear where that faith begins. Your Father knows what things you need, before you ask him (Matthew 6:8). And on the cross, with His breath running short, Jesus looked at His mother and the disciple He loved and said, Behold, your mother (John 19:27). The Savior provided for His mother while He was paying for you.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: A HOUSE WHERE NO ONE IS FORGOTTEN
paras: Let no one be enrolled as a widow under sixty years old, having been the wife of one man, being approved by good works. The church kept a list. A widow on it was supported, and her life was already known: she had brought up children, been hospitable to strangers, washed the saints’ feet, relieved the afflicted. She had spent her strength on others. Now others would spend theirs on her. The church honored a life already poured out, and it did not make her beg.

The younger widows Paul handles differently, and without contempt. He knows a young woman freshly bereaved may want to marry again, and he wants her to: I desire therefore that the younger widows marry, bear children, rule the household, and give no occasion to the adversary for insulting. His concern is that a list meant for the old would leave the young with empty days and the slow harm of going from house to house with nothing to do but talk. He is guarding them, not shaming them.

Then the closing word, which comes back around to men like you: If any man or woman who believes has widows, let them relieve them, and don’t let the assembly be burdened, that it might relieve those who are widows indeed. When a family carries its own, the church has hands free for the woman who has no one. That is a household where nobody is forgotten because everybody is carrying somebody. Christ, who had compassion on the widow of Nain and gave him to his mother (Luke 7:13, 15), still moves that way through His people. The widow’s need is His concern before it is yours, and He has decided to meet it with your hands.

stations.verse: Don’t rebuke an older man, but exhort him as a father; the younger men as brothers.
stations.question: When an older man in my church is plainly in the wrong, what does my tone toward him sound like?
stations.gloss: to strike at; to rebuke sharply
stations.live: Think of the older man you have been tempted to dismiss or cut down. Before you say anything to him this week, pray for him by name, then speak to him as you would want your own father spoken to.
body: Epiplēssō can mean to strike at, to punish; it also means to rebuke, to reprove. The New Testament has no other verse with it. Paul does not forbid Timothy to correct an older man. He forbids the kind of rebuke that lands like a blow.

Instead Timothy is to exhort him as a father — to come alongside and appeal. The same truth can be said either way. One leaves a bruise. The other leaves a way back. An older man who has gone wrong usually knows it. What he rarely gets is a younger man who still honors him while telling him so.

The dust says that being right gives you license to swing. But God did not deal with you by striking you down. He sent His Son to take the blow in your place. A man who has been spared like that has no business striking his brothers with his words.

stations.verse: But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let them learn first to show piety toward their own family and to repay their parents, for this is acceptable in the sight of God.
stations.question: What return am I making this year to the parents or grandparents who poured their years into me?
stations.live: Make one concrete return to a parent or grandparent this week — a visit, a repair, a meal, a bill paid. If yours are gone, make it to an old saint at church who has no one close by.
body: Amoibē means a requital, a recompense; it comes from a verb meaning to repay. This verse is the only place it turns up in the New Testament. Paul does not ask children to pay off their parents. He asks them to make a return — to give something back for what was given.

That return is what Paul calls piety toward their own family, and it is acceptable in the sight of God. Some men had parents who gave them little but scars. Honor may then look like a careful phone call, a bill quietly paid, a prayer for a father who never prayed for you. Grace does not ask you to pretend. It asks you to give what you can.

The dust keeps a ledger. It says you owe nothing to people who failed you, or that you owe everything and can never pay. Christ paid the debt you owed to God. A man freed from that debt can make small returns gladly.

stations.verse: Now she who is a widow indeed and desolate, has her hope set on God, and continues in petitions and prayers night and day.
stations.question: Who in my church has been left alone, without family close enough to look in on her each week?
stations.live: Learn the name of one widow or widower in your church who lives alone. Visit this week with your wife or a friend. Fix something, bring something, and ask what you can pray for.
body: Monoō means to leave alone, to forsake. Paul uses the perfect passive participle of a widow with no children: she has been left alone, and she remains alone. No other New Testament writer uses the word.

Paul sets another phrase right beside it: she has her hope set on God. Being left alone did not leave her hopeless. With no one to lean on, she leaned on God, and she continues in petitions and prayers night and day. Some of the strongest praying in your church comes from a small house with one coffee cup in the sink.

The dust tells the lonely that they have been forgotten. God does not forget. When my father and my mother forsake me, then Yahweh will take me up (Psalm 27:10). Christ was forsaken on the cross so that no one who hopes in God would be finally left alone. And He often answers that widow’s prayers by sending a man to her.

stations.verse: But she who gives herself to pleasure is dead while she lives.
stations.question: Where am I spending my money on my own comfort while someone near me goes without?
stations.gloss: to live for pleasure; to live in soft luxury
stations.live: Pick one comfort you spend on every week — the takeout, the gear, the streaming bill. Skip it once and put the money toward a widow’s need. Do it quietly, and let the Father who sees in secret keep the record.
body: Spatalaō comes from a noun meaning wantonness or luxury, and it means to live riotously. Besides this verse, only James has it. In James 5:5 it is the word behind taken your pleasure, spoken to rich men who held back their workers’ wages. The Greek Old Testament uses it in Ezekiel 16:49 of Sodom, where prosperous ease was in her and in her daughters.

Ezekiel finishes that sentence: She also didn’t strengthen the hand of the poor and needy. That is the edge of Paul’s warning. Pleasure-living is never only a private waste. It sits comfortable while others go without. A widow who lived that way was dead while she lives, and so is any man who has made his own ease the point of his days.
The dust offers comfort as life and hands you a grave. Christ, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9). Real life runs in His direction: down, toward need.

stations.verse: But if anyone doesn’t provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith, and is worse than an unbeliever.
stations.question: What need in my own household have I seen coming for months and kept putting off until later?
stations.gloss: to think ahead; to provide for
stations.live: Sit down this week with your wife, or alone, and name one need coming down the road — a will, a parent’s care, a debt, a child’s next season. Take the first concrete step on it before Sunday.
body: Pronoeō first means to foresee, then to provide. In its two other New Testament verses Paul uses it for taking thought for what is right: Respect what is honorable in the sight of all men (Romans 12:17). Here, with a person as its object, it means to provide for someone.

So providing in this verse is more than a paycheck left on the counter. It is a man looking down the road for the people God gave him: the will not yet written, the mother who will need help next winter, the son who needs his father’s time this year. Foresight is one of the shapes love takes.

The dust makes provision a matter of pride — never needing help, never being caught short. Your Father provides for you before you ask. My God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus (Philippians 4:19). A man resting in that can look ahead without fear and carry his own without strutting.

practices.title: SPEAK TO THE OLD AS FAMILY
practices.body: Paul tells Timothy to exhort an older man as a father, not strike at him. This week, seek out one older man in your church — not to fix him, but to honor him. Ask him how he came to faith and what he learned in his hard years. Listen longer than is comfortable, even if you have heard the story before. If you have a correction for him, carry it the way you would want a son to carry one to you.

practices.title: MAKE A RETURN AT HOME
practices.body: Your parents or grandparents gave you years you can never repay. Paul says to make a return anyway, and he calls it godliness. Call your mother. Fix your father’s porch step. Pay a bill without being asked. Mow the yard he can no longer mow. If your parents failed you, start smaller — a prayer, a card, a phone call kept short and kind. God counts that acceptable in His sight, because Christ has already made you acceptable.

practices.title: KNOCK ON ONE DOOR
practices.body: Somewhere in your church there is a widow, or an old man, who has been left alone and keeps praying anyway. Find out who. Go this week with your wife or a friend. Take a hot meal or a toolbox. Change the furnace filter, clean the gutters, sit at the table. Ask what she is praying for, and ask her to pray for you. You may be part of God’s answer to her nights. Go back next month.

practices.title: CUT ONE COMFORT
practices.body: Pleasure-living leaves a man dead while he lives. Pick one comfort that has hardened into habit — the evening scroll, the second takeout order, the gear you keep buying. Give it up this week, all seven days. Put the time toward your household and the money toward someone in need. Christ became poor for your sake, and He did not do it halfway. Let a small piece of His direction show up in your bank statement.

practices.title: LOOK DOWN THE ROAD
practices.body: Providing means seeing ahead. Sit down this week and name the need coming toward your household that you have been putting off: a will, life insurance, a parent’s care, a child who needs your time before he leaves. Write it down where you will see it. Take one step on it before Sunday — a phone call, an appointment, an evening blocked off. Do it not to prove yourself, but because your Father has provided for you, and sons learn their father’s ways.

title: The Household of God
subtitle: from dust to a family that provides
keyVerse: But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let them learn first to show piety toward their own family and to repay their parents, for this is acceptable in the sight of God.

passage.text: Don’t rebuke an older man, but exhort him as a father; the younger men as brothers;
the elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, in all purity.
Honor widows who are widows indeed.
But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let them learn first to show piety toward their own family and to repay their parents, for this is acceptable in the sight of God.
Now she who is a widow indeed and desolate, has her hope set on God, and continues in petitions and prayers night and day.
But she who gives herself to pleasure is dead while she lives.
Also command these things, that they may be without reproach.
But if anyone doesn’t provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith, and is worse than an unbeliever.
Let no one be enrolled as a widow under sixty years old, having been the wife of one man,

being approved by good works, if she has brought up children, if she has been hospitable to strangers, if she has washed the saints’ feet, if she has relieved the afflicted, and if she has diligently followed every good work.
But refuse younger widows, for when they have grown wanton against Christ, they desire to marry,
having condemnation, because they have rejected their first pledge.
Besides, they also learn to be idle, going about from house to house. Not only idle, but also gossips and busybodies, saying things which they ought not.
I desire therefore that the younger widows marry, bear children, rule the household, and give no occasion to the adversary for insulting.
For already some have turned away after Satan.
If any man or woman who believes has widows, let them relieve them, and don’t let the assembly be burdened, that it might relieve those who are widows indeed.

stationsIntro: These five words move from the way a man speaks to an older brother to the way he carries his own. Let each verse land, answer it as a son and a provider, then let the Greek sharpen what you heard.
lifeIntro: God has made you His son, set you in His household, and promised to supply every need you have in Christ. Everything below starts with what He has already done, not with what you owe. These practices are a son of that house carrying his share — in his words, in his own family, and toward the ones who have no one left.
lifePulls: The church is a household because the Son of God is not ashamed to call you His brother. Every widow, every old man, every younger brother in it belongs to the same Father.
prayer: Father, You have made me Your son and set me in Your household. Your Son is not ashamed to call me His brother. Teach me to speak to older men as fathers and to younger men as brothers. Make me a son who makes a return to those who raised me. Show me the one who has been left alone, and send me to her. Keep me from living for my own comfort while others go without. Give me eyes to see ahead and hands to provide for my own. You have supplied every need of mine in Christ; let me carry others gladly. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You have made me Your son and set me in Your household.
Your Son is not ashamed to call me His brother.
Teach me to speak to older men as fathers and to younger men as brothers.
Make me a son who makes a return to those who raised me.
Show me the one who has been left alone, and send me to her.
Keep me from living for my own comfort while others go without.
Give me eyes to see ahead and hands to provide for my own.
You have supplied every need of mine in Christ; let me carry others gladly.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: The church is a household, and God is its Father. Speak to older men as fathers and younger men as brothers. Make a return to the parents who raised you. Find the widow who has no one and carry her. Do not live for comfort. Provide for your own, because the Savior provided for His mother from the cross while He was paying for you. No one is shamed into this house. Everyone in it was carried in.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, from the narrow line you drew around yourself. Lift them to the Father of the fatherless, who sees the widow in her small house and the old man in his chair and the son who forgot to call. Lift them to the household He has built out of people the dust had sorted and thrown away. Lift them to the table where you have a place you did not earn, a chair with your name on it, set by a Father who wanted you there.

The dust told you that your obligations end at your own skin, and that the people who cannot pay you back are not worth the drive. God answered by doing the opposite. He came for those who could give Him nothing. He sets the lonely in families. He wrote the widow and the aging father into His church’s first business. And He called you, a man who owed Him everything and had paid Him nothing, His son. He did not wait for you to become useful before He brought you in.

Look at the cross. Jesus hung there carrying the sin of His people, and with the breath He had left He turned to His mother and gave her a son to take her home. He did not stop being a provider while He was being a sacrifice. Death could not keep Him; the grave let Him go, and He is still caring for His household — every widow, every brother, every man who has failed his own and come home to the Father. Nothing you owe anyone is larger than what He has already paid for you. So go and carry someone this week. Call your mother. Honor the old man. Sit at the widow’s table and drink her weak coffee. Look ahead for your own household and take the first step. You are not buying your way into God’s family. You are already in it. The Father of the fatherless keeps the widow’s name before Him every night she prays, and He has never once forgotten yours. The Son who said from the cross, Behold, your mother, still gives His people to one another, and He has given some of them to you. A man carried home like that can afford to carry. Every grocery sack you set on a widow’s counter this week rides on what He finished on that hill.
closingVerse: But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let them learn first to show piety toward their own family and to repay their parents, for this is acceptable in the sight of God.
carry: Who has God placed near you — a parent, a widow, an old man at church — whom you have been treating as someone else’s problem rather than as family in the household of God?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Most men keep two ledgers on honor. One lists what is owed to them — the credit for the job that came in under budget, the thanks for twenty years of Sunday mornings, the respect a foreman ought to get from a crew half his age. The other ledger lists what they owe, and that one stays mostly blank. It works the same way at church. You notice when the pastor misses your father’s funeral. You do not notice the forty hours he spent on the sermon you half heard. You know which book you open more often.

The dust works both ledgers. It tells you the man who preaches to you every week is overhead, a line on the budget the church could trim. It tells you the elder who fell should be covered quietly if you like him and hung out to dry if you don’t. It tells you the boss who signs your check has earned the hours from you and nothing more, and that the hours nobody checks are your own. And it tells you the sin no one has found will never be found.

That is a man face-down in the dirt, keeping score with his finger: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) The reviving word here is that honor in God’s house does not start with what you are owed. It starts with the God who looked at a blasphemer and a persecutor, showed him mercy, and counted him faithful (1:12–13). Every piece of honor in these verses runs downhill from that mercy — to the man who labors in the word, to the man who stands accused, to the master at the end of the row.

sections.heading: Honor in the Household
pulls: The dust tells you honor is a wage you collect. In God’s house it is a debt you pay — because the God who owns the house first counted a blasphemer faithful and put him to work.
paras: Paul left Timothy at Ephesus to set a household in order (1:3; 3:15). He has just finished with the widows, and the word he used there was honor: Honor widows who are widows indeed (5:3). Now he carries the same word up to the men who lead and down to the men who serve under a yoke. Elders get double honor. Masters get all honor. Nobody in the house is beneath it.

Watch what holds the section together. Paul does not ground any of it in rank. He grounds it in the eyes of God — in the sight of God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the chosen angels (5:21) — and in the name of God, which a man’s work either adorns or drags through the mud (6:1). Read 5:17 through 6:2 in one sitting before you go on. It moves fast. It covers pay, discipline, ordination, a sick stomach and a hard boss — one household, under one Lord. And every line of it assumes what 1:15 declared: the people in this house are sinners Christ came into the world to save.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE OX ON THE THRESHING FLOOR
paras: Let the elders who rule well be counted worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in the word and in teaching. Start with who gave these men. Christ did not leave His church to run itself. He gives men to rule and to teach, and a congregation with a faithful elder holds a gift it did not earn. Double honor covers both things such a man needs: respect for the office and bread for his table. The next verse makes the second plain.

You shall not muzzle the ox when it treads out the grain. That is Moses (Deuteronomy 25:4). Picture an ox walking circles on a threshing floor, grain under his hooves, grain at his nose, and a farmer who straps his mouth shut so he cannot eat while he works. God wrote a law against that. Paul sets a second word beside it: The laborer is worthy of his wages. Jesus said it first, when He sent His workers out ahead of Him into the harvest (Luke 10:7).

So the man who studies all week and opens the Book to you on Sunday is not overhead. He is an ox on your floor, not a hired hand you keep around while the numbers work. Ask whether you think of his pay as a cost to keep low or a debt to honor. Ask whether you have ever thanked him for the sermon that cut you, or only grumbled about the one that ran long. And notice the word Paul uses for his work — labor, the kind that leaves a man tired. Your pastor is not the only one who has worked that way for you. Christ labored for your soul all the way to death, and He sent you no bill.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: TWO OR THREE WITNESSES
paras: Don’t receive an accusation against an elder, except at the word of two or three witnesses. A man who stands up front draws fire. Somebody always has a story. Paul shuts the door on the rumor mill: no charge against an elder moves forward on one voice. Moses set the same standard for any man in Israel (Deuteronomy 19:15), and it is mercy. A church that believes every whisper will eat its shepherds alive. And a man who passes every whisper along has already sat as judge with no witnesses at all.

But the door does not swing only one way. Those who sin, reprove in the sight of all, that the rest also may be in fear. When the charge is true and the sin goes on, the title does not protect the man. The rebuke is public because the office was public. Leaders get a fair hearing. They do not get a free pass.

Then Paul raises his voice. I command you in the sight of God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the chosen angels, that you observe these things without prejudice, doing nothing by partiality. Picture the court. Timothy is not alone at the bench. God sits there. Christ sits there. The angels watch. In that room there is no leaning toward the man you hunt with or the man who gives the most. Here the gospel lands hard. The God who judges without partiality is the God who sent His Son to bear the judgment of men who had no case. You were not shown favor because someone liked you. You were shown mercy when you had nothing to plead. A man who knows that can stop grading people by how much he likes them.

parts.label: PART THREE
