parts.heading: A LITTLE WINE AND A LONG VIEW
pulls: Some sin walks in ahead of a man and some trails him by years. Nothing is hidden from God — the worst news for a man still pretending, and the best news for a man already covered by Christ.
paras: Lay hands hastily on no one. The laying on of hands set a man apart for his work in the church. Paul tells Timothy to slow down. Charm is not character, and one good season is not a tested life. If you hurry a man into leadership, you share the blame for what follows: Don’t be a participant in other people’s sins. Keep yourself pure.

Then, in the middle of a charge about church order, a word about a stomach. Be no longer a drinker of water only, but use a little wine for your stomach’s sake and your frequent infirmities. Timothy was often sick, and Paul cared about his body. That is all the verse needs to say. Keeping yourself pure does not mean punishing yourself. The God who calls a man to holiness also made his stomach. He takes no pleasure in a man who ruins his health to look strict. Holiness is a clean heart before God, not a show for the men watching.

Some men’s sins are evident, preceding them to judgment, and some also follow later. Here is why Timothy must not hurry. Some sin walks in the front door ahead of a man. Some trails him by years. Timothy cannot see all of it, and neither can you. But the other half of the saying is good news: there are good works that are obvious, and those that are otherwise can’t be hidden. The quiet faithfulness nobody praised — the years of night shift, the Saturdays with your aging father, the giving no one knows about — God has all of it in plain view. He sees the hidden sin and covers it in Christ. He sees the hidden good and will bring it to light.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: UNDER THE YOKE
paras: Let as many as are bondservants under the yoke count their own masters worthy of all honor, that the name of God and the doctrine not be blasphemed. Say it plainly. Paul is writing to men who were owned. He is not blessing the system that owned them; in this same letter he lists slave-traders among the lawless whom the law condemns (1:9–10). He is telling believers how to carry Christ inside a hard arrangement they did not choose and could not end.

Your situation is not theirs. You can quit. But the yoke still fits the shape of your days — a boss, a schedule, a pay stub, work that belongs to someone else. And Paul’s reason still holds. The way you work either honors the name of God or hands the men around you a reason to mock it. The hour padded on the timesheet. The tool that rides home in your lunch pail. The sneer at the foreman behind his back. Every one of those preaches a sermon about your God.

Then a harder word: Those who have believing masters, let them not despise them because they are brothers, but rather let them serve them. A Christian boss is no excuse to coast. Brotherhood is a reason to work better. And here is where all of it rests. The Son of God took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7) and wore a yoke heavier than any you will carry. He bore it to the cross for you without one word of complaint. Now He offers you His own: my yoke is easy, and my burden is light (Matthew 11:30). A man under that yoke can honor a hard boss without crawling, because he knows whom he serves.

stations.verse: Let the elders who rule well be counted worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in the word and in teaching.
stations.question: What would change in how I treat the man who teaches me God’s Word if I counted the weariness his labor costs him?
stations.gloss: to grow weary; to toil with effort
stations.live: Write your pastor or one of your elders a short note this week. Name one sermon or one conversation that helped you, thank him for the labor behind it, and ask what he needs.
body: Kopiaō first meant to grow weary. From there it came to mean the work that makes a man weary — toil with effort and sweat in it. Paul reaches for it often for the labor of ministry. Jesus uses it for the men He calls to Himself: all you who labor and are heavily burdened (Matthew 11:28).

So the elder who labors in the word and in teaching is not doing light work. He is tired from it. Study, prayer, the hospital at midnight, the hard talk with a straying man — it costs him. Paul knew that cost firsthand, and he knew where the strength came from: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me (1 Corinthians 15:10).

The dust wants you to think every tired man is on his own. The word that names the elder’s toil also names the men Jesus calls to come and rest. The One who calls the tired to Himself also holds up the men who wear themselves out for your soul.

stations.verse: For the Scripture says, “You shall not muzzle the ox when it treads out the grain.” And, “The laborer is worthy of his wages.
stations.question: Where have I let someone keep working for my good while I quietly hold back what they are owed?
stations.gloss: to muzzle; to put to silence
stations.live: Find one muzzle you have strapped on someone — a raise you could give, a debt you could pay early, a thank-you you have held back. Take it off before the week is out.
body: Phimoō comes from the word for a muzzle, and it means to muzzle. The New Testament also uses it for putting something to silence. Matthew uses it when Jesus had silenced the Sadducees with one answer (Matthew 22:34). Peter uses it for silencing the ignorance of foolish men by doing good (1 Peter 2:15).

Here it is the farmer’s strap on the ox. The law forbade it, and Paul lays that law alongside the men who feed the church. A muzzle is a small cruelty. It saves the owner a few mouthfuls of grain. But it tells the ox exactly what he is worth to the man: work, and no wages.

The dust wants you to muzzle whatever costs you — the thanks you keep back, the pay you keep thin, the praise you never say out loud. God has never measured His mercy to you by the mouthful. The God who would not let an ox go hungry has fed you at His own table.

stations.verse: I command you in the sight of God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the chosen angels, that you observe these things without prejudice, doing nothing by partiality.
stations.question: Whose sin am I quick to excuse simply because I like the man who committed it?
stations.live: Think of a dispute where you took a side because of who is in it. Before you speak of it again, hear the other man out in full, and say: ‘God sees this, and He does not lean.’
body: Prosklisis means an inclination — a leaning to one side, a tilt. Paul uses it for partiality, and this verse is its lone New Testament appearance.

Picture a scale that leans before anything is set on it. That is partiality. A man’s friendship, his money, his years in the church, his firm handshake — they tip the judgment before the facts come in. Paul says Timothy must do nothing that way, and he says it in the sight of God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the chosen angels.

The dust tells you everybody leans, so leaning is fine. But you were never weighed on a tilted scale. God did not lean toward you because you were likable. He found you guilty and then laid your guilt on His Son. A man saved by that kind of justice can afford to be fair to the man he likes least.

stations.verse: Some men’s sins are evident, preceding them to judgment, and some also follow later.
stations.question: What sin in me is following behind, out of sight, that I need to bring into the light now?
stations.live: Name to God, out loud, the one sin you are counting on staying hidden. If it wronged someone, go make it right this week. Then say: ‘Christ carried this. I will not carry it in the dark.’
body: Prodēlos means evident beforehand, or clearly evident. Paul uses it in two verses back to back, first for sins and then for good works. Hebrews uses it for what is plain about Christ’s family line: it is evident that our Lord has sprung out of Judah (Hebrews 7:14).

Some sin is plain before the judgment ever comes. Some is not plain at all — yet. It trails a man the way a stray dog trails him down a gravel road, out of sight around the bend, but coming. Paul tells Timothy this so he will be slow to judge by first looks.

The dust says what is buried stays buried. It does not. But the same saying that warns you holds a promise: good works that are not plain now can’t be hidden either. Bring your hidden sin into the light and lay it at the cross while it is still behind you. Christ has already carried it. Trust Him with the hidden good.

stations.verse: Let as many as are bondservants under the yoke count their own masters worthy of all honor, that the name of God and the doctrine not be blasphemed.
stations.question: When I work under another man’s authority, whose yoke do I believe I am really wearing?
stations.gloss: a yoke; the beam of submission
stations.live: Pick the task at work you most resent. Do it this week as well as you would if Christ had handed it to you, because He did. Say: ‘My yoke is His, and it is easy.’
body: Zygos is a yoke, the wooden beam that binds an animal to its load. The New Testament uses it as a picture of bondage or of submission to authority. It can also mean a balance, the beam of a set of scales (Revelation 6:5).

Paul uses it here for men who were owned. Peter in Acts and Paul in Galatians use it for the law laid on men’s necks as a way to be saved — a yoke of bondage (Galatians 5:1). And Jesus uses it for Himself: Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me (Matthew 11:29). Every man wears one. The only question is whose.

The dust tells you the yoke you wear at work is the one that defines you. Under it, a man either grovels or rebels. But a man freed from the yoke of earning his salvation, who has taken Christ’s yoke instead, can work hard for a hard boss without being owned by him.

practices.title: PAY THE OX
practices.body: Look at what your church gives the men who labor in the word, and at what you give your church. If you have treated your pastor’s pay as a cost to keep low, confess it. Then do something concrete this week: a gift toward his family, a word to the elders about his salary, a meal at your table with his name on the invitation. Paul calls it honor, and honor costs something. The ox has been treading your grain for years.

practices.title: STARVE THE RUMOR
practices.body: When you hear a story about a leader this week, ask one question before you repeat it: who are the two or three witnesses? If the answer is nobody, the story stops with you. If the matter is real, take it to the man himself or to the elders, not to the parking lot. Paul set a guard around his shepherds. Do not be the man who slips past it. A shepherd guarded from gossip can afford to tell you the truth.

practices.title: TAKE THE TILT OUT
practices.body: Name the man you never correct because you like him, and the man you never cut slack because you don’t. Write both names down. This week, give each what the other usually gets — hard truth for the friend, a fair hearing for the one you resent. Remember who sits in the room when you judge: God, Christ Jesus, and the chosen angels, and none of them leans. You were judged by that same level court and spared in Christ.

practices.title: WORK AS IF HE ASSIGNED IT
practices.body: Pick one ordinary task at work — the report, the cleanup, the job nobody checks. Do it all the way this week, not because the boss is watching but because the name of God rides on how you work. Keep your hours straight on the timesheet. Bring back what isn’t yours. Speak of your boss behind his back the way you would speak to his face. A man who works this way preaches without opening his mouth.

practices.title: LEAVE THE HIDDEN GOOD WITH GOD
practices.body: Do one good thing this week that no one will see — cover a widow’s bill, split a neighbor’s firewood, pray by name for the man who runs your crew. Tell nobody. Paul says the good works that are not obvious now can’t be hidden in the end. Let God keep the record. Your Father sees in secret, and He forgets nothing done in His Son’s name. The record He keeps is safer than the one you would keep yourself.

title: The Ox and the Yoke
subtitle: from dust to honest honor
keyVerse: Let the elders who rule well be counted worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in the word and in teaching.

passage.text: Let the elders who rule well be counted worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in the word and in teaching.
For the Scripture says, “You shall not muzzle the ox when it treads out the grain.” And, “The laborer is worthy of his wages.”
Don’t receive an accusation against an elder, except at the word of two or three witnesses.
Those who sin, reprove in the sight of all, that the rest also may be in fear.
I command you in the sight of God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the chosen angels, that you observe these things without prejudice, doing nothing by partiality.
Lay hands hastily on no one. Don’t be a participant in other people’s sins. Keep yourself pure.
Be no longer a drinker of water only, but use a little wine for your stomach’s sake and your frequent infirmities.
Some men’s sins are evident, preceding them to judgment, and some also follow later.
In the same way also there are good works that are obvious, and those that are otherwise can’t be hidden.
Let as many as are bondservants under the yoke count their own masters worthy of all honor, that the name of God and the doctrine not be blasphemed.

Those who have believing masters, let them not despise them because they are brothers, but rather let them serve them, because those who partake of the benefit are believing and beloved. Teach and exhort these things.

stationsIntro: Read each verse slowly and let it land before you answer. Where a Greek word is opened, let it press the verse further into the work of your hands this week.
lifeIntro: God has given His church shepherds, a fair court, and a name worth carrying into the shop and the field. These practices take that honor off the page and put it into your week.
lifePulls: Honor in God’s house runs downhill from mercy. A man counted faithful by grace can pay his pastor, judge without leaning, and work for a hard boss without crawling.
prayer: Father, You counted me faithful when I was a blasphemer, and You put me to work in Your house. Thank You for the men who labor in Your Word for my soul. Teach me to honor them with my words and with my money. Take the tilt out of my judgments, and let me see men the way You see them. Bring my hidden sin into the light, and cover it with the blood of Your Son. Keep the hidden good in Your hands, and free me from needing to be seen. Make my work an honor to Your name, under every boss You give me. Thank You that Christ carried the heavy yoke and gives me His easy one. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You counted me faithful when I was a blasphemer, and You put me to work in Your house.
Thank You for the men who labor in Your Word for my soul.
Teach me to honor them with my words and with my money.
Take the tilt out of my judgments, and let me see men the way You see them.
Bring my hidden sin into the light, and cover it with the blood of Your Son.
Keep the hidden good in Your hands, and free me from needing to be seen.
Make my work an honor to Your name, under every boss You give me.
Thank You that Christ carried the heavy yoke and gives me His easy one.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Honor in God’s house flows from mercy, not rank. Pay the men who labor in the word, because God would not even muzzle an ox. Guard your leaders from rumor, and do not shield them from the truth. Judge without leaning; you stand before God, Christ and the angels. Some sin and some good are slow to show, and God sees both. At work, carry His name well. You wear Christ’s yoke now, and it is easy.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, past the two ledgers you keep. Lift them to the One who never kept two on you. You kept count of what you were owed; He kept count of what you owed, and paid it Himself. You leaned toward the men you liked; He leaned toward no one, and still He showed you mercy. You hid what you hoped no one would find; He saw every bit of it, and He did not turn away.

The dust told you honor was a wage to collect. It told you the man in the pulpit was overhead, the accused man was fair game, and the boss was someone to outlast. But look at the household Paul describes. Shepherds fed like oxen on the threshing floor. A court with no thumb on the scale. Servants whose work makes the name of God look good in a place where it costs them. That house is not built by ambitious men. It is built by forgiven ones. The dust lied about the hidden things too. It said what is buried stays buried and what nobody sees does not count. Paul says God sees both, and He is not fooled by either.

And look at the Master of the house. The Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). He took the form of a servant. He labored for your soul all the way to death. False witnesses spoke against Him, and a governor eager to please the crowd handed Him over. He bore that crooked judgment so that you could stand before God’s bench with no case against you. He rose from the grave with the verdict reversed, and He stands now as your advocate. Every honor you pay this week, you pay out of what He paid first.

So go to work under His yoke. Pay the ox. Give the accused man a fair hearing. Do the hidden thing well and leave it with your Father. Carry His name onto the loading dock as a man who has nothing left to prove. And when the labor wears you down, hear the word He spoke to men exactly like you: Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. His yoke is easy. His burden is light. And the good you did today that no one saw can’t be hidden from Him — He will bring it out on the day He comes.
closingVerse: Let the elders who rule well be counted worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in the word and in teaching.
carry: Where are you still keeping a ledger of the honor you are owed, when Christ has already paid every debt you owed and handed you His easy yoke to wear?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Every man has a number. He may never say it out loud, but it is there — the figure in the retirement account, the paid-off house, the second piece of land, the raise that would finally let him breathe. The number always sits a little past where he stands. When he reaches it, it moves.

Watch how it works in a man. He takes the overtime and misses the ballgames, and calls it providing. He checks the account before he checks on his wife. He gives to the church and keeps a quiet tally, waiting for the return. None of it looks like greed from the outside. From the inside it feels like responsibility.

The dust tells you enough is just ahead. It tells you contentment is something you can buy once the money comes in. And it tells a worse lie in church clothes: that godliness pays — that if you tithe and pray and keep your nose clean, God owes you a better harvest. Paul says that is the thinking of men destitute of the truth, who suppose that godliness is a means of gain (6:5). The lie wears a tie on Sunday, but it is the same lie.

Follow that lie far enough and a man’s fists close on nothing but dirt. Then an old prayer becomes his own: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) The reviving word in this last chapter is that you came into the world with nothing, you will carry nothing out, and in Christ you have already been given the one life worth holding. Godliness is not your wage. It is what grace grows in a man who has stopped chasing the number.

sections.heading: The Letter Comes Home
pulls: The number always moves. Paul’s answer is not a bigger number but a different treasure: you came with nothing, you leave with nothing, and in Christ you already hold the one life worth taking hold of.
paras: Paul opened this letter by leaving Timothy at Ephesus to stop certain men from teaching a different doctrine (1:3). He closes it on the same note: If anyone teaches a different doctrine (6:3). Between those two lines he has shown Timothy the mercy that reached the chief of sinners, the one Mediator who gave Himself as a ransom, men who lift holy hands in prayer, a household that cares for its own, God revealed in the flesh, and godliness trained like a body. Now he comes home to the danger under so much false teaching — the love of money — and to the charge that stands over every faithful life. This is the last stretch of road Paul walks with Timothy in this letter, and he wants the young man’s hands in the right place when it ends.

Read 6:3–21 straight through before you go on. Listen to Paul’s voice rise. He moves from warning to command, from command to praise, and from praise to a last word for the rich and a last word for Timothy. And after all the charges, the final line of the letter is not an order. It is Grace be with you.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: GODLINESS IS NOT A WAGE
paras: If anyone teaches a different doctrine, and doesn’t consent to sound words, the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the doctrine which is according to godliness. Notice whose words are sound. They are the words of the Lord Jesus. The church is not sent out to invent a new message. It is sent to say again what He said and what He did. And true teaching always bends a man toward godliness, because it carries the voice of the One who saves. A man does not need a clever teacher. He needs a faithful one, who hands him what Christ said and then gets out of the way.

Then Paul draws the false teacher. He is conceited, knowing nothing, but obsessed with arguments, disputes, and word battles. He loves the fight more than the truth. Watch what comes up in the field he plows: envy, strife, insulting, evil suspicions — constant friction. False doctrine never stays in a man’s head. Sooner or later it ends up in a church fight, with brothers who will not speak to each other across the fellowship hall.

At the bottom of it is money. These men suppose that godliness is a means of gain. They treat the faith like a trade — something you work to get something else. You do not have to stand in a pulpit to think that way. A man who serves God to get the bills paid, the marriage fixed or the son home has made godliness a means of gain. But grace cannot be turned into a trade. It was given free, and it keeps giving itself away. Withdraw yourself from such — and from the part of you that thinks the same way.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: GREAT GAIN
paras: But godliness with contentment is great gain. Paul takes their word and turns it over in his hand. There is gain in godliness, but the gain is godliness itself, held with a quiet heart. Contentment is not a mood that comes and goes with the weather. It is a man who has found in Christ what he used to hunt for in his bank balance.

Then Paul gives the reason in a line a man could cut into a barn beam. For we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can’t carry anything out. You came in with empty hands. You will leave with empty hands. Everything in between is on loan. A man who has buried his father knows it; the pockets of the burial suit are empty. But having food and clothing, we will be content with that. Paul does not despise bread and a coat. He simply will not let them become the treasure.

Now the warning. Those who are determined to be rich fall into a temptation, a snare, and many foolish and harmful lusts, such as drown men in ruin and destruction. Paul does not say the rich man is lost. He says the man set on getting rich is walking toward a snare. The wanting is the trap, and the end of it is drowning. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Money is a tool; the love of it is a root, and roots grow. Paul says those who love it have pierced themselves through with many sorrows. They did it to themselves. And Christ, who though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9), came to pull men like that out of the water.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: FIGHT, AND TAKE HOLD
pulls: You do not fight to earn eternal life. You fight because it has already been given, and the world wants to pry your fingers off it. Christ held His confession before Pilate, and He will hold you.
paras: But you, man of God, flee these things, and follow after righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance, and gentleness. Paul does not only tell Timothy what to run from. He tells him what to run after. Flight without pursuit leaves a man empty, and an empty man drifts back to the snare. Righteousness, faith, love, gentleness — none of these can be bought, and every one was first given to you in Christ.

Fight the good fight of faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called. Look at the order. You were called first. God called you to eternal life and gave it to you, and now He tells you to grip what He has given. You do not fight to earn the life. You fight because it is already yours and the world wants to pry your fingers off it. Timothy made his confession in the sight of many witnesses. So did you, the day you first said out loud that Jesus is Lord.

Then Paul gives Timothy a picture to fight by: Christ Jesus, who before Pontius Pilate testified the good confession. Jesus stood before a Roman governor with His life on the line and did not take back one word. He walked from that room to the cross. Your confession stands on His. So Paul charges Timothy to keep the commandment without spot, blameless, until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ. The fight has an end. He will appear. And Paul cannot help himself — he breaks into praise of God, the blessed and only Ruler, the King of kings, and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality, dwelling in unapproachable light. The man who fights is fighting toward that light.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: RICH TOWARD THE TIME TO COME
paras: Charge those who are rich in this present world that they not be arrogant, nor have their hope set on the uncertainty of riches, but on the living God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy. Paul does not tell the rich to throw it all in the river. He tells them where to put their hope. Riches are uncertain — a hailstorm, a lawsuit, a bad year at the feed store. The living God is not. And He is not stingy. He richly provides, and He gives it to enjoy.

So the rich are to be rich in a different coin: that they do good, that they be rich in good works, that they be ready to distribute, willing to share. That is how a man lays up a good foundation against the time to come. He does not buy eternal life with it. He shows by an open hand that his hope sits somewhere other than his barn. Jesus told of a rich man who built bigger barns and died the same night (Luke 12:16–20). If you have more than food and clothing, this charge is for you.

Then the last word to Timothy: Timothy, guard that which is committed to you. The gospel was handed to him like a deposit. He did not write it. He was to keep it whole and turn away from empty chatter and from what is falsely called knowledge. Some had already traded the deposit for the chatter and wandered from the faith. The same gospel has been handed to you — in a pew, at a graveside, across a tailgate. Guard it. And hear how the letter ends, after all its charges: Grace be with you. The last word is a gift.

stations.verse: Constant friction of people of corrupt minds and destitute of the truth, who suppose that godliness is a means of gain. Withdraw yourself from such.
stations.question: In what part of my life have I been treating obedience to God as a way to get something from Him?
stations.gloss: a means of gain; a way of getting
stations.live: Name one thing you have been doing for God mainly to get something back. Keep doing it, but drop the deal. Say: ‘You owe me nothing. Christ is my gain.’
body: Porismos comes from a verb meaning to procure. It can mean a providing, and here it means a means of gain — a money-maker, a way to get ahead. The New Testament has it in just two verses, and they sit side by side.

Paul uses it twice on purpose. The false teachers suppose that godliness is a means of gain. Paul answers with the same word: godliness with contentment is great gain. They wanted godliness to pay out. Paul says godliness held with a quiet heart is itself the payment. One man wants godliness to buy something. The other finds it already holds what was worth buying.

The dust wants you to keep a deal with God: I give, You give back. That is a trade, and grace does not trade. The cross was a gift, handed to a man with nothing to offer in return. Godliness grows out of that gift, and it never buys more of it.

stations.verse: But those who are determined to be rich fall into a temptation, a snare, and many foolish and harmful lusts, such as drown men in ruin and destruction.
stations.question: What desire for more has been pulling me under while I tell myself I am only keeping my head above water?
stations.live: Look at the purchase or plan you have been chasing hardest. Put it on hold for thirty days. Each time it comes to mind, pray: ‘You filled the boats. You will feed my house.’
body: Bythizō means to make something sink, to send it to the bottom. Besides this verse, only Luke has it. Here the lusts that come with wanting riches drown men in ruin and destruction. In Luke it is used of boats.

The boats in Luke are full of fish. Peter had worked all night and caught nothing. At Jesus’ word he let down the net, and the catch was so heavy that both boats began to sink (Luke 5:7). Same word. One man goes under because he grabbed for more. Another nearly goes under from what Christ simply gave him.

The dust tells you that if you do not reach and grab, you will go under. Paul says the grabbing is what takes you down. The Lord who filled Peter’s boats can fill your table. Contentment does not mean you quit working. Peter still rowed out. It means you quit grabbing, and let Him be the One who loads the boat.

stations.verse: For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some have been led astray from the faith in their greed, and have pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
stations.question: What sorrow am I carrying right now that I drove into myself by loving money?
stations.gloss: to put on a spit; to pierce through
stations.live: Write down one sorrow you brought on yourself through money. Bring it to Christ in prayer. If it involves someone you wronged, take one step this week to make it right.
body: Peripeirō means to put on a spit, to run a skewer through, and so to pierce. No other New Testament verse has it. Paul uses it as a picture, and the picture is meant to hurt.

The love of money does not only lead a man into sin. It turns his own hand against him. Paul says these men have pierced themselves through with many sorrows — the debt that keeps him awake, the marriage gone cold while he worked every weekend, the partner he shorted, the son who learned what his father really loved. No enemy did it. He did it to himself.

The dust tells you the sorrow is just the price of getting ahead. But there is another piercing in this story. Christ was pierced, not for any greed of His own, but for yours. His wounds can heal the ones you gave yourself. Bring Him the wound, and stop calling it the cost of doing business.

stations.verse: Fight the good fight of faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called, and you confessed the good confession in the sight of many witnesses.
stations.question: What would it look like this week for me to grip the eternal life God has already given me?
stations.gloss: to lay hold of; to take hold
stations.live: Set aside one hour this week to fight for. Read 1 Timothy 6 and pray it back to God. When you are tempted to skip it, say: ‘He took hold of me first.’
body: Epilambanomai means to lay hold of, to take hold. In the Greek Old Testament and the New it always comes in the middle voice. Paul uses it twice in this chapter, here and in 6:19: that they may lay hold of eternal life. Luke uses it when Jesus took a little child, and set him by his side (Luke 9:47).

The same word describes Jesus on the water. Peter looks at the wind and starts to go under, and Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him (Matthew 14:31). Before Peter grabbed anything, Christ had grabbed him. Your fight to take hold is the fight of a man who is already held.

The dust tells you your grip is what keeps you safe, and your grip is weak. True enough. But you are taking hold of a life that has already taken hold of you. Fight with both hands. The hand that holds you will not let go.

stations.verse: Charge those who are rich in this present world that they not be arrogant, nor have their hope set on the uncertainty of riches, but on the living God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy.
stations.question: Where am I setting my hope on something that could be gone by the end of the month?
stations.live: Look at where your money goes this month and give one portion of it away to someone in need. As you do, say: ‘My hope is not in this. It is in the living God.’
body: Adēlotēs means uncertainty. It comes from adēlos, and Paul is the only New Testament writer to use it, here and nowhere else. Paul does not call riches evil. He says the hope a man sets on them rests on the uncertainty of riches. Last week’s prodēlos named what is plain to see. This word names what cannot be counted on.

Riches are uncertain. A market falls. A storm takes the crop. A body fails and the savings go to the hospital. A man can do everything right with his money and still watch it go. Paul is not being gloomy. He is being plain about what money is and what it is not.

The dust tells you the more you have, the surer you can be. Paul turns your eyes to the living God, who richly provides. Money cannot promise you tomorrow. God has. Christ is risen, and your life is hidden with Him in God, where no market can reach it.

practices.title: NAME YOUR NUMBER
practices.body: Write down the amount you have believed would finally settle you. Set it beside 6:7: we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can’t carry anything out. Then cross the number out. Thank God by name this week for the food and clothing in your house, and say with Paul, we will be content with that. Contentment starts the day a man stops moving the line. Your Father knows what you need before you ask.

practices.title: CHECK THE DEAL
practices.body: Ask where your obedience has turned into a bargain — giving to get, praying to be paid back, serving God to fix something at home. Confess it plainly. Grace is not a trade, and godliness is not a wage. Then keep doing the good thing without the deal attached. You will find it lighter to carry once it is no longer an invoice you are waiting on God to pay. He already paid you in His Son.

practices.title: FLEE ONE, FOLLOW ONE
practices.body: Paul gives you two lists. Pick one thing from the first — the money, the argument, the conceit — and cut it off this week. Pick one thing from the second — righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance, gentleness — and do one concrete act of it. Gentleness toward your wife when you would rather be right. Perseverance on the job you want to walk off. Flight and pursuit go together, so do both on the same day.

practices.title: OPEN YOUR HAND
practices.body: Paul tells the rich to be ready to distribute, willing to share. Find one need this week — a neighbor’s fuel bill, a family in your church short on groceries, a missionary who needs support — and meet it before anyone asks. Do it quietly. You are laying up a good foundation against the time to come, and you are showing where your hope really sits. The God who richly provides will not run short on you.

practices.title: GUARD THE DEPOSIT
practices.body: Paul’s last charge is to guard that which is committed to you. Write out the gospel in five plain sentences: who God is, what you have done, what Christ has done, how a man receives it, and the day He will appear. Read it aloud until you can say it without the page. Then tell it to one person this week — a son, a friend, the man on your crew who asked. The deposit was handed to you so you could hand it on whole.

title: Take Hold
subtitle: from dust to the life that is truly life
keyVerse: Fight the good fight of faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called, and you confessed the good confession in the sight of many witnesses.

passage.text: If anyone teaches a different doctrine, and doesn’t consent to sound words, the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the doctrine which is according to godliness,
he is conceited, knowing nothing, but obsessed with arguments, disputes, and word battles, from which come envy, strife, insulting, evil suspicions,
constant friction of people of corrupt minds and destitute of the truth, who suppose that godliness is a means of gain. Withdraw yourself from such.
But godliness with contentment is great gain.
For we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can’t carry anything out.
But having food and clothing, we will be content with that.
But those who are determined to be rich fall into a temptation, a snare, and many foolish and harmful lusts, such as drown men in ruin and destruction.
For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some have been led astray from the faith in their greed, and have pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
But you, man of God, flee these things, and follow after righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance, and gentleness.
Fight the good fight of faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called, and you confessed the good confession in the sight of many witnesses.
I command you before God, who gives life to all things, and before Christ Jesus, who before Pontius Pilate testified the good confession,
that you keep the commandment without spot, blameless, until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ,
which in its own times he will show, who is the blessed and only Ruler, the King of kings, and Lord of lords.
He alone has immortality, dwelling in unapproachable light, whom no man has seen, nor can see: to whom be honor and eternal power. Amen.

Charge those who are rich in this present world that they not be arrogant, nor have their hope set on the uncertainty of riches, but on the living God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy;
that they do good, that they be rich in good works, that they be ready to distribute, willing to share;
laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come, that they may lay hold of eternal life.
Timothy, guard that which is committed to you, turning away from the empty chatter and oppositions of what is falsely called knowledge,
which some profess, and thus have wandered from the faith. Grace be with you. Amen.

stationsIntro: Read each verse slowly and let it settle before you answer. Where a Greek word is opened, let it loosen your grip on what you cannot keep and tighten it on what you were given.
lifeIntro: God has called you to eternal life, given it to you in Christ, and promised the appearing of His Son. These practices are how a content man fights, holds on and gives while he waits for that day.
lifePulls: Contentment is not having enough. It is having Christ and knowing He is enough — and a man who knows that can fight the good fight with open hands.
prayer: Father, You had mercy on me as You had mercy on Paul, and You gave me eternal life in Christ. I came into the world with nothing, and You have given me all I need. Forgive me for the number I keep chasing and the deals I keep trying to make with You. Pull me out of the water where my wanting has dragged me. Teach me to flee what is killing me and to follow after righteousness, faith, love and gentleness. Give me strength to fight the good fight, and keep my grip on the life You called me to. Make me rich in good works and quick to open my hand. Keep the gospel safe in me, and keep me faithful until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, You had mercy on me as You had mercy on Paul, and You gave me eternal life in Christ.
I came into the world with nothing, and You have given me all I need.
Forgive me for the number I keep chasing and the deals I keep trying to make with You.
Pull me out of the water where my wanting has dragged me.
Teach me to flee what is killing me and to follow after righteousness, faith, love and gentleness.
Give me strength to fight the good fight, and keep my grip on the life You called me to.
Make me rich in good works and quick to open my hand.
Keep the gospel safe in me, and keep me faithful until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: The dust says godliness should pay and enough is just ahead. Paul says godliness with contentment is the gain, and you will carry nothing out. The love of money drowns men and pierces them through. So flee it. Follow after righteousness. Fight the good fight, and take hold of the life God already gave you. Open your hand to the man in need. Guard the gospel. Christ held His confession before Pilate, and He will appear.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, to the end of the letter and the end of the fight. Paul began with a blasphemer who obtained mercy, and he ends with a King who will appear. In between, the letter showed you the one Mediator who paid the ransom. It showed you hands lifted in prayer and a household that honors its widows and feeds its shepherds. It showed you a mystery Paul could only sing — God was revealed in the flesh. It showed you godliness trained the way a man works a stubborn field, and contentment that no longer needs a number.

The dust told you to grab. It told you more would settle you, that godliness ought to pay, that your grip on God was the only thing holding you up. But look at what you hold. You came in with nothing, and you will carry nothing out — and still you have been called to eternal life, and the God who called you richly provides everything you need along the way. The deposit is in your hands. The fight is real. The life is already yours. Nothing you hold in Christ can be repossessed, foreclosed on or lost in a bad year.

And look at the One who went first. Christ Jesus, who before Pontius Pilate testified the good confession. He stood before a governor who had power to free Him, and He did not flinch. He walked from that room to the cross and paid the ransom for sinners like you. He came up out of the grave with death broken under His feet, and He is not finished with you. The same Jesus who stood in that courtroom is coming back, and He has not lost track of one man who confessed His name.

So keep the commandment, and keep fighting. Flee the snare. Follow after righteousness. Guard what was handed to you. You will not fight forever. Paul gave Timothy a date with no number on it: until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ. God will show Him in its own times — the blessed and only Ruler, the King of kings, and Lord of lords. Christ will appear once, in His own body, in glory, and every man who took hold of the life He gave will see Him face to face. Until that day, carry the letter’s last word with you into Monday’s work and into the dark: Grace be with you.
closingVerse: Fight the good fight of faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called, and you confessed the good confession in the sight of many witnesses.
carry: What are you gripping so hard this week that your hands are too full to take hold of the eternal life God has already called you to?
